en: The Golden Light Most Victorious King Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śramaṇa Yijing by Imperial Decree.
Part One: The Introduction (1). Chapter One: The Introduction.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Bhagavān was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, within the most pure and profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the domain of all Buddhas and the abode of the Tathāgatas. He was accompanied by a great assembly of ninety-eight thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—well-tamed like great elephant kings, whose outflows (*āsrava*) had been eliminated, who were free from further afflictions, whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated, who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, achieved great mastery, dwelt in pure precepts, were skilled in expedient means, adorned with wisdom, realized the eight liberations, and had reached the further shore. Their names were as follows:

The Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Bhadrayaśas, Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Śāriputra, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
only Ānanda remained on the stage of training.

These and other great śrāvakas each arose from meditative concentration in the late afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, who possessed great majestic power like that of great nāga kings;
their fame was widely renowned and they were known by all. Their practice of giving and morality was pure, and they constantly delighted in upholding them.
They were diligent in the practice of patience and had, throughout immeasurable kalpas, transcended all meditative concentrations.
With mindfulness firmly established before them, they open the gateway of wisdom, skillfully cultivate expedient means, and sport with mastery in subtle supernatural powers.
Having attained dharanis and inexhaustible eloquence, they sever all afflictions and eliminate all defilements;
before long, they shall realize all-knowledge and subdue the hosts of Māra.
Beating the Dharma drum, he subdues all heterodox paths, causing pure minds to arise; he turns the wondrous wheel of Dharma, delivering the multitudes of humans and devas.
All Buddha-lands in the ten directions have been fully adorned, and there are no sentient beings within the six realms who do not receive benefit.
They achieve great wisdom, are endowed with great patience, abide in a heart of great compassion, and possess great...
Possessing the power of firm resolve, they have served successive Buddhas without entering parinirvāṇa;
having aroused the heart of great vows, they will cultivate pure causes deeply under the Buddhas until the end of the future;

they have realized the patience of non-arising regarding the dharmas of the three periods of time, surpassing the spheres of practice of the two vehicles, and they guide and transform the world through great skillful means.
They were all able to expound upon the teachings of the Great Master;
they had thoroughly understood the secret dharmas and the profound emptiness, being free from all doubt—their names were:
the Bodhisattva Unobstructed Turning of the Dharma Wheel, the Bodhisattva Constantly Resolving to Turn the Dharma Wheel, and the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent...
The Bodhisattva Progression, the Bodhisattva Unceasing, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja, the Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhānālaṃkārarāja,
the Bodhisattva Sumerurāja, the Bodhisattva Mahāsāgaragambhīrarāja, and the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu.
Sā, the Bodhisattva Mahāratnaketu, the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja,
the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇivibhu, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Pramuditabala,
the Bodhisattva Mahādharmanubhāva, the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūhaprabha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsuvarṇaprabhāvyūha, and the Bodhisattva Viśuddha...
Bodhisattva Śīlavat, Bodhisattva Nityasamāhita, Bodhisattva Suviśuddhamati,
Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavīrya, Bodhisattva Gaganacitta, Bodhisattva Anupacchinnamahāpraṇidhāna, Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyadāna,
Bodhisattva Sarvakleśavyādhipraśamanakara, Bodhisattva Vaidyarāja, and Bodhisattva Pramuditottamarāja.
Sā, the Bodhisattva Attaining the Supreme Prediction, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Pure Radiance,
the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Upholder of the Dharma, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Renowned Joy, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Manifesting Boundless Fame,
the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Lion’s Roar, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Bull-King’s Roar, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Auspicious...
Bodhisattva Śrī, Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-ratnaguṇa, Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-sūryagarbha, Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-candragarbha,
Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-jyotiṣprabha, Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-arcisprabha, Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-vidyutprabha,
Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-nirghoṣasvara, and Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-prajñāvarṣaspharaṇa.
Sā, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Pure Rain King, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Flower-Tree King,
the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Blue Lotus Fragrance, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Jewel-Candana Fragrant Cool Body,
the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Dispelling Darkness, and the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Breaking Cataracts.

These and other such immeasurable multitudes of great bodhisattvas each arose from meditative concentration at the hour of late afternoon, proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
Furthermore, there were five hundred and eighty million Licchavi youths, whose names were:

the youth Siṃhaprabha, the youth Siṃhamati, the youth Dharmadatta, the youth Indradatta, the youth Mahāprabha, the youth Mahāvikrama, the youth Buddhagupta, the youth Dharmagupta, the youth Saṅghagupta, the youth Vajragupta, the youth Gaganagupta, the youth Gaganasvara, the youth Ratnagarbha, and the youth Śrīgarbha. With these as their leaders, they all dwelt securely in unsurpassed bodhi and possessed deep faith and joy in the Mahāyāna.
Each at the hour of *pradoṣa*, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there were forty-two thousand devaputras, headed by such as Devaputra Priyadarśana, Devaputra Pramoda, Devaputra Sūryaprabha, Devaputra Candracūḍa, Devaputra Prajñābhāsa, Devaputra Gaganaviśuddhaprajña, Devaputra Kleśāpaha, and Devaputra Śrī; these and others as their leaders had all made great vows to protect and uphold the Mahāyāna, to ensure the flourishing of the True Dharma so that it would never be interrupted.
Each at the hour of *pradoṣa*, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
and withdrew to sit on one side. Furthermore, there were twenty-eight thousand nāga kings—

headed by the nāga kings Padma, Śalapatra, Mahābala, Mahārava, Parīttavīci, Vegadhārin, Suvarṇamukha, and Manasvin— who always delighted in receiving and upholding the Mahāyāna Dharma, having conceived deep faith, and praising and protecting it.
Each at the hour of late afternoon, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
There were also thirty-six thousand hosts of yakṣas, with the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa as their leader.
Their names were:

the yakṣa Āmra, the yakṣa Āmradhara, the yakṣa Padmaprabhāgarbha, the yakṣa Padmavaktra, the yakṣa Bhṛkuṭī, the yakṣa Mahābhayadarśana, the yakṣa Kṣitiprakaṃpa, and the yakṣa Grāsaka. All these yakṣas delighted in the True Dharma of the Tathāgata; with profound resolve, they protected and upheld it, never giving rise to weariness or indolence.
Each at the hour of *pradoṣa*, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.

Furthermore, there were forty-nine thousand *garuḍa* kings, with the king Gajendrabala as their leader, along with other *gandharvas*, *asuras*, *kiṃnaras*, *mahoragas*, and all the sages of the mountains, forests, rivers, and seas, as well as the assemblies of kings from all the great nations, the queens and consorts of the inner palace, men and women of pure faith, and the great multitudes of humans and devas—all gathered like clouds, each vowing to protect the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, to read, recite, receive, uphold, transcribe, and disseminate it.
Each at the hour of *pradoṣa*, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.

Once this great assembly of śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, humans, devas, and the eight classes of nāgas and spirits had gathered like clouds, each with a sincere heart joined their palms in reverence; gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, their eyes never once left him, as they longed to hear the sublime and wondrous Dharma.
At that time, in the late afternoon, the Bhagavān arose from his meditative concentration, surveyed the great assembly, and spoke these verses:
“The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the wondrous Dharma, Is the most supreme among all kings of sūtras;
Profound and difficult to hear, it is the realm of all Buddhas.”
I shall now, for the sake of the great assembly, proclaim this sūtra;
and may the four Buddhas of the four directions, through their majestic spiritual power, provide joint protection:
the Honored One Akṣobhya in the east, and the Buddha Ratnaśrī in the south.
In the west is Amitāyus; in the north, the Sound of the Heavenly Drum.
I further expound this sublime Dharma, the most excellent among auspicious repentances, which can extinguish all transgressions and purify all evil karma.
It dispels all suffering and affliction, Constantly bestowing immeasurable bliss;
It is the root of omniscience, Adorned with all meritorious virtues.
When sentient beings lack physical completeness, And their lifespans are about to diminish,
When various evil omens appear before one, the celestial deities all abandon them.
Friends harbor resentment, and kinsmen are entirely estranged;
they fall into mutual discord, and all precious wealth is lost.
When malevolent stars portend calamities, or one is afflicted by evil sorcery,
or if one is further burdened by much sorrow and oppressed by manifold sufferings,
such that one sees evil dreams during sleep, afflictions arise therefrom.
This person should bathe and wear fresh, clean clothes;
regarding this wondrous King of Sutras, profound and praised by the Buddha,
they should recite, listen to, and uphold it with a focused mind free from distraction.
By the power of this sutra, one can remain free from all calamities and misfortunes, as well as other manifold sufferings and hardships; there is none that is not entirely extinguished.
The Four World-Protecting Kings, along with their ministers and retinues, [will likewise provide protection].
Immeasurable yakṣas all protect him with one mind;
The goddess Mahāprajñāpāramitā, The river deity of the Nairañjanā,
The mother-goddess Hārītī, And the host of the firm earth-deity.
The Brahma King and Śakra, Lord of the Gods; the Dragon Kings and Kinnaras,
as well as the Garuḍa Kings and the hosts of Asuras and devas—
such celestial beings, together with their retinues.
All shall come to protect this person, never departing by day or night.
I shall now proclaim this sutra, the profound sphere of the Buddhas' practice;
it is the secret teaching of all Buddhas, difficult to encounter even in ten million kalpas.
If there are those who hear this sutra, And are able to expound it for others,
Or give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, Or provide offerings;
such persons as these Shall, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
They shall always be revered by devas and humans, And by nāgas and spirits.
This accumulation of merit is immeasurable, Exceeding the sands of the Ganges in number;
Those who read and recite this sutra Shall obtain such virtues and merits.
The Honored Ones of the ten directions and the bodhisattvas of profound practice shall protect those who uphold this sutra,
causing them to be free from all suffering and hardship.
Those who make offerings to this sutra should first bathe their bodies as previously described.
With food, drink, incense, and flowers, always give rise to thoughts of compassion.
If you wish to hear this sutra, cause the mind to be pure and free from defilement;
constantly generate thoughts of joy, for this can increase all merits.
Those who, with a heart of reverence, listen to this sutra,
will be born well in the human realm and remain far removed from all suffering and hardship.
Such people have ripened roots of goodness and are praised by all Buddhas.
Only then can one hear this sutra, as well as the method of repentance. **Chapter Two:

The Lifespan of the Tathāgata (1)** From the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the King of Sutras, Chapter Two: The Lifespan of the Tathāgata. At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Subhaketu, who had already served and made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas in the past, planting all manner of roots of goodness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Banner was alone in a quiet place and reflected thus:
"By what causes and conditions is the lifespan of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni so short, lasting only eighty years?"
He further thought:
"As the Buddha has taught, there are two causes and conditions for attaining a long life.
What are these two?"
First, not harming living beings; second, giving food and drink to others.

Indeed, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of countless great kalpas, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni refrained from harming life, practiced the ten paths of wholesome action, and constantly bestowed food and drink upon all hungry sentient beings. He even gave away his own flesh, blood, marrow, and bones to satisfy them, let alone other forms of food and drink.

At that time, as that bodhisattva was forming this thought in the presence of the World-Honored One, by the Buddha’s majestic power, his chamber suddenly became vast, magnificent, and pure. Adorned with various jewels such as indranīla and lapis lazuli, and interspersed with diverse colorful decorations, it resembled a buddha-field. A wondrous fragrance, surpassing all celestial incenses, filled the space with its sweet perfume.
On each of its four sides there was a supreme and exquisite lion throne, composed of the four precious substances and spread with celestial jewel-cloths.
Upon these thrones were wondrous lotus flowers, adorned with various kinds of rare jewels, equal in size to the Tathāgata, appearing spontaneously.
Upon the lotus flower are four Tathāgatas: Akṣobhya in the east, Ratnaketu in the south, Amitāyus in the west, and Dundubhisvara in the north.

These four Tathāgatas each sat cross-legged upon their respective seats, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the great city of Rājagṛha, as well as this trichiliocosm and even the Buddha-lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; celestial flowers rained down, and celestial music was played.
At that time, by the Buddha’s majestic power, all sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa and throughout the trichiliocosm experienced supreme and wondrous bliss, lacking nothing whatsoever.

Those with incomplete physical faculties all attained full completion: the blind were able to see, the deaf were able to hear, the mute were able to speak, and the ignorant attained wisdom; those with distracted minds regained their original minds, and those without clothing obtained garments. Those who were treated with contempt and disdain came to be respected by others; those with filth and impurity became physically clean. All manner of benefits for this world, such as had never occurred before, were fully manifested.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, having beheld the four Tathāgatas and these rare events, leaped for joy with great exultation. With palms joined and a single-minded focus, he gazed up at the extraordinary marks of the Buddhas and further contemplated the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni; yet, regarding his lifespan, he gave rise to a mind of doubt, wondering:
"How is it that while the Tathāgata’s merits are immeasurable, his lifespan is so brief, lasting only eighty years?"
At that time, the four Buddhas addressed the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, saying: "Good son!
You should not now speculate upon the length or brevity of the Tathāgata’s lifespan."
Why is this? Good son!

Among all those in the world of devas—Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—as well as humans and non-humans, we do not see anyone who is able to calculate or know the lifespan of the Buddha, nor can they determine its limit.
"Except for those who possess unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, as the four Tathāgatas were about to declare the lifespan of Śākyamuni Buddha, through the Buddha’s majestic power, the devas of the desire and form realms, along with nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all came together and entered the pure and wondrous chamber of Bodhisattva Subhadhvaja.
At that time, the four Buddhas, within the great assembly, wishing to reveal the full extent of the lifespan of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, spoke these verses:
"The number of drops in all the waters of the oceans may be known;
but there is no one able to calculate or know the lifespan of Śākyamuni."
The various Sumeru mountains could be divided until their number were known as easily as mustard seeds;
yet no one is able to calculate or know the lifespan of Śākyamuni.
All the soil of the great earth may have its particles counted; [but the lifespan of Śākyamuni cannot.]
No one is able to calculate or know the lifespan of Śākyamuni.
Even if one were to measure the expanse of space, its limits might be reached;
yet no one is able to fathom or know the lifespan of Śākyamuni.
If a person were to dwell for a hundred million eons, constantly calculating with all their might,
they still could not know the lifespan of the World-Honored One.
By not harming the lives of sentient beings and by giving them food and drink;
By virtue of these two causes, one attains a long life.
Therefore, the lifespan of the Great Awakened Honored One is difficult to calculate;
like an eon that has no limit, his measure of life is likewise.
“O Miaodang, you should know that you ought not to give rise to doubt or confusion;
the lifespan of the Most Victorious One is immeasurable, such that no one can know its number.
At that time, having heard the four Tathāgatas explain that the lifespan of Śākyamuni Buddha was limitless, the Bodhisattva Miaodang addressed them, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the Tathāgata manifests such a brief lifespan?
At that time, the four World-Honored Ones addressed the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, saying:

“Good son! When that Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world of the five turbidities, the lifespan of humans was one hundred years; their natures were base and inferior, their roots of goodness were meager, and they lacked faith and understanding.”

These sentient beings possess many views of a self, a person, a being, a life-sustainer, and a nourisher; they hold false views of "I" and "mine," as well as views of annihilationism and eternalism. Desiring to benefit these various ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and similar classes, so that they may give rise to correct understanding and swiftly attain the realization of unsurpassed bodhi, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni manifests such a short lifespan.
"Good son!

However, that Tathāgata wishes to cause sentient beings, after seeing his parinirvāṇa, to give rise to the thought that he is difficult to encounter and thoughts of sorrow and suffering, so that they will swiftly receive, uphold, read, recite, and master the sūtras and teachings spoken by the Buddha, World-Honored One, and explain them to others without giving rise to slander or destruction. For this reason, the Tathāgata manifests such a short lifespan."

Why is this? If those sentient beings were to see that the Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa, they would not give rise to thoughts of reverence or the perception of his being difficult to encounter; consequently, they would neither uphold, recite, master, nor explain for others the profound sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata.
Why is this? It is because they have seen the Buddha constantly and thus do not treat him with respect. Good son!

For example, suppose there is a person who sees that his parents possess great wealth and an abundance of precious treasures; he would not conceive the thought that such property is rare or difficult to encounter.
Why is this? Because they conceive the notion of permanence regarding their father’s wealth. Good son!
Those sentient beings are likewise; if they see the Tathāgata not entering parinirvāṇa, they do not give rise to the thought that he is rare and difficult to encounter. Why is this?
Because of the perception of permanence, son of good family!

It is, for example, as if there were a person whose parents were poor and who lacked material wealth; yet that poor person might go to the house of a king or the residence of a great minister and see their granaries and treasuries filled to overflowing with all kinds of rare jewels, thereby conceiving a sense of wonder and the thought that such things are difficult to encounter.
At that time, that poor man, desiring to seek wealth, extensively employed skillful means and exerted himself with untiring diligence. Why was this?
It was because he wished to abandon poverty and attain peace and happiness.

Good son! Those sentient beings are also like this: if they see the Tathāgata entering parinirvāṇa, they conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter, up to and including thoughts of sorrow and suffering, and further reflect:
"In immeasurable kalpas, the appearance of Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower, appearing only once in a long time."
Those sentient beings will give rise to a sense of wonder and the realization that such an encounter is difficult to find.

If they meet a Tathāgata, they will conceive a heart of reverent faith; hearing the preaching of the True Dharma, they will regard it as words of truth, receiving and upholding all the sūtras without ever giving rise to slander.
"Good son!
For these reasons, that Buddha, the World-Honored One, will not remain long in the world, but will quickly enter parinirvāṇa.
Good son!"
"These Tathāgatas bring sentient beings to maturity through such skillful means as these.
At that time, after the four Buddhas had spoken these words, they suddenly vanished from sight.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Subhaketurāja, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas and immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, went as one group to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner reported all these matters in detail to the World-Honored One.

Then the four Tathāgatas also proceeded to Vulture Peak, arriving at the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was; each took his seat according to his respective direction and addressed their attendant bodhisattvas, saying:
"Good sons!..."
"You should now go to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha is and inquire on my behalf:
'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?'"
He further spoke these words:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Tathāgata Śākyamuni!

You may now expound the profound essential teachings of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, eliminating famine, and enabling them to attain peace and happiness; I shall rejoice in this with all my heart.
Then those attendants each went to where Śākyamuni Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Teacher of Gods and Humans sends these boundless inquiries:
'Are you free from much illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?'"
He further spoke these words:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Śākyamuni Tathāgata!

You may now expound the profound essential teachings of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, eliminating famine, and causing them to attain peace and happiness.
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni addressed those attendant bodhisattvas, saying:
"Excellent!"
“Excellent!
Those four Tathāgatas are indeed able to bring benefit, profit, and peace and happiness to all sentient beings, and they have exhorted me to proclaim the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I am always at Vulture Peak, proclaiming this jewel of a sutra;
for the sake of maturing sentient beings, I manifest parinirvāṇa.
Ordinary people give rise to false views and do not believe what I have taught."
"In order to bring that to fulfillment, he manifests parinirvāṇa.

At that time, within the great assembly, there was a brahmin of the Kauṇḍinya clan named Dharmabhāṇaka Vyākaraṇa. Together with an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of brahmins, having made offerings to the Buddha and hearing the World-Honored One speak of entering parinirvāṇa, his tears flowed profusely. He went before the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
"World-Honored One!"

If it is true that the Tathāgata possesses great compassion for all sentient beings, out of pity and for their benefit, enabling them to attain peace and happiness; if you are like parents, with no one else equal to you, able to serve as a place of refuge for the world; if you can provide illumination through great wisdom like the rising sun; and if you regard all sentient beings universally with impartial love like Rāhula—then I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me this one wish!
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent.
By the Buddha’s majestic power, there was among this assembly a Licchavi youth named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, who spoke to the brahmin Kauṇḍinya, saying:
"Great Brahmin!..."
"What vow do you now wish to ask of the Buddha?
I am able to grant it to you.
The brahmin said:
“O Youth! I wish to make offerings to the Unsurpassed World-Honored One; I now request from the Tathāgata a relic the size of a mustard seed.
For what reason?
I have heard it said:

"If a son or daughter of good family obtains even a portion of the Buddha’s relics the size of a mustard seed and reverently makes offerings to them, that person shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as Śakra."
At that time, the youth said to the brahmin:
"If you wish to be born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three and receive supreme retribution, you should listen to this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* with a sincere heart."
Among all sutras, this is the most supreme; it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter, beyond the comprehension of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
This sutra can produce immeasurable and boundless fruits of merit and retribution, even leading to the accomplishment of unsurpassed bodhi.
"I shall now briefly explain this matter for you.
The brāhmaṇa said: "Excellent!"
"O youth!

This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is profoundly deep and supreme; it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. Even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot comprehend it, let alone people like us from the remote frontiers, whose wisdom is so slight and shallow that we could ever understand it."

Therefore, I now seek even a portion of the Buddha’s relics as small as a mustard seed to take back to my own land, place them within a precious casket, and pay them reverent homage; thus, after my life ends, I shall become Śakra and constantly enjoy peace and happiness.
"Why is it that you now cannot seek this one wish for me from the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct?
Having spoken these words,
the youth then addressed the brahmin in verse:
"The swift-flowing waters of the Ganges might give birth to white lotuses;
yellow birds might take on white forms, and black birds might turn crimson.
Even if the Jambū tree were to produce tāla fruit,"
From within the branches of the *kṣīravṛkṣa*, the leaves of the *āmra* tree may emerge;
such rare and wondrous things might perhaps undergo transformation.
Yet the relics of the World-Honored One can never, under any circumstances, be obtained.
Even if one were to weave a most exquisite garment from tortoise hair and wear it during the cold season,
only then would one seek the relics of the Buddha.
Even if one were to construct a multi-storied pavilion using the legs of mosquitoes, [only then would one seek the relics of the Buddha].
Only when it is firm and unshakable shall one seek the relics of the Buddha.
Even if a leech were to grow white teeth within its mouth,
long, sharp, and like a blade, only then might one seek the relics of the Buddha.
Suppose one were to take rabbit horns and use them to construct a ladder,
by which one might ascend to the celestial palaces and there seek the relics of the Buddha.
A mouse might climb this ladder and drive away the asuras.
One who seeks the relics of the Buddha while still being able to obstruct the moon in the sky;
one who seeks the relics of the Buddha while like a fly drunk on wine,
wandering through villages and towns and building vast dwellings.
If a donkey’s lips were as red as the *bimba* fruit,
and it were skilled in song and dance, only then might one seek the relics of the Buddha.
If a crow and an owl were to roam together in one place, [only then might one find the Buddha's relics].
Only when you act in mutual harmony and compliance can you seek the relics of the Buddha.
Even if the leaves of the *pāla* tree could be fashioned into a parasol capable of shielding one from the great rain, only then might you seek the relics of the Buddha.
Even if one were to take a great ship, filled to the brim with all manner of treasures,
and cause it to travel across dry land, only then might one seek the relics of the Buddha.
Or suppose a *jiaoliao* bird were to take up Mount Xiangshan in its beak—
"Roam freely wherever you wish, And then seek the relics of the Buddha.
At that time, having heard this verse, the Dharma Master bestowed a prophecy upon the brahmin and replied to the youth Sarvasattvapriyadarśana with a gāthā:
"Excellent, great youth! You are the auspicious one within this assembly;
With a mind of skillful means, one attains the unsurpassed prediction of Buddhahood.
The Tathāgata of great majesty and power is able to rescue and protect the world;
you, O Benevolent One, should listen with a sincere heart as I now explain this in sequence.
The realm of all Buddhas is inconceivable; there is nothing in the world equal to it.
The nature of the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, and its cultivation is without distinction.
The essence of all Buddhas is identical, and the teachings they proclaim are likewise so.
The Buddhas have no creator, nor are they originally born.
The World-Honored One’s vajra-body manifests through expedient means as transformation bodies;
therefore, the Buddha’s relics are not even as much as a mustard seed.
The Buddha is not a body of blood and flesh; how, then, could there be śarīra?
It is through skillful means that he leaves behind bodily bones to benefit all sentient beings.
The Dharma-body is true awakening; the Dharma-realm is the Tathāgata.
"This is the true body of the Buddha, and he also teaches such a Dharma.

At that time, thirty-two thousand devaputras in the assembly, hearing it said that the Tathāgata’s lifespan is so long and far-reaching, all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they leaped for joy and experienced what they had never known before.
With one voice and in unison, they spoke this verse:
"The Buddha does not enter parinirvāṇa, Nor does the True Dharma perish;
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, He manifests the appearance of extinction."
“The World-Honored One is inconceivable; His wondrous body has no marks of difference.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, He manifests various kinds of adornments.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, having personally heard before the Buddha—and in the presence of the four Tathāgatas, the two Great Beings, and the sons of the gods—the account of the lifespan of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, rose again from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If it is truly as you say—that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not enter parinirvāṇa and possess no śarīra—then why does the sūtra speak of nirvāṇa and the Buddha’s śarīra, causing all humans and devas to pay them reverence and make offerings?”
The Buddhas of the past have left behind physical relics that circulate in the world; humans and devas make offerings to them and thereby obtain boundless merit.
Now, you further state that they do not exist, which gives rise to doubt and confusion.
“We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and explain this in detail!
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner and the great assembly:
“You should know this!”

As for the statement that there are *śarīra* relics in *parinirvāṇa*, this is a teaching of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). You should listen with a single-minded focus to the significance of this.
Son of good family!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should know that there are ten dharmas by which one can understand the true principle of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who speaks of ultimate *mahāparinirvāṇa*.
What are the ten?
First, because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have ultimately and completely severed all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is called *nirvāṇa*.
Second, because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are well able to understand the non-substantiality of sentient beings and the non-substantiality of phenomena, it is called nirvāṇa.
Third, because they are able to transform the basis of the person and the basis of phenomena, it is called nirvāṇa.
Fourth, because the causes and conditions for transforming sentient beings have ceased spontaneously, it is called nirvāṇa.
Fifth, because one has realized the true, undifferentiated, and equal dharmakāya, it is called nirvāṇa.
Sixth, because one realizes that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are non-dual in nature, it is called nirvāṇa.
Seventh, because one understands the fundamental root of all phenomena and realizes their purity, it is called nirvāṇa.
Eighth, because one skillfully practices the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena, it is called nirvana.
Ninth, because one attains right wisdom through the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is called nirvana.
Tenth, because one attains the non-differentiation between the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the nature of nirvāṇa, it is called "nirvāṇa.
These are the ten dharmas that speak of the existence of nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should know that there are ten further dharmas by which one can understand the true principle of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who speaks of the ultimate Great Parinirvāṇa."
What are the ten?
First, all afflictions have desire as their root and arise from desire;
because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have severed desire, this is called nirvāṇa.

Second, because all Tathāgatas have severed all desires and attachments and do not grasp at a single dharma, and because they do not grasp, they neither go nor come; since there is nothing to be grasped, this is called nirvāṇa.
Third, because there is no coming or going and nothing to be grasped, this is the Dharma-body, which is neither born nor extinguished; because it is without birth or extinction, it is called Nirvana.
Fourth, this absence of arising and ceasing cannot be proclaimed by words because all verbal expression has been cut off; therefore, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
Fifth, there is no self or person, but only the arising and ceasing of phenomena; because one attains the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), it is called *nirvāṇa*.

Sixth, the afflictions and secondary delusions are all adventitious dusts, whereas the dharma-nature is the host; being neither coming nor going, it is called nirvana because the Buddha understands this.
Seventh, suchness is real while all else is false; that which is the essence of reality is suchness, and the nature of suchness is the Tathāgata, which is called nirvāṇa.

Eighth, the nature of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is free from conceptual proliferation (prapañca); only the Tathāgata realizes the dharma of the limit of reality, and with the eternal cessation of conceptual proliferation, it is called nirvāṇa.
Ninth, non-arising is reality, while arising is delusion; foolish people drift and drown in birth and death, whereas the Tathāgata’s essence is real and free from delusion, which is called nirvāṇa.
Tenth, unreal phenomena arise from conditions, whereas true phenomena do not arise from conditions; the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is, in its essence, true, and is thus called nirvāṇa.
"Good son! These are called the ten dharmas that speak of the existence of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son!"

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that there are furthermore ten dharmas which enable one to understand the true principle of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the teaching of ultimate Great Parinirvāṇa.
What are the ten?

First, the Tathāgata thoroughly knows giving and the fruit of giving as being without self or what belongs to a self; because he has forever eliminated and extinguished incorrect conceptualization regarding this giving and its fruit, it is called nirvāṇa.

Second, the Tathāgata thoroughly knows the precepts and the fruits of the precepts as being without self or what belongs to a self; because he has eternally eliminated and extinguished incorrect conceptualization regarding these precepts and their fruits, it is called nirvāṇa.

Third, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands patience and the fruit of patience as being devoid of self and what belongs to self; because he has eternally eliminated and extinguished incorrect conceptualization regarding this patience and its fruit, it is called nirvāṇa.

Fourth, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands diligence and the fruits of diligence as being without self or what belongs to a self; because he has eternally eliminated the improper conceptualization regarding this diligence and its fruits, it is called nirvāṇa.

Fifth, the Tathāgata thoroughly knows meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the fruits of concentration, being free from the notions of "self" and "mine. Because false conceptualizations regarding this concentration and its fruits have been forever eliminated, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

Sixth, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands wisdom and the fruit of wisdom, which are devoid of self and what belongs to a self; because false discrimination regarding this wisdom and its fruit has been forever eliminated, it is called nirvāṇa.

Seventh, because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are well able to thoroughly understand that all sentient beings are non-sentient and that all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature, and because they have forever eliminated and extinguished improper conceptualization, this is called nirvāṇa.
Eighth, if one cherishes oneself, one gives rise to seeking; because of this seeking, one undergoes manifold suffering and affliction.
Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have eliminated self-love, they have forever severed seeking; because there is no seeking, it is called nirvāṇa.

Ninth, all conditioned phenomena possess measure and number, whereas unconditioned phenomena are entirely free from measure and number. Because the Buddha has transcended the conditioned and realized the unconditioned, being without measure or number, it is called Nirvana.

Tenth, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands that the essence of both sentient beings and phenomena is entirely empty; since they do not exist apart from emptiness, and emptiness itself is the true Dharma-body, it is called nirvāṇa.
“Good son! These are called the ten dharmas that speak of the existence of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son!”
Is it only that the Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa that is rare?
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of rare dharmas that constitute the conduct of the Tathāgata. What are these ten?

First, regarding the faults of saṃsāra and the tranquility of nirvāṇa: because one realizes the equality of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, one neither dwells in the cycle of existence nor remains fixed in nirvāṇa, and does not give rise to aversion toward sentient beings; this is the conduct of a Tathāgata.
Second, the Buddha does not form such thoughts regarding sentient beings as:
"These foolish people practice perverted views and are entangled and oppressed by various afflictions;
I shall now awaken them and cause them to attain liberation."

Nevertheless, by the power of the roots of virtue from his past kindness, he spontaneously delivers those sentient beings according to their faculties, inclinations, and resolutions, without giving rise to conceptual discrimination; he instructs, benefits, and gladdens them until the end of the future, never ceasing—this is the conduct of a Tathāgata.
Third, the Buddha has no such thought as:
"I shall now expound the twelvefold teaching to benefit sentient beings.

Nevertheless, by the power of the roots of goodness from his past acts of charity, he extensively teaches for the sake of those sentient beings until the end of the future, without exhaustion; this is the practice of the Tathāgata.
Fourth, the Buddha has no such thought:
"I shall now go to those cities, towns, and villages, to the houses of kings, ministers, brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, and there beg for alms."

Nevertheless, due to the power of habitual practice from his past conduct of body, speech, and mind, he proceeds spontaneously to those places to beg for alms for the sake of benefiting others; this is the conduct of a Tathāgata.

Fifth, the body of the Tathāgata is free from hunger and thirst, nor does it exhibit any signs of excretion, weakness, or exhaustion. Although he goes on almsround, he consumes nothing and has no conceptual discrimination; yet, in order to spontaneously benefit sentient beings, he manifests the appearance of eating—this is the practice of the Tathāgata.
Sixth, the Buddha has no such thought:
"These sentient beings are of superior, middling, or inferior capacity; I shall preach the Dharma to them according to their respective faculties and natures."

"Yet the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is free from discrimination; according to their capacities and in skillful response to their conditions, he preaches the Dharma for them—this is the conduct of a Tathāgata.
Seventh, the Buddha has no such thought:
'These types of sentient beings do not respect me and constantly utter words of abuse toward me; I cannot engage in discourse with them.'"
"Those beings revere me and constantly praise me together in my presence; I shall engage in conversation with them.
Nevertheless, for the Tathāgata to give rise to a mind of compassion that is impartial and without duality—this is the conduct of a Tathāgata.

Eighth, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are free from love and hatred, pride, greed, and all afflictions; nevertheless, the Tathāgata always delights in tranquility, praises few desires, and remains aloof from clamor and bustle—this is the practice of the Tathāgata.

Ninth, there is not a single dharma that the Tathāgata does not know or fail to master; in all circumstances, the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) manifests before him, free from all conceptual discrimination.

Nevertheless, when the Tathāgata perceives the activities of those sentient beings, he accords with their inclinations and employs skillful means to guide and lead them toward liberation; this is the conduct of the Tathāgata.
Tenth, when the Tathāgata sees some sentient beings attain wealth and prosperity, he does not give rise to joy;
when he sees them suffer decline and loss, he does not give rise to sorrow or distress.
Nevertheless, when the Tathāgata perceives that sentient beings are practicing right conduct, his unimpeded great loving-kindness spontaneously rescues and gathers them in;
if he perceives that sentient beings are practicing wrong conduct, his unimpeded great compassion spontaneously rescues and gathers them in.
This is the practice of the Tathāgata.
Son of good family!
You should know that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, teaches such boundless right practices as these.
You should know that this is called the true characteristic of nirvāṇa.

Whenever one perceives someone attaining parinirvāṇa, this is a skillful means; and the leaving behind of śarīra relics so that all sentient beings may revere and make offerings to them—all of these are the power of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness born of compassion.

If you make offerings, in future lives you will be far removed from the eight difficulties, encounter the Buddhas, meet spiritual friends, and never lose your virtuous mind. Your meritorious rewards will be boundless, and you shall swiftly attain liberation, no longer entangled by birth and death. You should diligently cultivate such sublime practices and not be negligent.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, having heard the Buddha personally declare that he would not enter parinirvāṇa and [teach] the profound practice, joined his palms in reverence and said:

"Only now do I know that the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, does not enter parinirvāṇa, and that he leaves behind relics to universally benefit all sentient beings. My body and mind leap with joy; I marvel at this unprecedented occurrence."

When this "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata" was being spoken, immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is equal to the unequaled.
At that time, the four Tathāgatas suddenly vanished. Having prostrated at the feet of the Buddhas, the Bodhisattva Subhaketur rose from his seat and returned to his own place.
*The Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Fascicle One;
*The Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śramaṇa Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Three: The Analysis of the Three Bodies (Part Two).

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha rose from his seat amidst the great assembly. He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and made offerings with exquisite flowers of gold and jewels, as well as jeweled banners, streamers, and canopies. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice in accordance with the Dharma regarding the profound secrets of all Tathāgatas?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
Reflect upon this well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
"Good son! All Tathāgatas possess three kinds of bodies."
What are the three?
First, the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body); second, the saṃbhogakāya (enjoyment body); and third, the dharmakāya (dharma body).
When these three bodies are fully perfected, they encompass anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; if one understands them correctly, one will swiftly transcend birth and death.
"How does a bodhisattva thoroughly understand the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)? Good son!

When the Tathāgata was formerly on the stage of practice, he cultivated various dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings. Having practiced in this way until his cultivation was perfected, through the power of that practice, he attained great mastery."

By virtue of sovereign power, he discerns the inclinations of sentient beings, their conduct, and their realms—all of them—without waiting for the right time and without missing the proper occasion; his teachings correspond to place, time, conduct, and the Dharma itself. He manifests various bodies; this is called the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
"Good son! How does a bodhisattva thoroughly understand the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body)?

It is that which the Tathāgatas manifest for the sake of enabling bodhisattvas to attain thorough penetration; which they teach as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) in order to cause them to understand that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are of one flavor; which serves to remove the fear of sentient beings with the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and to inspire joy; and which acts as the foundation for the boundless Buddha-dharmas. Because it accords with reality, by virtue of the power of the original vows of suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness, this body appears endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and a circular halo behind the neck and back. This is called the *nirmāṇakāya*."
Good son! How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva thoroughly understand the dharma-body?

It is because, for the purpose of eliminating all obstacles such as the afflictions and for the purpose of possessing all wholesome dharmas, there is only suchness and the wisdom of suchness; this is called the dharma-body.
The first two types of bodies exist as provisional designations; this third body exists as ultimate reality and serves as the foundation for the former two. Why is this so?

Apart from the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*) and apart from non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), there is no other distinct dharma for all Buddhas. All Buddhas are fully endowed with wisdom, have utterly extinguished all afflictions (*kleśa*), and have attained the pure Buddha-ground; therefore, the suchness of phenomena and the wisdom of suchness encompass all Buddha-dharmas.
"Furthermore, good son!
All Buddhas bring benefit to themselves and others to ultimate completion.
That which benefits oneself is the suchness of dharmas (dharmatā-tathatā); that which benefits others is the wisdom of suchness (tathatā-jñāna)."

Because one attains mastery over matters that benefit oneself and others, thereby accomplishing various and boundless functions, all Buddha-dharmas are thus distinguished as having immeasurable and boundless varieties of differentiation.
Good son! It is like depending upon conceptualization and discursive thought that one speaks of various afflictions, speaks of various karmic functions, and speaks of various retributive fruits.

Thus, in accordance with the suchness of the Dharma and in accordance with the wisdom of suchness, one teaches various teachings of the Buddhas, various teachings of the Pratyekabuddhas, and various teachings of the Śrāvakas.

Relying on the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatā-tathatā*) and relying on the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*), all Buddha-dharmas are accomplished with sovereign mastery; this is the first inconceivable [aspect].
For example, it is inconceivable to paint decorative ornaments upon the sky;
likewise, relying on the suchness of phenomena and relying on the wisdom of suchness to accomplish the Buddha-dharmas is also inconceivable.
“Good son! How is it that the dharmatā-tathatā and tathatā-jñāna are non-dual, yet achieve mastery and the accomplishment of enlightened activities? Good son!
For example, when a Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa, because of his mastery over vows, all manner of activities are accomplished;
likewise, the dharmatā-tathatā and the mastery of the wisdom of suchness accomplish their tasks in the same way.

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters the concentration of non-thought, by virtue of their prior power of aspiration, they arise from meditative absorption and perform various activities; thus, these two dharmas are without distinction, and their tasks are accomplished with mastery."

Good son! For example, the sun and moon have no discrimination; likewise, water and mirrors have no discrimination, and light also has no discrimination. Through the conjunction of these three, a reflection arises.

Thus, both the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) are without conceptual differentiation; yet, through the sovereignty of their vows, when sentient beings have a karmic resonance, they manifest response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and transformation-bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), appearing like the conjunction of the sun, the moon, and their reflections.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like immeasurable and boundless water-mirrors; by relying upon light, various different forms of empty reflections appear. That which is 'empty' is itself signless."
"Good son!

These various disciples who have been transformed by this teaching are reflections of the Dharma-body. By the power of their vows, they manifest various forms within these two kinds of bodies, yet within the ground of the Dharma-body, there are no distinct characteristics."
"Good son!
Based on these two bodies, all Buddhas speak of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder);
based on this *dharmakāya*, they speak of *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder)."
Why is this? Because all other dharmas have reached ultimate exhaustion;
based on these three bodies, all Buddhas speak of non-abiding nirvana.
For the sake of the two bodies (nirmāṇakāya and sambhogakāya), they do not abide in nirvāṇa; apart from the dharma-body (dharmakāya), there is no separate Buddha.
Why do the two bodies not abide in nirvāṇa?

Because the two bodies are provisional designations lacking substantial reality, arising and ceasing moment by moment, and thus do not abide permanently; they appear repeatedly precisely because they are not fixed.

The Dharma-body is not thus; therefore, the two bodies do not abide in nirvāṇa. Because the Dharma-body is non-dual, it does not abide in nirvāṇa; hence, one speaks of "non-abiding nirvāṇa" based upon the three bodies.
“Good son! Because all ordinary beings are subject to the three marks, they possess bondage and hindrances; they remain far removed from the three bodies and do not attain the three bodies.
What are these three?
First is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*), second is the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), and third is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Because these various natures cannot be understood, cannot be extinguished, and cannot be purified, one consequently fails to attain the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Because these three characteristics can liberate, extinguish, and purify, all Buddhas are fully endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Son of good family!
Because ordinary beings have not yet been able to eliminate these three minds, they remain far removed from the three bodies and cannot attain them.
What are these three?
First, the mind that initiates activity; second, the mind that relies upon the fundamental mind; and third, the fundamental mind itself.
By relying on the various paths of subduing, the mind that initiates activity is exhausted.
By relying on the path of severance, one exhausts the fundamental mind;
by relying on the supreme path, the fundamental mind is exhausted.
Because the mind that gives rise to phenomena ceases, one attains the manifestation of transformation bodies.
Because the fundamental mind is extinguished, the response body (nirmāṇakāya) is manifested;
because the fundamental mind is extinguished, one attains the dharma body (dharmakāya).
Therefore, all Tathāgatas are fully endowed with the three bodies.
“Good son! All Buddhas, in their first body, share the same activities as all Buddhas;
in their second body, they share the same intention as all Buddhas.”
In the third body, one is of the same essence as all Buddhas. Good son!
Because this first Buddha-body manifests various forms according to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings, it is said to be manifold.
The second Buddha-body has disciples with a single-minded intent; therefore, it manifests a single appearance, and for this reason it is called "one.
The third Buddha-body transcends all kinds of appearances and is not an object of grasping at characteristics; therefore, it is called "neither one nor two."
Good son! This is the first body, for it is manifested in dependence upon the response body (nirmāṇakāya);
this is the second body, for it is manifested in dependence upon the dharma body (dharmakāya).
This Dharma-body is truly existent because it has no basis. "Good son!
These three bodies are said to be permanent for certain reasons, and are said to be impermanent for certain reasons."

The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) constantly turns the wheel of Dharma, appearing everywhere in accordance with conditions through a continuous succession of skillful means without interruption; for this reason, it is said to be permanent.
However, because it is not the fundamental [body] and its great function is not fully manifested, it is said to be impermanent.

As for the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body): because it has continued uninterruptedly from time immemorial, and because it is able to sustain all the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the Buddhas; and because sentient beings are inexhaustible, its activity is likewise inexhaustible—for these reasons, it is said to be "permanent.
However, because it is not the fundamental [body] and its full activity is not manifest, it is said to be "impermanent."

The Dharma-body is not a conditioned phenomenon; it is devoid of differentiated characteristics because it is the fundamental source, just like space. For this reason, it is said to be eternal. Good son!
Apart from non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), there is no superior wisdom; apart from the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*), there is no superior realm.

This suchness of phenomena is the suchness of wisdom; these two kinds of suchness are neither identical nor different. Therefore, because the Dharma-body is pure in wisdom and pure in cessation, these two purities constitute the complete purity of the Dharma-body.
"Furthermore, son of good family, there are four distinctions in the differentiation of the three bodies:

there is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) which is not the response body (saṃbhogakāya); there is the response body which is not the transformation body; there is that which is both the transformation body and the response body; and there is that which is neither the transformation body nor the response body."
What is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) that is not the response body (saṃbhogakāya)?
It refers to that which, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, benefits beings according to conditions through the mastery of vows; this is called the transformation body.
What is the response body (saṃbhogakāya) that is not the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya)?
It is the body prior to the stages (bhūmi).
What is the transformation body that is also the response body?
This refers to the body that abides in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
What is neither a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) nor a response body (*saṃbhogakāya*)?
It is the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).
“Good son! This Dharma-body is manifested by the non-existence of duality.
What is meant by the non-existence of duality?

Regarding these characteristics of the dharmakāya and the locus of those characteristics, both are non-existent; they are neither existent nor non-existent, neither identical nor different, neither numerical nor non-numerical, and neither luminous nor dark.

In this way, suchness-wisdom does not perceive characteristics or the locus of characteristics; it does not perceive that which is neither existent nor non-existent; it does not perceive that which is neither one nor different; it does not perceive that which is neither numerical nor non-numerical; it does not perceive that which is neither light nor darkness.

Therefore, one should know that the purity of the objective realm and the purity of wisdom are indivisible and without interval; as they constitute the foundation of the path to cessation, this Dharma-body is able to manifest the various activities of the Tathāgata.

“Good son! This body, with its causes, conditions, objects, and locations, has its fruit dependent upon its basis; because this is difficult to conceive, if one understands this meaning, this body is itself the Mahāyāna, the nature of the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgatagarbha.”

Based upon this body, the initial resolve is generated; the mind of the stages of practice (*bhūmi*) becomes manifest, and the mind of the stage of non-retrogression likewise appears. The mind of the single-birth-to-enlightenment (*ekajātipratibaddha*), the vajra-mind, and the Tathāgata-mind all become fully manifest, and the immeasurable, boundless, sublime Dharma of the Tathāgatas is entirely revealed.
Relying upon this Dharma-body, the inconceivable Mahāsamādhi is manifested;
relying upon this Dharma-body, all great wisdoms are made manifest.
Therefore, the two bodies manifest based upon samādhi and wisdom.

Thus, this dharmakāya is described as permanent and self in terms of its own essence; it is described as bliss because of great samādhi, and it is described as pure because of great wisdom. Consequently, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, sovereign, blissful, and pure.

Based upon the Great Samādhi, all meditative concentrations such as Śūraṅgama, all foundations of mindfulness such as the Great Dharma Mindfulness, the Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion, all dhāraṇīs, all supernormal powers, all masteries, and the impartial embrace of all dharmas—such Buddha-dharmas as these all manifest.

Relying upon this great wisdom, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered analytical knowledges, the one hundred and eighty unique qualities, and all rare and inconceivable dharmas are fully manifested.
Just as, by relying on a wish-fulfilling jewel, immeasurable and boundless varieties of rare treasures all appear, so too,
by relying on the jewel of the great samādhi and the jewel of great wisdom, one can bring forth the various, immeasurable, and boundless sublime dharmas of all Buddhas.

“Good son! This Dharma-body samādhi and wisdom transcend all marks; they do not cling to marks and cannot be conceptually differentiated. They are neither eternal nor annihilated; this is called the Middle Way.”
Although there is conceptual differentiation, its essence is without differentiation.

Although there are three numbers, there are no three entities; it neither increases nor decreases. Like a dream or an illusion, it is without anything grasped and without any grasper. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such a state of liberation, which transcends the realm of the King of Death and overcomes the darkness of birth and death. It is a place that all sentient beings are unable to practice or reach, yet it is the dwelling place of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Good son!

It is like a person who, desiring to obtain gold, searches everywhere until he finds a gold ore. Having obtained the ore, he immediately crushes it, selects the purest portion, and smelts it in a furnace to produce refined gold. He may then fashion it at will into various ornaments such as rings and bracelets; although it serves many purposes, the nature of the gold does not change.
"Furthermore, noble son!
If a good man or a good woman seeks supreme liberation and practices worldly goodness, they shall behold the Tathāgata and his assembly of disciples."
Having approached him, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is wholesome?"
"What is unwholesome?
What is right cultivation that leads to pure conduct?
When the Tathāgatas and their assemblies of disciples see him ask this, they reflect as follows:
"If these sons and daughters of good family desire to seek purity and wish to hear the true Dharma," he then explains it for them,
causing them to attain awakening.

Having heard this, they maintain it with right mindfulness, resolve their minds upon practice, and attain the power of diligence. They eliminate the obstacle of indolence, extinguish all sins, and regarding the various points of training (*śikṣāpada*), they abandon disrespect. They stifle the mind of agitation and regret and enter the First Ground (*prathamabhūmi*).
Relying on the mind of the First Ground, they eliminate the obstacles to benefiting sentient beings and attain entry into the Second Ground.
Within this ground, they eliminate the obstacle of not being free from affliction and enter the Third Ground.
In this stage, by removing the obstacle of the mind’s lack of pliancy and purity, one enters the fourth stage;
in this stage, by removing the obstacle to skillful means, one enters the fifth stage;
in this stage, by removing the obstacle to seeing the ultimate and conventional truths, one enters the sixth stage.
In this stage, by removing the obstacle of perceiving the aspect of activity, one enters the seventh stage;
in this stage, by removing the obstacle of not seeing the aspect of cessation, one enters the eighth stage;
in this stage, by removing the obstacle of not seeing the aspect of arising, one enters the ninth stage.
In this stage, one removes the obstacles to the six supernormal powers and enters the tenth bhūmi;
in this stage, one removes the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), eliminates the fundamental mind, and enters the stage of the Tathāgata.
The stage of the Tathāgata is called "utterly pure" because of three kinds of purity.
What are these three?
First, the purity of afflictions; second, the purity of suffering; and third, the purity of marks.

For example, when genuine gold is melted, refined, and smelted, and has been subjected to heating and hammering so that it is free from dust and impurities, its purity is revealed because the nature of gold is inherently pure; thus, the substance of the gold is pure, yet this does not mean that the gold itself is non-existent.

For example, when turbid water settles and becomes clear and pure, free from all sediment and impurities, this is to reveal that the nature of water is fundamentally pure; it does not mean that there is no water.

In the same way, when the Dharmakāya is separated from afflictions and the suffering and its accumulation have been eliminated, leaving no further residual habits, this is to reveal that the Buddha-nature is fundamentally pure; it does not mean that it lacks substance.

For example, just as the realm of space is obscured by smoke, clouds, dust, and mist, yet once these are removed, that spatial realm is pure— without implying that space itself does not exist— so too,
because all sufferings have been entirely exhausted within the Dharmakāya, it is described as "pure," without implying that it lacks substantiality.

For example, suppose there is a person who, in a dream, sees a great river sweeping over his body; he moves his hands and feet to cut across the current and reaches the other shore. Because his body and mind did not slacken or retreat, even after waking from the dream, he no longer perceives the water or the distinction between this and that shore, yet it is not that he lacks a mind.
Once the delusive thoughts of birth and death have been completely extinguished, this awakening is pure; it does not mean that there is no awakening.
Because all such delusive thoughts within the dharma-realm no longer arise, it is described as pure; it is not that the Buddhas lack actual substance.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

This Dharma-body, when purified of the afflictive hindrances, can manifest the Response-body; when purified of the karmic hindrances, it can manifest the Transformation-body; and when purified of the cognitive hindrances, it can manifest the Dharma-body."

For example, just as lightning arises depending on the sky and light arises depending on lightning, so too does the response body (nirmāṇakāya) manifest depending on the reality body (dharmakāya), and the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) manifests depending on the response body.

Because of the purity of its nature, it can manifest the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); because of the purity of wisdom, it can manifest the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); and because of the purity of samādhi, it can manifest the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

These three purities are the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*), not different from suchness, the single-flavor suchness, the liberation suchness, and the ultimate suchness; therefore, the essence of all Buddhas has no difference.
"Good son! If there are good sons or good daughters who declare that the Tathāgata is their Great Teacher,
and if they maintain such firm conviction, these persons should, with a profound mind, understand that the body of the Tathāgata is without any distinction."
"Good son!

For this reason, one completely eliminates all improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) toward various objects; thus one knows that those phenomena possess no dual characteristics and are without discrimination. This is the practice of the noble ones: suchness remains as it is within them, devoid of dual characteristics."
Because of correct practice, all such obstacles are completely eliminated;

as each obstacle is eliminated, so too does the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena and the *tathatājñāna* (wisdom of suchness) attain supreme purity, resulting in the purity of the correct wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm).
In this manner, all such sovereign powers are fully embraced and brought to accomplishment; all obstacles are entirely extinguished.

Because all obstacles have been purified, this is called the true characteristic of True Suchness (tathatā) and Right Knowledge (samyag-jñāna). One who perceives thus is said to possess the noble vision (ārya-darśana); this is what is meant by truly seeing the Buddha.
Why is this? Because they perceive the true suchness (*tathatā*) of phenomena as it truly is; therefore, all Buddhas are able to universally behold all Tathāgatas. Why is this?

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, though they have already transcended the triple world and seek the realm of ultimate reality, are unable to know or see it. Regarding that which such noble ones do not know or see, all ordinary beings give rise to doubt and confusion, engaging in inverted discrimination; thus they cannot attain liberation, just as a rabbit attempting to swim across the ocean will certainly fail to cross.
Why is this? Because their power is weak and inferior.
Ordinary persons are likewise; they are unable to penetrate the suchness of phenomena (dharmatā-tathatā).

However, all Tathāgatas possess a non-conceptual mind and have attained great mastery over all phenomena; because they are endowed with pure and profound wisdom, this is their own domain, not shared with others.

Therefore, throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have not spared their own bodies or lives, but have performed difficult practices and ascetic austerities before finally attaining this body—which is supreme and peerless, inconceivable, beyond the realm of verbal expression, wondrously tranquil, and free from all fears.

“Good son! One who thus knows and sees the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena has no birth, aging, or death; their lifespan is limitless; they have neither sleep nor hunger or thirst; their mind is always in meditative concentration, free from distraction or agitation.”
If one gives rise to a contentious mind toward the Tathāgata, one will be unable to see the Tathāgata.

All that the Buddhas have spoken is capable of benefiting others; those who hear it will all attain liberation. One shall not encounter evil birds and beasts, wicked people, or malevolent spirits; because of hearing the Dharma, the karmic fruition thereof is inexhaustible.

However, all Tathāgatas have no records of indeterminate matters; they have no desire to know all objective realms, and they harbor no conceptual distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Whatever the Tathāgata has predicted is invariably certain.

In the four modes of deportment of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, there is nothing that is not encompassed by wisdom; among all dharmas, there is nothing that is not embraced by compassion and mercy, and nothing that does not bring benefit and peace to all sentient beings.

“Good son! If there are good sons or good daughters who hear, believe, and understand this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, they shall not fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras. They will always dwell among humans and devas, never being born into lowly or inferior conditions. They will constantly have the opportunity to draw near to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, listen to and receive the True Dharma, and will always be reborn in the pure lands of the Buddhas.”

Why is this? Because by hearing this profound Dharma, these sons and daughters of good family have already been known and prophesied by the Tathāgata; they shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If a son or daughter of good family hears this profound and subtle Dharma even once, you should know that such a person does not slander the Tathāgata, does not destroy the True Dharma, and does not disparage the Noble Assembly. Because they cause all sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them, and cause those who have already planted roots of goodness to increase and mature them, they exhort all sentient beings in every world to practice the six pāramitās.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, along with Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Great Kings, and the assembly of devas, rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In whatever place this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is expounded, there shall be four kinds of benefits for that land.
What are the four?

First, the king’s military forces shall be powerful and flourishing; he shall be free from enemies, liberated from disease, enjoy longevity, and abide in auspiciousness and peace, while the True Dharma shall flourish and manifest.

Second, the ladies of the inner palace, the queen, the princes, and all the ministers will be harmonious and joyful, free from contention; they will be devoid of flattery and deceit, and will be cherished and respected by the king.

Third, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all the people of the land will practice the True Dharma; they will be free from illness and live in peace and happiness, with no one dying an unjust death, and they will fully establish themselves in all fields of merit.

Fourth, throughout the three periods of the day and night, their four great elements remain in harmony; they are constantly protected by the various devas, who act with compassion and equanimity, free from any intent to harm, causing all sentient beings to take refuge in and revere the Triple Gem, and wishing for them all to cultivate the practices of Bodhi.
These are the four kinds of beneficial matters.
World-Honored One!
We, too, shall constantly follow those who uphold this sutra for the sake of propagating it, and wherever they dwell, we shall provide them with benefit.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Good son! It is so! It is so!"
"You all should diligently propagate this wondrous King of Sutras with a devoted mind, so that the True Dharma may long abide in the world.

**Chapter Four: Repentance upon Dreaming of the Golden Drum** At that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, having personally heard this sublime Dharma in the presence of the Buddha, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. With single-minded contemplation, he returned to his own abode.

In a dream during the night, he saw a great golden drum, its radiance dazzling like the orb of the sun; within this light, he beheld immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, seated upon lapis lazuli thrones beneath jeweled trees, surrounded by assemblies of countless hundreds of thousands as they preached the Dharma for them.
He saw a brahmin striking a golden drum with a mallet, which produced a great sound; within that sound, he recited subtle verses explaining the method of repentance.
Having heard them, Subhaketur memorized them all and remained there with his mind focused upon them.

When dawn had broken, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands, he took various offerings and departed from the city of Rājagṛha. He proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain and, having arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. After arranging incense and flowers and circumambulating him three times to the right, he withdrew to sit on one side. With palms joined in reverence, gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”

In a dream, I saw a brahmin holding a drumstick in his hand and striking a magnificent golden drum, producing a great sound; within that sound, he recited subtle verses explaining the method of repentance, all of which I have memorized and retained.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will bestow great compassion and grant me leave to speak.
He then spoke in verse before the Buddha:
"During the middle of last night, I dreamed of a great golden drum; I struck it with my hand, And its sound reached the ten directions."
Their forms are exceedingly beautiful and wondrous, Enveloped on all sides by golden light.
Like the blazing orb of the sun, Their radiance shines everywhere,
Pervading the realms of the ten directions, So that all may behold the Buddhas.
Beneath jeweled trees, each sat upon a lapis lazuli throne;
surrounded by hundreds of thousands of beings in infinite numbers, they paid him reverent homage.
There was a brahmin who struck a golden drum with a mallet.
Within the sound of that drum, this sublime gāthā was spoken:
"The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* drum produces a wondrous sound, Which reaches throughout the trichiliocosm;
It can extinguish the most grievous sins of the three miserable realms, As well as all the sufferings and calamities among human beings."
By the power of this sound of the golden drum, may all obstacles of affliction be forever extinguished;
may fear be severed and all be brought to peace, just like the Sovereign Muni.
Within the great ocean of birth and death, the Buddha accumulated practices and cultivated all-encompassing wisdom;
