he enables sentient beings to be complete in the factors of enlightenment, so that they ultimately all return to the ocean of merit.
From this golden drum emerges a wondrous sound, universally causing all who hear it to obtain the Brahma-voice;
may they realize the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi and constantly turn the pure, sublime wheel of Dharma.
Abiding for inconceivable eons, he preaches the Dharma according to capacities to benefit all sentient beings;
he can sever the flowing stream of afflictions and sufferings, so that greed, hatred, delusion, and the like are all extinguished.
If there are sentient beings dwelling in evil realms, With great fires and fierce flames enveloping their bodies;
If they should hear the sound of this wondrous drum, They will immediately be able to leave suffering behind and take refuge in the Buddha.
All have attained the wisdom of recollecting past lives, Able to remember hundreds of thousands of previous existences;
With right mindfulness of the Honored Muni, They have heard the Tathāgata’s most profound teaching.
By hearing the sublime and wondrous sound of the golden drum, one shall always be able to draw near to all Buddhas;
one will be able to completely abandon all evil karma and purely cultivate all categories of pure goodness.
All beings among gods and humans who pray with profound reverence and utmost sincerity—
upon hearing the wondrous sound of the golden drum, may all their aspirations be fulfilled.
Sentient beings fall into the Avīci Hell, Their bodies scorched by the fierce blaze of raging flames;
Having no protector, they wander in saṃsāra— Those who hear this can cause their suffering to be extinguished.
Among humans, devas, hungry ghosts, and animals, All those currently undergoing various sufferings and hardships—
Upon hearing the wondrous sound emitted by the golden drum, They shall all be freed from suffering and attain liberation.
In the worlds of the ten directions now, the Ever-Abiding Honored One among Two-Legged Beings—
may you, with a heart of great compassion, take pity on me and remember me.
Sentient beings have no refuge, nor is there any protector.
For those of such kinds, you are able to act as a great refuge.
Whatever sins I have previously committed, all those most grievous evil karmas—
I now confess them all with a sincere heart before the One of Ten Powers.
I did not believe in the Buddhas, nor did I revere my elders or kin;
I did not strive to cultivate various virtues, but constantly committed all manner of evil deeds.
Or, relying on my own high status, my noble lineage, and my wealth and rank, I was arrogant.
In the prime of life, one acts with heedlessness, constantly creating various evil karmas.
The mind perpetually gives rise to perverse thoughts, and the mouth utters evil words;
failing to see one's own transgressions, one constantly creates various evil karmas.
Constantly engaging in the conduct of fools, their minds shrouded by the darkness of ignorance,
they follow along with unwholesome friends and perpetually create various evil karmas.
Whether due to various forms of play and pleasure, or again, harboring sorrow and affliction, [they act thus].
Ensnared by greed and hatred, I have committed various evils.
Associating with unwholesome people, and driven by stinginess and envy, I practiced flattery and deception out of poverty; thus have I committed various evils.
Although I did not delight in these manifold faults,
I committed various evils because of my fearfulness and lack of self-mastery;
whether due to a restless mind or because of anger and resentment.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, I have committed various evils.
Driven by food, drink, clothing, and lust for women,
burning with the fires of affliction, I have committed various evils.
Toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, I failed to give rise to a heart of reverence;
for all such transgressions as these, I now confess them all.
Toward the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas, likewise I lacked a heart of reverence.
For all such various sins as these, I now repent them all.
Out of ignorance, I slandered the True Dharma; I was unfilial toward my parents;
for all such various sins as these, I now repent them all.
Out of ignorance and pride, and through the power of greed and hatred, I have committed such manifold transgressions; I now repent of them all.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, I have made offerings to countless Buddhas.
I vow to deliver all sentient beings, Causing them to be free from all suffering and hardship.
May all living beings Be established in the ten stages;
Once their merit and wisdom are perfected, May they attain Buddhahood to guide the deluded masses.
For the sake of all sentient beings, I have practiced asceticism for hundreds of thousands of kalpas;
by the power of great wisdom, I cause them all to emerge from the ocean of suffering.
For the sake of all conscious beings, I expound the most profound sutras.
The most supreme Golden Light can eliminate all evil karma.
If a person has committed various extremely grave offenses throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas,
by confessing them for even a brief moment, all their evils will be completely eradicated.
Relying upon this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, one performs such repentance;
by means of this, all karmas of suffering can be swiftly exhausted.
There are hundreds of thousands of supreme concentrations and inconceivable dhāraṇīs.
The faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and path-factors—may I practice these constantly without weariness.
May I reach the tenth stage, the place replete with precious jewels;
may I perfect the Buddha-qualities and ferry across the stream of birth and death.
Regarding the oceans of all Buddhas, The treasury of their most profound merit,
And their wondrous wisdom beyond conceptual thought— May I cause them all to be fully perfected.
I pray only that the Buddhas of the ten directions Will observe and protect me with mindful care.
With a heart of great compassion, Please accept my repentance with pity.
Whatever evil karma I have created Throughout many kalpas,
And the suffering that arises from it— Out of your compassion, I pray you, eliminate it.
I have committed various evil deeds, And my mind is constantly filled with sorrow and fear;
Throughout the four modes of conduct, I have never known a thought of joy.
The Buddhas, endowed with great compassion, Are able to remove the fears of sentient beings.
I pray that you accept my repentance, And cause me to be freed from sorrow and suffering.
I possess the hindrance of afflictions As well as various karmic retributions;
I pray that with the water of great compassion, You will wash them away until they are pure.
The various sins I have committed in the past, And the evil karma I am now creating—
I confess them all with a sincere heart, And pray that they may all be cleared away.
Regarding all future evil karma, I shall guard against it so that it does not arise.
Even were there a transgression, I would never dare to conceal it.
The three types of bodily action, the four kinds of verbal action,
and the three types of mental karma bind all sentient beings, continuing perpetually from time immemorial.
Through these three types of conduct, I have committed the ten unwholesome karmas;
all such manifold transgressions, I now confess.
Whatever evil deeds I have committed, their bitter retribution I must receive myself.
Now, before all the Buddhas, I sincerely repent of all [faults].
Whatever roots of goodness exist here in Jambudvīpa and in worlds of other directions, I now rejoice in them all.
May I leave behind the ten unwholesome actions and practice the path of the ten virtues;
may I dwell securely within the ten stages and constantly behold the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Through the deeds of merit and wisdom cultivated by my body, speech, and mind—
By these roots of goodness, may I swiftly attain supreme wisdom.
Now, standing before the One of Ten Powers, I confess my many hardships and misfortunes:
the suffering of delusion within the three realms of existence, and the suffering of constantly committing the most grievous evil deeds.
The difficulty of the accumulation of my own desires and perversities, The difficulty of the constant arising of craving and the cycle of transmigration,
The difficulty of attachment to this world, The difficulty of the afflictions of all foolish beings,
The difficulty of the distracted and inverted mind, And the difficulty of associating with evil friends.
The difficulty of being stained by craving within birth and death; The difficulty of committing transgressions through the darkness and dullness of hatred and delusion;
The difficulty of being born in the eight states of no leisure or evil realms;
The difficulty of never having accumulated merit— I now, before the Most Victorious One, Repent of all these boundless sinful karmas.
I now take refuge in all the Sugatas; I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One, an ocean of virtue.
Like a great mountain of gold illuminating the ten directions, I pray only that you will compassionately accept me with pity.
The color of your body is pure golden light, free from stain; your eyes are like clear, deep-blue lapis lazuli.
You are the Honored One of auspicious majesty and renown; with the sun of great compassion and wisdom, you dispel all darkness.
The light of the Buddha-sun is ever-pervasive, Pure, stainless, and free from all dust;
The moon of the Muni shines with supreme coolness, Able to dispel the fever of afflictions for sentient beings.
Adorned throughout by the thirty-two marks, With all eighty secondary signs perfectly complete;
His inconceivable merit is beyond compare, Like the flowing light of the sun illuminating the world.
His form is like pure, stainless lapis lazuli, Like the full moon dwelling in the void;
A wondrous crystal net reflects his golden body, Adorned with manifold rays of light.
Within the torrential flood of the suffering of birth and death, beings are swept away by the waters of old age, sickness, and grief;
this ocean of suffering is difficult to endure, but the Buddha-sun extends its radiance to cause it to dry up forever.
I now prostrate to the Omniscient One, the rare and honored one of the trichiliocosm,
whose body of shimmering purple-gold radiates brilliant light, adorned with every kind of exquisite excellence.
As the volume of the great ocean is difficult to know, And the motes of dust upon the great earth cannot be numbered,
As Mount Sumeru is beyond measurement, So too is space without limit.
The virtues of all Buddhas are likewise such that all sentient beings cannot know them;
even if one were to contemplate them with earnest reflection for immeasurable eons, there would be none who could reach the shore of their ocean of merit.
All the mountains and peaks upon this great earth may be split into atoms and counted;
the drops of the oceans may be measured with the tip of a hair; yet the merit of the Buddha can never be reckoned.
All sentient beings together praise the World-Honored One’s fame and all his virtues;
his pure marks and signs are wondrously adorned, their measure and limits being beyond calculation.
By all my accumulated roots of goodness, may I swiftly attain the state of the Unsurpassed Honored One;
may I extensively proclaim the True Dharma to benefit all living beings, causing them all to be liberated from every suffering.
Having subdued the hosts of the powerful Māra armies, you shall turn the unsurpassed wheel of the True Dharma;
abiding for inconceivable kalpas, you shall satisfy all sentient beings with the flavor of the nectar of immortality.
Just as the most supreme ones of the past, Whose six pāramitās were all perfected;
Who extinguished all greed, hatred, and delusion, Subdued the afflictions, and eliminated all suffering.
May I always attain the knowledge of past lives, And be able to remember hundreds of thousands of past births;
May I also constantly recollect the Honored Muni, And hear the profound Dharma of all Buddhas.
By means of all these roots of goodness, may I serve the boundless and most supreme Honored Ones;
may I remain far removed from all causes of unwholesomeness, and constantly practice the truly wondrous Dharma.
May all sentient beings in every world be entirely freed from suffering and attain peace and happiness;
may those whose sense faculties are incomplete have their physical forms made fully perfect.
If there are sentient beings who encounter the suffering of illness, Their bodies emaciated and without support;
May all their ailments be eliminated, And their faculties, complexion, and strength be fully restored.
If one violates the king’s law and deserves execution, oppressed by manifold sufferings, they give rise to grief and distress;
when they undergo such extreme agony, there is no refuge that can provide protection.
If one is subjected to whips, staves, shackles, and fetters, And various instruments of torture cut into the body;
During immeasurable hundreds of thousands of moments of grief and affliction, Body and mind are oppressed, with not even a moment’s peace.
May all be freed from bondage, as well as the sufferings of whips and staves;
may those facing execution have their lives preserved, and may all their manifold sufferings be forever and entirely eliminated.
If there are sentient beings oppressed by hunger and thirst, may they obtain all manner of sublime flavors;
may the blind see and the deaf hear; may the lame be able to walk and the mute be able to speak.
May impoverished sentient beings obtain a treasure trove, With granaries overflowing so that they lack for nothing;
May they all attain supreme and wondrous bliss, And not a single sentient being suffer affliction.
All humans and devas delight in beholding them; their countenances and deportment are mild, elegant, and most majestic.
They all presently experience immeasurable bliss, enjoying abundant prosperity and endowed with merit.
According to the thoughts of those beings regarding music and dance, all manner of wondrous sounds appear before them;
when they think of water, there immediately appears a cool pond, with golden lotuses floating upon its surface.
According to the thoughts in the minds of those sentient beings, Food, drink, clothing, and bedding;
Gold, silver, precious gems, and exquisite lapis lazuli, As well as necklaces and ornaments—all are fully provided.
May sentient beings never hear evil sounds, nor shall they ever see anything discordant;
may their physical appearances all be dignified and majestic, and may each, with a heart of loving-kindness, cherish one another.
All the various means of worldly sustenance and enjoyment, Are fully satisfied whenever they are thought of;
Whatever precious wealth is obtained, without stinginess, Is distributed and given to all sentient beings.
Incense sticks, powdered incense, and unguents, along with various exquisite flowers of manifold colors, fall from the trees three times each day;
as they are enjoyed according to one’s heart, joy arises.
May all sentient beings universally make offerings to the most supreme Honored Ones of the ten directions,
to the pure and wondrous Dharma-gates of the Three Vehicles, and to the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
May I always vow not to dwell in lowliness or meanness, nor fall among the eight difficulties of the leisureless;
may I be born as a noble being among those who possess leisure, and may I forever have the opportunity to personally attend upon the Buddhas of the ten directions.
May I always be born into a wealthy and noble family, with treasuries and granaries all filled to overflowing;
may my countenance and renown be peerless, and may my lifespan extend through many kalpas.
May all women be transformed into men, Brave, intelligent, and possessed of great wisdom;
May they always practice the Bodhisattva path, Diligently cultivating the six perfections to reach the other shore.
Constantly seeing the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, Dwelling peacefully beneath the jewel-king trees;
Seated upon sublime lapis lazuli lion thrones, They always personally receive the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
Whatever karma I have created throughout the three realms of existence in the past and present,
which invites rebirth in the loathsome and unwholesome destinies— may it all be extinguished, leaving nothing behind forever.
All sentient beings within the ocean of existence Are firmly bound by the snare of birth and death;
I vow that with the sword of wisdom you shall sever them, Causing them to leave suffering behind and swiftly realize the state of Bodhi.
Whatever various causes for supreme merit beings have performed here within this Jambudvīpa,
or in other world-systems, I now rejoice in them all.
By means of this merit from rejoicing, And the manifold virtues created through body,
speech, and mind, May these supreme deeds ever increase, And may you swiftly realize unsurpassed, great enlightenment.
All the merits of praising the Buddha’s virtues, With a profound mind pure and free from stain;
Dedicated and vowed toward boundless blessings— One shall transcend sixty kalpas of the evil realms.
Whether they be men or women, or members of the noble lineages such as the Brahmins,
whoever joins their palms with single-minded devotion and praises the Buddha shall always remember the events of their past lives throughout every birth.
With sense faculties pure and body perfected, May all supreme virtues be fully accomplished;
In all future places of birth, May they always be gazed upon by gods and humans alike.
It is not by having cultivated various roots of goodness under one or ten Buddhas that one now hears this;
only by planting roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas does one finally hear this method of repentance.
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son!
Just as in your dream, the golden drum produced sounds praising the Tathāgata’s true merits along with the method of repentance;
whoever hears this shall obtain immense merit, bring vast benefit to sentient beings, and eliminate their karmic obstructions."

You should now know that these supreme karmic deeds are all due to past praise and the making of vows, the causal conditions of former habituation, and the protective empowerment of the Buddhas' majestic power; I shall explain these causal conditions for you.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the great assembly was filled with joy; they all believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
*Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Fascicle Two.
*Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Fascicle Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śramaṇa Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command.
Chapter Five: The Elimination of Karmic Obstructions (3). Chapter Five: The Elimination of Karmic Obstructions.

At that time, the World-Honored One abided in correct discernment and entered a profound, subtle, and tranquil meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). From the pores of his body, he emitted a great radiance of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various colors; within this light, all Buddha-fields appeared, such that they could not be matched by any analogies or comparisons, even those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.

The five turbidities of this evil world are illuminated by this light. All these sentient beings—who have committed the ten unwholesome actions, the five crimes of immediate retribution, slandered the Triple Gem, been unfilial toward their honored parents, and shown contempt for their teachers, elders, and the assembly of Brahmins; those who were destined to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals—each receive this light reaching their respective abodes. Upon seeing this light, by the power of the light, all these sentient beings attain peace and happiness; they become upright and exquisite, endowed with perfect physical marks, adorned with merit and wisdom, and come to behold the Buddhas.

At that time, Śakra, the lord of the devas, together with the entire assembly of devas, the goddess of the Ganges, and the great multitude, having been graced by this rare light, all approached the Buddha’s dwelling, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic authority, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms toward the Buddha.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

How should good sons and good daughters who aspire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, practice the Mahāyāna, and gather in all sentient beings who are deluded and inverted, as well as those who have committed karmic obstacles and transgressions in the past—how should they repent so that these may be eliminated?"
The Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Noble son!
You now practice the path, desiring to bring immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to pure liberation and peace, out of compassion for the world, to benefit and bring welfare to all."

If there are sentient beings who, due to karmic obstructions, have committed various transgressions, they should exert themselves with diligence throughout the six periods of day and night. With their right shoulders bared, their right knees touching the ground, and palms joined in reverence, they should single-mindedly focus their thoughts and speak these words:

"I take refuge and pay homage to all the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions—those who have already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, who turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma, uphold and illuminate the wheel of Dharma, rain down the great rain of Dharma, beat the great drum of Dharma, blow the great conch of Dharma, raise the great banner of Dharma, and hold aloft the great torch of Dharma."

For the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, they constantly practice the gift of Dharma, guiding and encouraging the deluded masses so that they may attain the great fruit and realize eternal bliss.
To all such Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, I bow my head with body, speech, and mind, and take refuge with sincerity, paying homage with a devoted heart.

Those World-Honored Ones, through their true wisdom, their true eye, their true realization, and their true equanimity, fully know and fully see the wholesome and unwholesome karma of all sentient beings.

Since beginningless saṃsāra, I have followed along with the evil currents, committing karmic obstacles and transgressions together with all sentient beings, bound and fettered by greed, hatred, and delusion.

When one has not yet recognized the Buddha, not yet recognized the Dharma, and not yet recognized the Sangha, and does not yet distinguish between good and evil, one may commit crimes of immediate retribution through body, speech, and mind; with an evil mind, shed the blood of a Buddha, slander the true Dharma, cause schism in the harmonious Sangha, kill an Arhat, or kill one’s father or mother.

Regarding the three types of physical, four types of verbal, and three types of mental actions, they commit the ten unwholesome deeds—whether performing them themselves, inciting others to do so, or rejoicing upon seeing them done.

They recklessly slander virtuous people, deceive others with false weights and measures, and pass off the counterfeit as the genuine. They give impure food and drink to all beings, and within the six realms of existence, they further afflict and harm their own parents.

Or they may steal the property of a stūpa, the property of the Saṃgha from the four quarters, or the property of the present Saṃgha, using it as they please; they take no pleasure in practicing the Dharma and Vinaya of the World-Honored One, and they do not comply with the instructions of their teachers.
Seeing practitioners of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Mahāyāna vehicles, they take pleasure in insulting and reviling them, causing those who practice the path to feel regret and distress.

Seeing those superior to themselves, they harbor jealousy; regarding the gift of Dharma and material gifts, they constantly give rise to stinginess and parsimony. Enveloped by ignorance, their minds deluded by false views, they do not cultivate virtuous causes, allowing evil to increase. They slander the Buddhas, declaring the Dharma to be non-Dharma and non-Dharma to be Dharma.
Regarding these manifold transgressions, the Buddha, by means of his true wisdom, true eye, true realization, and true equanimity, knows them all and sees them all.
I now take refuge before all the Buddhas and disclose everything without daring to conceal it; I shall not commit again any sins not yet committed, and I now repent for all those already committed.

Regarding the karmic obstructions created by my past actions, which would otherwise cause me to fall into the evil realms—the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the hosts of asuras, and the eight states of no leisure—I pray that all such karmic obstructions in this life may be completely extinguished, and that I shall not undergo any of these evil retributions in the future.

Just as all the great Bodhisattvas of the past, while practicing the conduct of enlightenment, have already repented of all their karmic obstructions, so too do I now repent of my karmic obstructions. I reveal them all and dare not conceal them; may the sins already committed be extinguished, and may I never again dare to create future evils.

Just as all the great Bodhisattvas of the future cultivate the practices of enlightenment and repent all their karmic obstructions, so too do I now repent my karmic obstructions; I reveal them all and dare not conceal them. May the sins already committed be extinguished, and may I never again dare to create evil in the future.

Just as all the great Bodhisattvas currently in the worlds of the ten directions have already repented all their karmic obstructions while practicing the path to enlightenment, so too do I now repent my own karmic obstructions. I disclose them all and dare not conceal them; may the sins already committed be extinguished, and I vow never again to create future evil.
“Good son! For this reason, if one has committed a transgression, one must not conceal it for even a single kṣaṇa, let alone for a day and night, or for a long period of time.”

If one has committed an offense and seeks purification, feeling shame and remorse in one's heart, and with faith that there will inevitably be retribution for evil in the future, giving rise to great terror, one should perform repentance in this manner.
It is like a person whose head or clothing is set on fire; they must seek to extinguish it immediately, for as long as the fire is not extinguished, the mind cannot find peace.
If a person commits an offense, it is likewise: they should immediately repent so that it may be swiftly eliminated.

If there are those who wish to be born into a wealthy and prosperous family with abundant riches and treasures, and further desire to resolve their minds to practice the Mahāyāna, they too should perform repentance to eliminate their karmic obstructions.

If one wishes to be born into a noble and wealthy Brahmin lineage or a Kṣatriya family, or to become a Wheel-Turning King endowed with the seven treasures, one must likewise repent and eliminate karmic obstructions.

“Good son! If there are those who wish to be born among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, they too should perform repentance to eliminate their karmic obstructions.”

If you wish to be born among the gods of the Brahma Assembly, the Ministers of Brahma, Great Brahma; the Heaven of Limited Light, Infinite Light, and Pervasive Radiance; the Heaven of Limited Purity, Infinite Purity, and Universal Purity; the Heaven of No Clouds, Merit-Born, and Vast Fruit; or the Heavens of No Affliction, No Heat, Good Appearance, Good Vision, and the Ultimate of Form, you should likewise repent and eliminate your karmic obstructions.
If one desires to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, one should likewise repent and eliminate karmic obstructions.

If you wish to seek the three knowledges (*traividyā*) and six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), or the sovereign enlightenment of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas up to the ultimate stage; or if you seek the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), pure knowledge, inconceivable knowledge, immovable knowledge, and the perfect, universal knowledge of right and complete enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), you should likewise repent and eliminate your karmic obstructions.
Why is this? Son of good family!

All dharmas arise from causes and conditions, as the Tathāgata has taught: they arise with distinct characteristics and cease with distinct characteristics, because their causes and conditions are distinct.

Thus, all dharmas of the past have already ceased and perished, so that no karmic obstructions remain; these conditioned phenomena that had not yet manifested in the present now arise, and future karmic obstructions shall never arise again.
Why is this? Son of good family!

All dharmas are empty; that which the Tathāgata has taught contains no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span; furthermore, there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor are there any conditioned phenomena.
Good son! All dharmas depend upon the source, yet they cannot be described. Why is this?
Because it transcends all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

If there are sons or daughters of good family who thus enter into this subtle and wondrous True Principle and give rise to a mind of faith and reverence, this is called "having no sentient beings while possessing the fundamental. For this reason, it is said that through repentance, one eliminates karmic obstructions.
“Good son! If a person accomplishes four dharmas, they can eliminate karmic obstructions and attain eternal purity.
What are these four?

First, not giving rise to deviant thoughts and achieving right mindfulness; second, not engendering slander toward the profound principle; third, giving rise to the mind of omniscience toward beginner bodhisattvas; fourth, giving rise to immeasurable loving-kindness toward all sentient beings—these are called the four.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Guard the three karmas with single-minded devotion, And do not slander the profound Dharma;
Conceive the thought of omniscience, And purify karmic obstacles with a compassionate heart."
“Good son! There are four karmic obstacles that are difficult to extinguish and eliminate.
What are these four?

First, committing extremely grave transgressions against the bodhisattva vows; second, giving rise to slander toward the Mahāyāna sūtras; third, being unable to increase one's own roots of goodness; and fourth, being greedily attached to the three realms of existence and lacking the mind of renunciation.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of remedial actions for karmic obstacles. What are the four?
First, one should with a sincere heart draw near to all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions and confess all transgressions.
Second, to exhort all Buddhas on behalf of all sentient beings to preach the profound and wondrous Dharma;
third, to rejoice in all the merits and virtues possessed by all sentient beings;
fourth, to dedicate all roots of goodness and merit toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Among all men and women in the world, there are those who are able to practice the Mahāyāna and those who are not. How can they come to rejoice in the roots of merit and goodness of all sentient beings?”
The Buddha said, "Good son! If there are sentient beings who,

though unable yet to practice the Mahāyāna, nevertheless, during the six periods of day and night, bare their right shoulders, place their right knees upon the ground, join their palms in reverence, and with single-minded concentration, cultivate sympathetic joy, they shall obtain immeasurable merit."
One should speak thus:
"I now deeply rejoice in all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions who are currently practicing giving, ethical discipline, mental cultivation, and wisdom."
"By virtue of performing such rejoicing in merit, one will certainly obtain a result that is honored, sublime, unsurpassed, peerless, and most excellent.
In this way, I rejoice in all the roots of goodness belonging to all sentient beings of the past and the future."

Furthermore, regarding all the merits of those bodhisattvas currently at the initial stage who have resolved their minds toward enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), as well as the great merits of those who, having practiced the bodhisattva path for more than a hundred great eons, have attained the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), reached the stage of non-retrogression, or are in their final birth before Buddhahood—I wholeheartedly rejoice in and praise this entire mass of merit.
The rejoicing in and praising of all the merits of all bodhisattvas of the past and future is likewise so.

Furthermore, regarding all Buddhas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the worlds of the ten directions in the present, who have realized wondrous Bodhi and, for the sake of delivering boundless sentient beings, turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, practice unimpeded Dharma-giving, beat the Dharma drum, blow the Dharma conch, erect the Dharma banner, and rain down the Dharma rain; who out of compassion exhort and transform all sentient beings, causing them all to believe and accept, so that they may all receive the gift of Dharma and obtain sufficient, inexhaustible peace and happiness—[I rejoice in their merits].

Furthermore, whatever roots of goodness have been accumulated as the merits of all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, may all sentient beings who have not yet possessed such merits come to possess them entirely; I rejoice in this with all my heart.
In this same way, one should also with a sincere heart rejoice in and praise all the merits of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas of the past and future.
"Good son!

Such rejoicing shall result in an accumulation of immeasurable merit, equal to that of all sentient beings throughout as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, were they all to sever their afflictions and become arhats."

If there were a son or daughter of good family who, for the remainder of their life, constantly made offerings of the most excellent clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, such merit would not equal even one-thousandth part of the merit previously mentioned from sympathetic joy.

Why is this? The merit of making offerings is finite and measurable, for it does not encompass all merits; whereas the merit of sympathetic joy is immeasurable and infinite, and is able to encompass all merits of the three periods of time.
Therefore, if anyone wishes to increase their superior roots of goodness, they should cultivate such merit through sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).

If there is a woman who aspires to transform her female body into that of a man, she too should practice the cultivation of the merit of sympathetic joy; she will certainly, according to her wish, manifest as a man.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have already understood the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*). I now pray that you will explain the merit of exhortation (*adhyeṣaṇā*), so as to cause all bodhisattvas of the future to turn the wheel of Dharma, and for the sake of the bodhisattvas of the present who are correctly practicing.”
The Buddha told Śakra:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who aspire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should practice the paths of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Mahāyāna."
This person, during the six periods of day and night, maintaining the aforementioned dignified posture and with single-minded devotion, should speak these words:

"I now take refuge in all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions. To those who have already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* but have not yet turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, and who wish to relinquish their reward-body (*vipākakāya*) and enter *nirvāṇa*—to all such ones, I most sincerely prostrate and entreat them to turn the great wheel of Dharma, to rain down the great rain of Dharma, to kindle the great lamp of Dharma, to illuminate the principles of the Way, and to bestow the unimpeded Dharma. Do not enter *parinirvāṇa*; remain long in the world to deliver, liberate, and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, as previously described, until they reach inexhaustible peace and happiness."

I now dedicate these merits from my exhortation toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, just as the great bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present have dedicated their merits from exhortation toward bodhi; I likewise dedicate these merits from my exhortation toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Good son! Suppose there were someone who offered the seven treasures filling the entire trichiliocosm as an offering to the Tathāgata; yet if another person were to exhort and request the Tathāgata to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, the merit obtained by the latter would surpass that of the former."
Why is this? That is the gift of material wealth; this is the gift of the Dharma.
O son of good family!

Setting aside the gift of the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm, if a person were to offer the seven treasures filling as many great trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River to all the Buddhas and entreat them [to teach], that merit would still surpass the former; for the gift of Dharma possesses five superior benefits.
What are the five?
First, the gift of Dharma benefits both oneself and others, whereas the gift of material wealth does not;
second, the gift of Dharma enables sentient beings to transcend the three realms, whereas the merit of the gift of material wealth does not extend beyond the realm of desire.
Third, the gift of Dharma can purify the Dharma-body, whereas the gift of material wealth merely increases physical form;
fourth, the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible, whereas the gift of material wealth is finite;
fifth, the gift of Dharma can sever ignorance, whereas the gift of material wealth merely suppresses craving and attachment.
Therefore, noble son!
The merit of exhortation is immeasurable and boundless, beyond easy analogy.

Just as when I formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, I exhorted all Buddhas to turn the great wheel of Dharma, by virtue of those roots of goodness, all the Śakras and Brahmā kings of today now exhort me to turn the great wheel of Dharma.
"Noble son!
Please turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of delivering, liberating, and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
In the past, while practicing for the sake of Bodhi, I entreated the Tathāgata to remain long in the world and not enter parinirvāṇa."

By virtue of these roots of goodness, I shall attain the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered analytical knowledges, and great loving-kindness and great compassion; I shall realize countless unique dharmas, enter into nirvana without remainder, and my True Dharma shall abide long in the world.

My Dharma-body is incomparably pure, possessing various wondrous marks, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable sovereignty, and immeasurable merit; it is inconceivable, benefiting all sentient beings, and could not be fully described even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas.
The Dharma-body encompasses and stores all dharmas, yet all dharmas do not encompass the Dharma-body.
The Dharma-body is eternally abiding and does not fall into the view of permanence; although it appears to cease, it is also not the view of annihilationism.

It can shatter the various divergent views of sentient beings and give rise to their various true insights; it can untie the bonds of all sentient beings—though there are no bonds to be untied—and plant the roots of all manner of goodness in sentient beings, bringing those who are immature to maturity and those already matured to liberation.
Unconditioned and immovable, far removed from clamor and bustle, quiescent and uncreated, sovereign and blissful, transcending the three periods of time while being able to manifest within them;

beyond the realm of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is that which all great bodhisattvas practice, and in essence is no different from that of all Tathāgatas—all of this is due to the power of the roots of goodness resulting from the merit of exhortation and entreaty; such a Dharma-body as this, I have now attained.

Therefore, if anyone who wishes to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* explains even a single sentence or a single verse from among the various sūtras for others, their merit and roots of goodness are already immeasurable; how much more so when they exhort the Tathāgata to turn the great wheel of Dharma, to remain long in the world, and not enter parinirvāṇa.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, cultivate all roots of goodness belonging to the path of the three vehicles, how should they dedicate them toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)?”
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas: “Good son!

If there are sentient beings who seek bodhi and cultivate the path of the three vehicles, and who wish to dedicate all their roots of goodness, they should, during the six periods of day and night, with earnest and sincere hearts, speak as follows:”

"From beginningless saṃsāra until now, whatever roots of goodness I have cultivated and accomplished in relation to the Triple Gem—whether it was giving even a single morsel of food to an animal, or reconciling disputes with kind words, or receiving the three refuges and the various precepts, or performing repentance, making requests, and rejoicing in all roots of goodness—I now bring them all to mind and gather them together, dedicating them for the benefit of all sentient beings without any regret or stinginess."

These are comprised within the roots of goodness conducive to liberation; as known and seen by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they are immeasurable, unimpeded, and pure. All such meritorious roots of goodness he dedicates entirely to all sentient beings, with a mind that does not dwell on signs and a mind that does not abandon signs.

I likewise dedicate all these roots of merit and virtue to all sentient beings, wishing that they may all obtain hands that fulfill their desires, drawing forth jewels from space to satisfy the aspirations of all beings; that their wealth and joy be inexhaustible and their wisdom infinite; that their eloquence in the subtle Dharma be entirely unimpeded; and that together with all sentient beings, they may equally realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and attain all-knowledge.
Consequently, these roots of goodness further give rise to immeasurable wholesome dharmas, all of which are dedicated toward unsurpassed bodhi.

Furthermore, just as the merits and roots of goodness cultivated by the great bodhisattvas of the past were entirely dedicated toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), so too shall it be for those of the present and the future.

Nevertheless, I shall dedicate all my merits and roots of goodness toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; by means of these roots of goodness, may I together with all sentient beings attain perfect enlightenment.

Just as other Buddhas sit at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree—wondrously inconceivable, unimpeded, and pure; abiding in the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the *dhāraṇī* of the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma; destroying the immeasurable hosts of the Māra Pāpīyān; and that which should be seen, known, and thoroughly penetrated—all such things they fully illuminate and realize in a single kṣaṇa. In the final watch of the night, they attain the Dharma of Ambrosia and realize the meaning of Ambrosia. May I and all sentient beings likewise realize such wondrous awakening.
Just as with Amitāyus Buddha, Śālendrarāja Buddha, Sūryaprabha Buddha, Akṣobhya Buddha, Guṇasuprabha Buddha,
Siṃhaprabha Buddha, Śataprabha Buddha, Jālaprabha Buddha, Ratnaketu Buddha,
Ratnārcis Buddha, Arciṣmat Buddha, Arciḥpradīpa Buddha, and Kṣema...
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas such as Śaṅkara-rāja Buddha, Sūkṣma-svara Buddha, Su-vyūha-rāja Buddha,
Dharma-dhvaja Buddha, Uttama-kāya Buddha, Priya-varṇa-kāya Buddha, Samanta-prabhāsa Buddha, Brahma-śuddha-rāja Buddha, and Uttama-bhava Buddha—
these and others, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past...
Just as [the Buddhas] manifest in the future and the present through their responsive transformations, attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment,
and turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings, so too shall I do.
The detailed exposition is as above. "Good son!

If there are men or women of pure faith who receive, uphold, read, recite, remember without forgetting, and extensively explain for others this 'Chapter on the Extinction of Karmic Obstructions' from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, they shall obtain an immeasurable and boundless mass of great merit."
For example, suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were simultaneously to attain a human body, and having attained a human body, were to achieve the path of a pratyekabuddha.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, for as long as their lives last, respectfully revere and honor each individual Pratyekabuddha with the four types of offerings, giving to each of them seven precious jewels as vast as Mount Sumeru; and after these Pratyekabuddhas have entered Nirvana, they build stupas out of rare treasures to make offerings to them, those stupas being twelve yojanas in height and breadth, constantly making offerings with various flowers, incense, precious banners, flags, and canopies.
"Good son! What do you think?
Is the merit obtained by this person not indeed great?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: “Very many,
World-Honored One!”

“Good son! If there is another person who, regarding this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra—the king of all sūtras—specifically the ‘Chapter on the Extinction of Karmic Obstructions,’ receives, maintains, reads, recites, remembers it without forgetting, and explains it extensively for others, the merit they obtain cannot be matched by even a hundredth part of the merit previously described from making offerings; nor can it be reached by a hundred-thousand-myriad-bilions part, or even by any calculation, comparison, or analogy.”

Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family abide in right practice and entreat all Buddhas of the ten directions to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; for this reason, they are all gladdened and praised by the Buddhas.
"Good son!
As I have taught, among all forms of giving, the gift of Dharma is supreme.
Therefore, good son!"
Even if one were to make various offerings to the Triple Gem, they could not be compared [to this].

Even if one were to encourage others to receive the Three Refuges and maintain all the precepts without violation, such that the three karmas were never in vain, these could not be compared [to this].

To exhort all sentient beings in all worlds, according to their strength, their capacity, and their aspirations and inclinations, to resolve upon bodhicitta within the Three Vehicles—this cannot be compared [to anything else].
Within all worlds throughout the three periods of time, may all sentient beings attain unimpededness and swiftly accomplish immeasurable merit, such that nothing can be compared to it.
To cause all sentient beings in the lands of the three periods of time to be free from obstacles and attain *sambodhi* cannot be compared [to anything else].
To exhort all sentient beings in the lands of the three periods of time to swiftly emerge from the suffering of the four evil realms cannot be compared [to anything else].
Exhorting all sentient beings throughout the lands of the three periods of time to eliminate their most grievous evil karma cannot be compared [to this].
Exhorting them to be liberated from all suffering and affliction cannot be compared [to this].
It cannot be compared to causing all those who are oppressed by every form of fear and suffering to attain liberation;
nor can it be compared to exhorting all sentient beings before the Buddhas of the three periods of time to rejoice in all their merits and to resolve to attain Bodhicitta.

One should exhort others to abandon the karma of evil conduct and verbal abuse, and vow that all merits be fully accomplished. In every lifetime, one should exhort others to offer worship, honor, and praise to the Triple Gem, and urge sentient beings to purely cultivate meritorious deeds and bring enlightenment to fulfillment; this cannot be compared to anything else.

Therefore, you should know that exhorting the Triple Gem of all worlds throughout the three periods of time; exhorting them to fulfill the six pāramitās; exhorting them to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; and exhorting them to remain in the world for immeasurable kalpas to expound immeasurable, profound, and wondrous teachings—these merits are so profound that none can compare with them.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, the Goddess of the Ganges, immeasurable Brahmā kings, and the four classes of devas rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and joined their palms in prostration at his feet.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We have all heard this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the King of Sutras; we now all receive, uphold, read, recite, and master it, and we explain it extensively for others, dwelling in accordance with this Dharma.”
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
We desire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by practicing in accordance with the Dharma, following these various superior characteristics of this meaning.

At that time, Brahmā, Śakra the Lord of Devas, and the others scattered various kinds of māndārava flowers over the Buddha at the place where the Dharma was being taught. The earth of this trichiliocosm shook violently; all celestial drums and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; they emitted golden light that filled the world and produced wondrous sounds.
Then Śakra, Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

All of this is due to the majestic spiritual power of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, which universally rescues through its compassion, provides manifold benefits, increases the various roots of goodness of bodhisattvas, and extinguishes all karmic obstructions.”
The Buddha said, “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said. Why is this?
O son of noble family!

I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, there was a Buddha named Ratnarāja Mahāprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world and remained for six hundred and eighty billion kalpas.

At that time, when the Tathāgata Jewel King Great Radiance appeared in the world, desiring to deliver and liberate all sentient beings—including humans, devas, Śakras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—and to establish them in peace and happiness, he first preached the Dharma at his inaugural assembly, delivering hundreds of thousands of billions of trillions of beings. They all attained the fruit of arhatship; their outflows were exhausted, and they possessed mastery and unimpeded freedom in the three knowledges and six supernormal powers.

In the second assembly, he further delivered ninety thousand *koṭi-nayuta* beings, all of whom attained the fruit of Arhatship; their outflows were exhausted, and they possessed mastery and unimpededness in the three knowledges and six supernormal powers.
In the third assembly, he further delivered ninety-eight trillion beings, all of whom attained the fruit of arhatship and fulfilled the aforementioned [qualities]. "Good son!

At that time, I was in the body of a woman named Puṇyaratnaprabhā; I personally attended upon the World-Honored One during the third assembly, received, upheld, read, and recited this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra*, and expounded it extensively for others, for the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, that Blessed One bestowed upon me this prediction:

"This girl Puṇyaratnaprabhā shall, in a future age, attain Buddhahood, and her name shall be Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

"After casting off the body of that woman, from that time forward, he transcended the four evil realms and was born among humans and devas, experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss. For eighty-four hundred thousand births, he served as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), until today he attained perfect enlightenment, his fame being universally renowned and filling the entire world."
At that time, the great assembly suddenly beheld the Tathāgata King of Jewel Radiance, who was turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
"O sons of good family!..."

To the east of this Sahā world, passing through as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in a hundred thousand Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Ratnavyūha. Therein dwells the Tathāgata Ratnarāja-prabhāsa, who is currently present and has not yet entered parinirvāṇa; he is preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma and extensively transforming all living beings. Those of you who see him are seeing that very Buddha.

“Good son! If there are good sons or good daughters who hear the name of this Tathāgata King of Jewels Great Radiance, they shall attain non-retrogression on the bodhisattva stages and proceed to great parinirvāṇa.”

If there are women who hear this Buddha’s name, at the time of their death they shall behold that Buddha arriving at their side; having seen the Buddha, they shall never again undergo birth in a female body.
“Good son! This subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* brings about manifold benefits, manifold increases the bodhisattva’s roots of goodness, and extinguishes all karmic obstructions.”
"Good son!

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who, wherever they may be, preach this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra for others, all within that land will obtain four kinds of beneficial roots of merit."
What are the four?
First, the king shall be free from illness and be spared from all calamities;
second, his lifespan shall be long and free from obstacles.
Third, there will be no enemies or adversaries, and the military forces will be brave and strong;
fourth, there will be peace, stability, abundance, and joy, and the True Dharma will circulate. Why is this?
"Such a king of men is constantly protected by Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, and the hosts of yakṣas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"O sons of good family!
"Is this fact?
At that time, immeasurable Śakras, Brahmās, the Four Great Kings, and the hosts of yakṣas all answered the World-Honored One with one voice: "It is so!"

"It is so! If there be any kingdom where this wondrous King of Sutras is preached, expounded, recited, and chanted, we four kings shall constantly come to protect its sovereigns, accompanying them in both movement and stillness. Should that king encounter any calamities, obstacles, or enemies, we four kings shall cause them all to be extinguished; we shall also ensure that grief, sorrow, and epidemics are eliminated, increasing his lifespan and bringing about auspicious responses. His wishes shall be fulfilled according to his heart, and he shall always dwell in joy. We shall also enable all the soldiers within his realm to become entirely brave and robust."
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Good son!
Practice as you have spoken. Why is this? Because..."

When these sovereigns of various kingdoms act in accordance with the Dharma, and all the people follow the king in practicing according to the Dharma, you shall all receive the benefits of physical strength and vitality, your palaces will be radiant, and your retinues will be powerful and flourishing.
Then Śakra, Brahmā, and the others addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“If there is a place where this wondrous sutra is lectured upon, read, and circulated, there shall be four kinds of benefit for the great ministers and high officials within that country.
What are these four?
First, they treat one another with mutual intimacy and harmony, honoring and cherishing each other;
second, they are always held in affection and esteem by kings, as well as revered by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the rulers of great and small nations;
third, they regard wealth lightly and value the Dharma, seeking no worldly profit, so that their excellent reputation spreads everywhere and they are held in high esteem by all.
Fourth, their lifespan will be extended, and they will dwell in peace, security, and happiness;
these are called the four kinds of benefits.
If this sutra is proclaimed in any land, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas shall obtain these four kinds of victory.
What are the four?
First, they shall lack nothing in terms of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine;
second, they shall all attain peace of mind for contemplation, recitation, and study.
Third, by relying on mountain forests, one attains a dwelling in peace and happiness;
fourth, whatever one’s heart desires, all shall be fulfilled.
These are called the four kinds of benefits.

If there be any land where this sutra is proclaimed, all its people shall attain abundance and joy; there shall be no epidemics, and merchants coming and going shall obtain much treasure and wealth, being fully endowed with supreme merit—this is called the manifold benefits of various merits.
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Great Kings, and the great assembly addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If this profound meaning of such a sutra as this exists in the present, one should know that the Tathāgata’s thirty-seven factors of enlightenment remain in the world and have not yet perished. When this sutra is extinguished, the True Dharma shall also perish.”
The Buddha said: "So it is! So it is!"
"Good sons!

For this reason, regarding this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, you should all with single-minded devotion correctly recite, correctly hear and uphold, correctly contemplate, and correctly practice even a single phrase, a single verse, a single chapter, or a single fascicle. You should widely proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of all sentient beings, so that they may enjoy peace and happiness throughout the long night, and that their benefit and merit may be boundless."
At that time, when the great assembly had heard what the Buddha had spoken, they all received supreme benefit and joyfully accepted and upheld it.
*Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Fascicle Three.
*Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Fascicle Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śramaṇa Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command.
Chapter Six: The Dhāraṇī of the Most Pure Ground (4). Chapter Six: The Dhāraṇī of the Most Pure Ground.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Lion-Mark Unobstructed Radiance, together with immeasurable billions of followers, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and having made offerings of various flowers, incense, precious banners, pennants, and canopies, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By how many causes and conditions is the bodhicitta attained?
What is this bodhicitta?”
World-Honored One!
Within enlightenment itself, the present mind cannot be apprehended, the future mind cannot be apprehended, and the past mind cannot be apprehended.
Apart from enlightenment, the bodhicitta likewise cannot be apprehended.
Awakening is ineffable; the mind, too, is without color and without marks, devoid of activity, and not something to be contrived. Sentient beings, likewise, cannot be apprehended and cannot be known.
“World-Honored One!
How can the profound meaning of all dharmas be known?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! It is so! It is so!”
Awakening is subtle and wondrous; its activities and fabrications are all unattainable.
Apart from awakening, even the bodhicitta is unattainable.
Awakening is inexpressible, and the mind is likewise inexpressible; it has no form or characteristics and no activity, and all sentient beings are also unattainable.

Why is this? Because awakening and the mind are identical with true suchness (*tathatā*), and because both the subject that realizes and the object realized are equal, it is not the case that there are no phenomena to be known.
"Good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who understands in this way is said to have attained penetration into all dharmas and is well-versed in explaining both awakening (bodhi) and the mind of awakening (bodhicitta)."
The bodhicitta is neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present.
The mind is likewise, and sentient beings are likewise; within this, two distinct characteristics cannot truly be found.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are without arising, awakening (bodhi) cannot be apprehended, nor can the name "awakening" be apprehended; sentient beings and the name "sentient being" cannot be apprehended; śrāvakas and the name "śrāvaka" cannot be apprehended; pratyekabuddhas and the name "pratyekabuddha" cannot be apprehended; bodhisattvas and the name "bodhisattva" cannot be apprehended; Buddhas and the name "Buddha" cannot be apprehended; conditioned activity and non-activity cannot be apprehended, nor can the names "conditioned activity" and "non-activity" be apprehended.
Because they are unattainable, one attains abiding within all dharmas of tranquility; this arises by relying upon all roots of merit and virtue.

“Good son! For example, just as the precious King of Mountains, Sumeru, benefits all beings, so too does this bodhicitta benefit sentient beings; therefore, it is called the first cause of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).”
"Good son! For example, because the great earth sustains all things, this is called the second cause: the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

For example, because a lion possesses great majestic power, walks alone without fear, and is free from alarm and terror, this is called the third cause: the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)."
For example, like the wind-wheel and the strength of Nārāyaṇa—being courageous, robust, and swift because the mind does not retreat—this is called the fourth cause of the *vīryapāramitā* (diligence).

For example, it is like a seven-jeweled tower with four stairways; as a cool breeze blows through its four gates, one experiences the bliss of peace and security. Because one seeks fulfillment in the Dharma-treasury of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is called the fifth cause: the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

Just as the orb of the sun blazes with intense radiance, this mind can swiftly destroy the darkness of ignorance regarding birth and death; therefore, this is called the sixth cause, the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).

Just as a caravan leader can fulfill all the heart's desires, this mind can cross the perilous path of birth and death because it attains the jewels of merit; therefore, this is called the seventh cause: the perfection of skillful means and supreme wisdom (*upāya-prajñā-pāramitā*).

Just as the pure moon is full and free from obscuration, because this mind is able to be pure and complete with respect to all objects, it is called the eighth cause: the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

For example, just as the Wheel-Turning Sage King’s minister of the military treasure exercises sovereign mastery according to his will, this mind is well able to adorn and purify Buddha-lands and extensively benefit all sentient beings through immeasurable merit; therefore, this is called the ninth causal perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).

Just as with space and the wheel-turning sage king, this mind is unimpeded regarding all objects and attains mastery in all places until reaching the stage of consecration; therefore, this is called the tenth cause, the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*).
"Good son! These are called the ten causes of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. You should practice and study these ten causes, good son!"
By relying on five kinds of dharmas, a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
What are these five?
First, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Second, compassion;
third, a mind free from desire for gain;
fourth, the gathering and sustaining of all sentient beings.
Fifth, they aspire to seek the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Son of good family!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
“Good son! Furthermore, by relying on five dharmas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
What are these five?
First, the purification of the three karmas;
second, not acting as a cause or condition for the afflictions of any sentient being;
third, closing the gates to all evil realms and opening the doors to the happy destinies.
Fourth, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
fifth, all their merits are entirely fulfilled.
Noble son!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). "Good son!
Furthermore, by relying on five dharmas, the bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*)."
What are the five?
First, the ability to subdue the afflictions of greed and anger;
second, not begrudging one’s body or life, and seeking neither personal security nor the thought of cessation.
Third, by reflecting upon past karma, one is able to endure suffering;
fourth, by giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, one brings to fulfillment the various roots of goodness in sentient beings;
fifth, for the sake of attaining the profound patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"Good son, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of patience. Good son!"
Furthermore, by relying on five dharmas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
What are these five?
First, they take no pleasure in dwelling together with the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second, not receiving peace and happiness because merit has not yet been fully accumulated;
third, not giving rise to a mind of weariness toward various difficult practices and ascetic austerities;
fourth, gathering and benefiting others through great compassion, and bringing all sentient beings to maturity through skillful means.
Fifth, they aspire to and seek the stage of non-retrogression.
Son of good family!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of exertion.
“Good son! Furthermore, by relying on five dharmas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
What are these five?
First, because they gather all wholesome dharmas so as not to allow them to be scattered;
second, because they constantly aspire for liberation and do not cling to the two extremes;
third, because they aspire to attain supernormal powers in order to bring sentient beings to maturity in their various roots of goodness.
Fourth, it is for the sake of purifying the dharma-realm by removing the defilements of the mind;
fifth, it is for the sake of severing the root of the afflictions of sentient beings. Good son!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the dhyāna-pāramitā. "Good son!
Furthermore, by relying on five dharmas, the bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the prajñā-pāramitā."
What are these five?
First, one constantly makes offerings to and draws near all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and wise ones, never giving rise to weariness or aversion;
second, when the Buddhas and Tathāgatas preach the profound Dharma, one’s mind always delights in hearing it, never reaching satiety.
Third, they possess the supreme wisdom of the ultimate and conventional truths, delighting in skillful discernment;
fourth, they swiftly sever all afflictions of both the views and the meditative paths;
fifth, they have attained complete mastery over all worldly arts and the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*).
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom. Good son!”
Furthermore, based on five dharmas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*). What are these five?
First, they thoroughly penetrate the differences in the inclinations, afflictions, and mental activities of all sentient beings.
Second, they clearly comprehend all the immeasurable gateways of remedial counteractions for various phenomena;
third, they possess the samādhi of great compassion, entering and emerging from it with mastery;
fourth, regarding all the pāramitās, they aspire to practice them all, achieving them to full completion.
Fifth, they vow to fully comprehend all Buddha-dharmas, embracing them without exception.
Son of good family!
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of the supreme wisdom of skillful means.
“Good son! Furthermore, by relying on five dharmas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
What are these five?
First, one’s mind attains stable abiding by realizing that all phenomena, from their very origin, are neither born nor extinguished, neither existent nor non-existent;
second, one’s mind attains stable abiding by contemplating the most sublime principle of all phenomena as stainless and pure;

third, one’s mind attains stable abiding by transcending all conceptualizations, [realizing] that this is the fundamental *tathatā* (suchness), which is without fabrication or activity, undifferentiated and immovable.
Fourth, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, the mind attains stable abiding within the conventional truth;
fifth, with respect to śamatha and vipaśyanā, they are practiced simultaneously, and the mind attains stable abiding.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of aspiration. Good son!”
Furthermore, based on five dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).
What are these five?
First, by means of the power of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna-bala*), he is able to fully comprehend the mental activities and the good or evil of all sentient beings.
Second, they are able to cause all sentient beings to enter the profound and subtle Dharma;
third, they truly understand the cycle of birth and death of all sentient beings according to their conditions and karma;
fourth, regarding the three types of spiritual faculties among all sentient beings, they are able to discern and know them through the power of correct wisdom.

Fifth, for all sentient beings, he teaches according to the truth so as to cause them to plant roots of goodness, bring them to maturity, and deliver them; all of this is due to the power of his wisdom. Good son!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of power.
“Good son, furthermore,
by relying on five dharmas, the bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the perfection of wisdom.”
What are these five?
First, being able to distinguish between good and evil among all phenomena;
second, distancing oneself from and embracing black and white dharmas respectively.
Third, being able to neither loathe nor rejoice in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
fourth, possessing the practices of merit and wisdom to reach the ultimate state;
fifth, receiving the supreme empowerment and attaining the unique dharmas of all Buddhas, as well as the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom. Good son!”
What is the meaning of *pāramitā*?
It is the meaning of the excellence of cultivation;
it is the meaning of fulfilling immeasurable, vast, and profound wisdom. This is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
The meaning of *pāramitā* is that the mind does not cling to the phenomena of conditioned activity or non-activity;
the meaning of *pāramitā* is the correct awakening and correct contemplation regarding the faults of birth-and-death and the virtues of *nirvāṇa*;
the meaning of *pāramitā* is the complete gathering and sustaining of both fools and the wise.
The ability to manifest various kinds of rare and wondrous Dharma-jewels is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
unimpeded liberation and the fulfillment of wisdom is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
the correct discernment and knowledge of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
That generosity and the other perfections, as well as wisdom, can lead one to the stage of non-retrogression is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
that the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) can bring them to fulfillment is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
and that the merit and roots of goodness of all sentient beings can be brought to maturity is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
To be able to fully accomplish the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the unique buddha-qualities, and so forth upon attaining enlightenment as a Buddha—this is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
To realize that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are entirely without dual characteristics—this is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
To deliver and liberate all beings—this is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
To skillfully explain and subdue all non-Buddhists who come to challenge and debate, this is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
to be able to turn the wheel of the twelve sublime practices, this is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
to be without attachment, without views, and without affliction or entanglement, this is the meaning of *pāramitā*.

“Good son! For a Bodhisattva of the first stage, this sign appears beforehand: the trichiliocosm is entirely filled with immeasurable and boundless varieties of jewel treasuries, all of which the Bodhisattva sees in their entirety.”
"Good son!

For a Bodhisattva of the second stage, these signs appear beforehand: the Bodhisattva sees the great trichiliocosm with its ground as level as the palm of a hand, adorned with immeasurable and boundless varieties of exquisite colors and pure, precious ornaments."
"Good son!
For a Bodhisattva of the third stage, this sign appears beforehand: he sees himself as courageous and strong, adorned with armor and weapons, capable of subduing all enemies and bandits."
"Good son!

To a Bodhisattva of the fourth stage, this sign appears beforehand: wind-circles from the four directions scatter all manner of wondrous flowers, which are strewn everywhere and cover the ground; the Bodhisattva sees them all."
"Good son!

For a Bodhisattva of the fifth stage, this sign appears beforehand: there is a woman of exquisite jewels, her body adorned all over with various precious necklaces, her head crowned with a tiara of choice flowers as ornament; the Bodhisattva sees all of this."

"Good son! To a bodhisattva of the sixth stage, this sign appears beforehand: there are lotus ponds made of the seven treasures with four flights of stairs, covered everywhere with golden sand, pure and free from impurity, filled to the brim with water possessing the eight virtues. Blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*kumuda*), and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) adorn them in every place. At these lotus ponds, one sports in joy and experiences incomparable coolness; the bodhisattva sees all of this."
"Good son!

For a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage, this sign appears beforehand: before the Bodhisattva, there are sentient beings who ought to fall into hell; yet by the power of the Bodhisattva, they do not fall, remaining free from injury and free from fear—all of which the Bodhisattva perceives."
"Good son!

To a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage, this sign appears beforehand: on both sides of his body, there are lion kings who act as his guardians; all other beasts are utterly terrified, and the Bodhisattva sees them all."
"Good son!

For a Bodhisattva of the ninth stage, this sign appears beforehand: he sees a Wheel-Turning Sage King surrounded and making offerings to him by immeasurable billions of followers, with a white parasol atop his head adorned with immeasurable varieties of jewels."
"Good son!

Before this stage, such signs appear to a Bodhisattva of the tenth ground: the body of the Tathāgata shines with a golden luster, and his immeasurable pure radiance is perfectly complete; surrounded by immeasurable billions of Brahmā kings who pay homage and make offerings, he turns the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous Wheel of Dharma—all of which the Bodhisattva sees."
“Good son! Why is the first stage named ‘Joy’ (*pramuditā*)?

It is because one has for the first time realized the supramundane mind; what was previously unattained is now attained for the first time. Regarding the great task, all that was wished for is fully accomplished, giving rise to supreme joy and bliss; therefore, the first is named ‘Joy.’”
All subtle defilements and the transgressions of violating the precepts are completely purified; therefore, the second stage is called the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

The light of immeasurable wisdom and samādhi is unshakable and cannot be overcome; with the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining as its foundation, the third stage is called the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).
Because one burns away all afflictions with the fire of wisdom, increases radiance, and cultivates the factors of enlightenment, the fourth stage is called the "Blazing Stage" (Arciṣmatī).

Because the mastery of superior wisdom through the cultivation of skillful means is extremely difficult to attain, and because one is able to subdue those afflictions—both those seen and those cultivated—that are otherwise difficult to subdue, the fifth stage is called the "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā).
