The continuity of the practice of the Dharma is clearly manifested, and the contemplation of the signless (*animitta-manasikāra*) appears entirely before one; therefore, the sixth stage is called "Manifest" (*Abhimukhī*).

Because the untainted, uninterrupted, and signless contemplation, as well as the liberating samādhi, have been practiced for a long time, this stage is pure and free from obstacles; therefore, the seventh stage is called "Far-Reaching" (*Dūraṅgamā*).
Through the cultivation of signless contemplation, one attains mastery such that the activities of all afflictions cannot cause one to waver; therefore, the eighth stage is named "The Immovable.

Having attained mastery over the various distinctions of all phenomena, being free from affliction and burden, and increasing wisdom with unimpeded sovereignty, the ninth stage is named "Excellent Intelligence."
The Dharma-body is like space, and wisdom is like a great cloud; because both are able to pervade and cover all things, the tenth stage is therefore named "Dharma Cloud" (Dharmameghā).

“Good son! The ignorance that clings to the characteristics of self and dharmas, and the ignorance that fears birth-and-death and the evil realms—these two types of ignorance obstruct the first stage.”
The ignorance regarding subtle transgressions of the precepts and the ignorance regarding the initiation of various karmic activities—these two ignorances obstruct the second bhūmi.

The ignorance regarding attachment to what has not yet been attained and what is now being attained, and the ignorance that can obstruct the sublime dhāraṇīs—these two ignorances obstruct the third bhūmi.

The ignorance that consists in attachment to the joy of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and the ignorance that consists in craving for subtle and pure phenomena—these two ignorances obstruct the fourth stage.
The ignorance that consists in the desire to turn one's back on saṃsāra and the ignorance that consists in the aspiration to enter nirvāṇa—these two ignorances obstruct the fifth stage.
The ignorance of the flowing of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) and the ignorance of the manifestation of coarse signs—these two ignorances obstruct the sixth stage.
The ignorance of the active manifestation of subtle signs and the ignorance of mental engagement that delights in signlessness—these two ignorances obstruct the seventh stage.
The ignorance regarding effort in the contemplation of the signless (*animitta*) and the ignorance regarding mastery over signs—these two ignorances obstruct the eighth stage.

The ignorance regarding lack of skill in these two types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) concerning the meaning, phrases, and syllables as they are taught, and the ignorance regarding speech and eloquence not being at will—these two ignorances obstruct the ninth stage.

The ignorance regarding the lack of mastery over the manifestation of great supernormal powers and the ignorance regarding activities for which subtle secrets have not yet been realized—these two ignorances obstruct the tenth stage.

Regarding all objects, there is the ignorance that constitutes a subtle obstacle to what is to be known, and the ignorance that constitutes the coarse heaviness of extremely subtle afflictions; these two types of ignorance obstruct the stage of Buddhahood.

“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving in the first stage; practices the perfection of ethical discipline in the second stage; practices the perfection of patience in the third stage; practices the perfection of diligence in the fourth stage; practices the perfection of meditative concentration in the fifth stage; practices the perfection of wisdom in the sixth stage; practices the perfection of skillful means and supreme knowledge in the seventh stage; practices the perfection of aspiration in the eighth stage; practices the perfection of power in the ninth stage; and practices the perfection of gnosis in the tenth stage.”
“Good son! The first generation of the bodhicitta, when embraced, can give rise to the Samādhi of Wondrous Jewels;
the second generation of the bodhicitta, when embraced, can give rise to the Samādhi of Lovely Joy.”
The third arousal of the mind, when embraced, can give rise to the samādhi of being difficult to move;
the fourth arousal of the mind, when embraced, can give rise to the samādhi of non-retrogression;
the fifth arousal of the mind, when embraced, can give rise to the jewel-flower samādhi.
The sixth arousal of the mind, when embraced, can give rise to the samādhi of the sun’s perfectly round radiant flames;
the seventh arousal of the mind, when embraced, can give rise to the samādhi of the fulfillment of all vows according to one's wish;
the eighth arousal of the mind, when embraced, can give rise to the samādhi of manifest realization and abiding.
The ninth arousal of the mind, through its integration, can give rise to the samādhi of the Treasury of Wisdom;
the tenth arousal of the mind, through its integration, can give rise to the samādhi of Valiant Progress.
"Good son! These are called the ten kinds of mental resolve of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Good son!"
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in this first stage, attain a dhāraṇī named ‘Relying on the Power of Merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke the mantra, saying:
*Tadyathā | pūṇe | manurati | dhuka dhuka dhuka | yava-suliyu | apavasa-ti | yava-candara | dyotati | tavad-rakṣa-maṃ | daṇḍa-pariharaṃ | kuru | svāhā.* “Good son!”
This dhāraṇī was spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of more than one Ganges River for the sake of protecting Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

If there are those who recite and uphold this dhāraṇī-mantra, they shall be liberated from all fears—namely, tigers, wolves, lions, and other such ferocious beasts; all evil spirits, humans, and non-humans; enemies, bandits, calamities, and adversities; and all forms of suffering and affliction. They shall be freed from the five hindrances and never forget the mindfulness of the first stage.
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva attains a dhāraṇī in the second bhūmi called ‘Abiding in Excellent Peace and Bliss.
It is as follows: *Tadyathā | uccūlī | cili cili | uccūla uccūla | nantu nantu uccūli | huru huru | svāhā.* Good son!”
This dhāraṇī was spoken by Buddhas numbering more than twice the sands of the Ganges River for the sake of protecting Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the second bhūmi.

If there are those who recite and uphold this dhāraṇī-mantra, they shall be freed from all fears—such as wild beasts, evil spirits, humans, and non-humans—as well as from enemies, thieves, calamities, misfortunes, and all forms of suffering and affliction. They shall be liberated from the five hindrances and shall never forget their mindfulness of the second bhūmi.
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva attains a dhāraṇī in the third stage called ‘Invincible Power.
It is as follows: *Tadyathā | danda | kimbha | dandaki | karaci | kokaraci | keyūri | dandari | svāhā* | Good son!”
This dhāraṇī was spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of three Ganges Rivers for the sake of protecting Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the third bhūmi.

If there are those who recite and uphold this dhāraṇī-mantra, they shall be freed from all fears—such as those caused by wild beasts, evil spirits, humans, and non-humans—as well as from enemies, thieves, calamities, misfortunes, and all forms of suffering and affliction; they shall be liberated from the five hindrances and shall never forget the mindfulness of the third bhūmi.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the fourth stage, they obtain a dhāraṇī named ‘Great Benefit.
It is as follows: *Tadyathā | śrī śrī | dharmiṇi dharmiṇi | dhari dhariṇi | śrī śrīṇi | viśarabhasi ṇa | vaṃdhami te | svāhā* | Good son!”
This dhāraṇī was spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of four Ganges Rivers for the sake of protecting Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the fourth stage.

If there be anyone who recites and maintains this dhāraṇī-mantra, they shall be freed from all fears—such as those caused by wild beasts, evil spirits, humans, and non-humans—as well as from enemies, thieves, calamities, misfortunes, and all forms of suffering and affliction; they shall be liberated from the five hindrances and shall never forget the mindfulness of the fourth stage.
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva attains a dhāraṇī in the fifth stage called ‘Adorned with Various Merits.
It is as follows: *Tadyathā | hara hara | nicara nicara | karmāṇi saṃkarmāṇi | saṃvāsani cchambhani | sitambhani muhaṃni | syamabuve svāhā* | Good son!”
This dhāraṇī was spoken by Buddhas numbering more than five *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges], for the sake of protecting Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the fifth stage (*pañcamī-bhūmi*).

If there be anyone who recites and maintains this dhāraṇī-mantra, they shall be liberated from all fears—such as those caused by fierce beasts, malevolent spirits, humans, and non-humans—as well as from enemies, thieves, calamities, misfortunes, and all forms of suffering and affliction; they shall be freed from the five hindrances and shall never forget the mindfulness of the fifth stage.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the *dhāraṇī* called ‘Perfect Wisdom’ (*paripūrṇajñāna*) in the sixth stage, it is as follows:
*Tadyathā | vistir vistari | marini kari kari | vidūhandi | ruru ruru | curu curu durubaduruba | śaśa śeṭha parisa svāhā | siddhi sarvasattvānām siddhyantu mantrapadāni svāhā.* Good son!”
This dhāraṇī was spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of more than six Ganges Rivers for the sake of protecting Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the sixth stage.

If there are those who recite and uphold this dhāraṇī mantra, they shall be freed from all fears—beasts of prey, evil spirits, humans, non-humans, and the like—as well as from enemies, thieves, calamities, adversities, and all forms of suffering and affliction; they shall be liberated from the five hindrances and never forget the mindfulness of the sixth stage.
“Good son! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains the *dhāraṇī* called ‘Supreme Practice of Dharma’ (*Dharmavara-caryā*) in the seventh stage, it is as follows:
*Tadyathā | śoca śoca | ruśoca śoca śoca ru | vṛkṣi vṛkṣi | amṛta-hūṃ-ni-bhṛśani | vṛkṣi-varu-vati | vidhehi | binda-vṛṇi | amṛti-kṣi | bhaṅkuru bhaṅkuru svāhā.* Good son!”
This dhāraṇī was spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of seven Ganges Rivers for the sake of protecting bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the seventh stage.

If there are those who recite and uphold this dhāraṇī-mantra, they shall be liberated from all fears—such as those caused by wild beasts, evil spirits, humans, and non-humans—as well as from enemies, thieves, calamities, misfortunes, and all forms of suffering and affliction; they shall be freed from the five hindrances and never forget the seventh stage.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the dhāraṇī named ‘Inexhaustible Treasury’ in the eighth stage, it is as follows:
‘Tadyathā | śrī śrī śriṇi | miti miti | kṛti kṛti hiru hirū | curu curu | vandami svāhā. Good son!”
This dhāraṇī was spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers for the sake of protecting bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the eighth stage.

If there are those who recite and uphold this dhāraṇī-mantra, they shall be liberated from all fears—such as wild beasts, evil spirits, humans, and non-humans—as well as from enemies, thieves, calamities, misfortunes, and all forms of suffering and affliction; they shall be freed from the five hindrances and never forget the mindfulness of the eighth stage.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the *dhāraṇī* named ‘Infinite Gate’ in the ninth stage, it is as follows:
*Tadyathā | haricandaki | kūlambalate | dūrasī | bhaṭa bhaṭasiri siri-kasiri-pisiri | svasti | sarvasattvānām svāhā.* Good son!”
This dhāraṇī was spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of nine Ganges Rivers for the sake of protecting Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the ninth stage.

If there are those who recite and uphold this dhāraṇī mantra, they shall be liberated from all fears—such as those caused by wild beasts, evil spirits, humans, and non-humans—as well as from enemies, thieves, calamities, misfortunes, and all forms of suffering and affliction; they shall be freed from the five hindrances and never forget the mindfulness of the ninth stage.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the tenth stage, they obtain a dhāraṇī named ‘Destroying the Diamond Mountain.’”

“Tadyathā | siddhe susiddhe | mucani mocani vidyāmale vimale nirmale | maṅgale hiraṇyagarbhe ratnagarbhe | samantabhadre | sarvārthasādhani | manasi mahāmanasi | abhyudgate ’bhyutthite | āśvāse vilāse adhviti amṛte | āśvāse vilāse | varame vara-haṃsa-ma-svāhā | rephurṇi phurṇa | manurati svāhā. “O son of good family!”

This auspicious phrase of the empowerment of the dhāraṇī was spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of more than ten Ganges Rivers, for the sake of protecting the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the tenth bhūmi.

If there are those who recite and uphold this dhāraṇī mantra, they shall be liberated from all fears—such as those caused by wild beasts, evil spirits, humans, and non-humans—as well as from enemies, thieves, calamities, and adversities; all poisonous harms shall be entirely extinguished, they shall be freed from the five hindrances, and they shall never forget the ten stages (daśabhūmi).

At that time, the Bodhisattva Lion-Mark Unobstructed Radiance, having heard the Buddha speak this inconceivable dhāraṇī, immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and praised him in verse:
"Homage to the peerless, To the profound dharma of signlessness;
Sentient beings have lost right knowledge— Only the Buddha can deliver them."
With the Tathāgata’s clear eye of wisdom, not a single dharma-characteristic is seen;
yet with the eye of the true Dharma, he universally illumines the inconceivable.
Not a single dharma is produced, nor does a single dharma cease.
Through this impartial vision, one attains the unsurpassed state;
neither destroying saṃsāra nor dwelling in nirvāṇa,
and being unattached to the two extremes, one thus realizes parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the categories of the pure and the impure, the World-Honored One knows them as a single flavor;
by not discriminating among phenomena, he has attained supreme purity.
The World-Honored One, whose body is boundless, does not utter a single word.
Causing all the assembly of disciples to be fully saturated by the rain of Dharma;
the Buddha observes the characteristics of sentient beings as being entirely devoid of any intrinsic nature,
yet he constantly extends protection and rescue to those who suffer.
Suffering and pleasure, permanence and impermanence, The existence of a self and the non-existence of a self;
Neither identical nor different, Neither arising nor ceasing.
Such manifold meanings Are differentiated according to how they are taught.
Just as an echo in an empty valley, only a Buddha can fully comprehend it.
The Dharma-realm is without discrimination; therefore, there are no distinct vehicles.
Yet, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they are distinguished and taught as being three.

At that time, the Great Brahmā King Maheśvara also rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the King of Sutras, is rare and immeasurable; it is excellent in its beginning, middle, and end, and its words and meanings are ultimate, for they can bring all Buddha-dharmas to fulfillment.
If anyone receives and upholds it, that person shall be repaying the kindness of all Buddhas.
The Buddha said, “Good son! It is so!”
So it is! It is just as you have said,
son of good family!
If anyone should hear this sutra, they shall all never regress from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Why is this?
O son of good family!

This can mature the sublime roots of goodness of non-regressive stage Bodhisattvas; it is the foremost Dharma-seal and the king of all sutras. Therefore, one should listen to it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it.
Why is this? Son of good family!

If all sentient beings have not yet planted roots of goodness, have not yet matured their roots of goodness, and have not yet drawn near to the Buddhas, they will be unable to hear this subtle and wondrous Dharma.

If good sons or good daughters are able to hear and receive this, all their karmic obstacles will be completely extinguished, and they will attain supreme purity. They will always behold the Buddhas and never be separated from the Buddhas and those of noble conduct who are spiritual friends. They will constantly hear the wondrous Dharma, abide on the stage of non-retrogression, and obtain such supreme *dhāraṇī* gates that are inexhaustible and undiminishing;
namely, the *dhāraṇī* of the Inexhaustible and Undiminishing Sublime Merits Emerging from the Ocean Seal;
the *dhāraṇī* of Inexhaustible and Undiminishing Penetration into the Mental Activities and Speech of Sentient Beings; and the *dhāraṇī* of Inexhaustible and Undiminishing Sun-like Pure Radiance.
The *Dhāraṇī of the Light of the Full-Moon Mark* is inexhaustible and undiminished;
the *Dhāraṇī that Subdues All Afflictions and Manifests a Stream of Merit* is inexhaustible and undiminished;
the *Dhāraṇī that Shatters the Diamond Mountains* is inexhaustible and undiminished.
The dhāraṇī of the treasury of causes and conditions for the ineffable meaning is inexhaustible and undiminished;
the dhāraṇī of penetrating the sounds of the principles of truthful speech is inexhaustible and undiminished;
the dhāraṇī of the seal of mental activity that is as stainless as space is inexhaustible and undiminished.
The dhāraṇī that can manifest the bodies of infinite Buddhas is inexhaustible and undiminishing. "Good son!

Because these and other such inexhaustible and undiminishing dhāraṇī-gates are accomplished, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to manifest the body of a Buddha in all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, expounding the various unsurpassed true Dharmas. While remaining unmoving and non-abiding within the *tathatā* of phenomena, neither coming nor going, he is well able to mature the roots of goodness of all sentient beings, yet he does not perceive even a single sentient being who is to be matured."
Although one speaks of various dharmas, within these words there is no moving or staying, no going or coming; thus, one is able to realize non-arising-and-ceasing within arising and ceasing.
"For what reason is it said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have neither coming nor going?
It is because the essence of all phenomena is without differentiation.

When this Dharma was spoken, three trillion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); immeasurable bodhisattvas did not regress from their resolve for enlightenment; immeasurable and boundless bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; and immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The supreme Dharma can go against the current of birth and death; It is profound, subtle, and difficult to perceive.
Sentient beings are blind and obscured by craving; Because they do not see it, they undergo manifold sufferings.”
At that time, the great assembly rose from their seats together, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In whatever place this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the King of Sutras, is preached, expounded, read, or recited, we, the great assembly, shall all go there to serve as listeners. We shall cause that Dharma-preacher to obtain benefit, peace, and happiness, free from obstacles, with body and mind at ease.”

We shall all offer our utmost devotion in making offerings, and we shall also cause the assembly to dwell in peace and happiness; in the lands where they reside, may there be no enemies, bandits, terrors, calamities, or the suffering of famine, and may the population flourish.
This ground of the site of enlightenment where this Dharma is preached must not be trodden upon nor defiled by any gods, humans, non-humans, or any other sentient beings.
For what reason?

The place where the Dharma is preached is itself a caitya; one should make offerings with incense, flowers, silken fabrics, banners, and canopies. We shall constantly provide protection for it, ensuring that it remains free from decay or loss.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"Sons of good family!
You should diligently practice this sublime sūtra; in this way, the True Dharma will abide long in the world."
The Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra, King of Sutras, Scroll Four;
The Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra, King of Sutras, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śramaṇa Yijing by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: Praise by the Lotus Simile (5). Chapter Seven: Praise by the Lotus Simile.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhi-tree deity:
"O Good Goddess!

"You should now know that last night, in a dream, Wondrous Banner saw a magnificent golden drum emit a great sound, praising the Buddha’s merits and the method of repentance. I shall explain the causes and conditions of this matter to you in detail; you should listen attentively and reflect upon it well."

"In the past, there was a king named Golden Dragon Lord who constantly praised and extolled the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time by means of the metaphor of the lotus flower.
He then spoke these verses of praise for the great assembly:
"The Buddhas of the past, future, and present, Dwelling peacefully within the worlds of the ten directions;
With utmost sincerity, I now prostrate in homage, Single-mindedly praising all the Most Victorious Ones.
The Unsurpassed, Pure Muni Honored One, His body’s radiance shines like the color of gold;
Foremost among all sounds, Like the resonance of Great Brahmā, thundering like the roar of clouds.
The color of his hair is like that of a king of black bees, curling in elegant spirals of deep azure-blue;
his teeth are white, even, and closely set like snow or white jade, perfectly aligned and radiant with light.
Your eyes are pure and stainless, most wondrously beautiful, like the broad petals of a great blue lotus;
your tongue is wide and long, exceedingly supple, like a red lotus emerging from the water.
Between his eyebrows there is always a white tuft of hair, curling to the right with the color of crystal;
his brows are fine, long, and like the crescent moon, their brilliant hue surpassing that of a king of bees.
The nose is high, long, and straight like a gold ingot; pure, wondrous, and lustrous, its features are flawless.
As for all the exquisite and sublime fragrances in the world, upon smelling them, he knows exactly where they originate.
The World-Honored One’s most supreme body is golden in color; each individual hair-tip is identical in its marks.
Deep blue, soft, and curling to the right, their subtle and radiant luster is beyond compare.
At his first birth, his body possessed a wondrous radiance, Universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions;
It was able to extinguish the suffering of sentient beings within the three realms of existence, Causing them all to receive peace, stability, and joy.
Within the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, Among the asuras, devas, and human beings—
May they cause all these various sufferings to be extinguished, And may they always experience spontaneous peace and bliss.
The radiance of his body’s hue shines universally at all times, like refined gold, wondrous beyond compare;
his face is perfectly bright like the full moon, and the color of his lips is as lovely as the *bimba* fruit.
His gait and majestic deportment resemble those of a lion; his bodily radiance is as brilliant as the rising sun.
His arms and forearms are slender and long, reaching past his knees, appearing like the drooping branches of a *sāla* tree.
A halo one fathom wide illuminates the boundless, Brilliant as hundreds of thousands of suns;
It reaches every Buddha-field, Awakening the deluded according to their conditions.
The net of pure radiance is peerless, Its flowing brilliance fills hundreds of thousands of worlds;
Shining everywhere throughout the ten directions without obstruction, All darkness and gloom are entirely dispelled.
The Sugata’s compassionate light bestows happiness; its wondrous form shines through, equal to a mountain of gold.
Its flowing radiance reaches hundreds of thousands of lands; all sentient beings who encounter it attain liberation.
The Buddha’s body has perfected immeasurable merit, adorned by all virtues;
transcending the three realms, he alone is honored as supreme, unrivaled in excellence throughout the world.
All Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the atoms within the great earth;
The Honored Ones of the ten directions in the future and present, likewise as many as the multitude of atoms in the great earth.
With my body, speech, and mind in perfect sincerity, I prostrate and take refuge in the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
I praise the ocean of their boundless merits and offer all manner of incense and flowers as worship.
Even if I were to have a thousand tongues in my mouth, And praise the Tathāgata for immeasurable eons, The virtues of the World-Honored One are inconceivable;
Most supreme and profound, they are difficult to describe.

Even if I were to possess a hundred thousand tongues, To praise but a single Buddha for a single virtue, I would still find it difficult to know even a small fraction of them; How much more so for the boundless virtues of all Buddhas?
Even if the great earth and all the heavens, up to the peak of existence, were turned into a sea of water;
though one could count its drops with the tip of a hair, the merit of a single quality of the Buddha remains exceedingly difficult to measure.
With my body, speech, and mind, I pay homage and praise the boundless virtues of all Buddhas;
may the inconceivable fruits of all this supreme merit be dedicated to sentient beings so that they may swiftly attain Buddhahood.
Having praised the Tathāgata, that king further deepened his resolve and made a great vow:
"May I, in future ages, live through immeasurable and incalculable kalpas."
In my dreams I constantly see a great golden drum, From which I hear the sound of the proclamation of repentance;
I praise the Buddha’s virtues as being like the lotus flower, Vowing to realize non-arising and attain perfect enlightenment.
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world occurs but once; they are extremely difficult to encounter even in hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
In dreams at night, I constantly hear the sound of the wondrous drum; by day, I repent in accordance with what is appropriate.
I shall fully cultivate the six perfections to rescue all beings from the ocean of suffering;
thereafter, I shall attain unsurpassed enlightenment, with a Buddha-field as pure and inconceivable as it can be.
I offered a wondrous golden drum to the Tathāgata, And praised the true merits of all Buddhas;
By this cause, I shall behold Śākyamuni Buddha, Who will grant me the prophecy that I shall succeed him as the Honored One among Men.
Golden Dragon and Golden Light are my sons; In the past, they were once my spiritual friends.
May they be born in my household in every lifetime, Together receiving the prediction of supreme enlightenment.
If there are sentient beings without protection, Wandering through the long night of saṃsāra and undergoing manifold sufferings;
May I become their refuge in future lives, Causing them to always attain peace and happiness.
May the manifold sufferings of the three realms of existence be extinguished, And may all beings find peace and happiness according to their hearts' desire;
Cultivating bodhi in future ages, May they all become Buddhas just like those who have attained Buddhahood in the past.
By the merit of this Golden Light Repentance, may the ocean of suffering be forever exhausted and all transgressions eliminated;
may karmic obstructions and afflictions be entirely extinguished, and may I swiftly attain the fruit of purity.
The great ocean of merit and wisdom is boundless in measure, pure, stainless, and bottomless;
may I attain this ocean of virtue and swiftly realize supreme, unexcelled Bodhi.
By the power of this confession with golden light, one shall obtain the pure radiance of merit;
having attained this pure and wondrous light, one shall always illumine all things with the light of wisdom.
May the radiance of my body be equal to that of all Buddhas, And may my merit and wisdom likewise be so;
May I alone be preeminent in all worlds, With sovereign power and majesty beyond compare.
May we transcend the ocean of suffering with outflows; may we forever roam the ocean of unconditioned bliss.
May the ocean of merit in the present remain ever full; may the ocean of wisdom in the future be brought to perfection.
May my buddha-field transcend the three realms, With sublime merits of boundless measure;
May all who possess the karmic affinity be born therein together, And may they all swiftly attain pure wisdom.
"O Subhaketu, you should know: The king, Golden Dragon Lord, Who once made such a vow, Is none other than your own self.
In former times there were two sons, Golden Dragon and Golden Light."
"Immediately, with silver marks and silver light, you shall receive my prediction.
When the great assembly heard these words, they all resolved their minds upon Bodhi;
may they, in the present and the future, always rely upon this repentance.
Chapter Eight: The Suvarṇottama Dhāraṇī At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Susthitamati within the assembly: “Good son!

There is a dhāraṇī called Suvarṇottama; if there are good sons or good daughters who wish to personally behold and respectfully make offerings to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, they should receive and uphold this dhāraṇī.
Why is this? This dhāraṇī is the mother of all Buddhas of the past, present, and future.

Therefore, you should know that whoever upholds this dhāraṇī possesses great merit and virtue; they have planted the roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas in the past and are now able to receive and uphold it. Their precepts will be pure, without violation or deficiency, free from obstacles, and they will certainly be able to enter the profound Dharma-gate.
The World-Honored One then explained the method for upholding the dhāraṇī: first invoke the names of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, pay homage with a sincere heart, and then recite the mantra:
"Namo to all Buddhas of the ten directions."
Homage to all the great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
Homage to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all worthy sages.
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha.
Homage to the Buddha Akṣobhya of the East.
Homage to the Buddha Ratnākara of the South.
Homage to the Buddha Amitābha of the West.
Homage to the Buddha Druma-kinnara-rāja-saṃgīti of the northern direction.
Homage to the Buddha Vipula-guṇa-saṃcaya of the upper direction.
Homage to the Buddha Guṇaprabha of the lower direction.
Homage to the Buddha Ratnagarbha.
Homage to the Buddha Samantaprabhāsa.
Homage to the Buddha Samantāvabhāsa.
Homage to the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭarāja.
Homage to the Buddha Padmottara.
Homage to the Buddha Samadarśin.
Homage to the Buddha Ratnaśikhin.
Homage to the Buddha Ratnottama.
Homage to the Buddha Ratnaprabha.
Homage to the Buddha Vimalaprabha.
Homage to the Buddha Pratibhānālaṃkāravicaya.
Homage to the Buddha Śaśikāntivigatābhāsa-lakṣaṇarāja.
Homage to the Buddha Avataṃsaka-prabha.
Homage to the Buddha Prabhāsa-rāja.
Homage to the Buddha Bhadrābhāsra-vimala-guṇa-rāja.
Homage to the Buddha Vīkṣaṇābhayavikrāmin.
Homage to the Buddha Abhayakīrti.
Homage to the Buddha Vararāja.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sudhi.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
"Namo ratnatrayāya. Tadyathā: kuṇḍe kuṇḍe, kuñjare kuñjare, iṭṭhili miṭṭhili, svāhā. The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Susthita:

"This dhāraṇī is the Mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. If there are good sons or good daughters who uphold this mantra, they will be able to generate an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of merit and virtue; this is equivalent to making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and praising countless Buddhas, and all such Buddhas will bestow upon these persons the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Excellent abiding!

If there are those who can uphold this mantra, they shall obtain whatever they desire—clothing, food, wealth, and treasures; extensive learning and wisdom; freedom from illness and long life—and shall gain immense merit. Whatever they seek or pray for, none of their wishes shall fail to be fulfilled."
"Excellent abiding!

Those who uphold this mantra shall, until they realize unsurpassed bodhi, always dwell together with the Bodhisattva Golden City Mountain, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Great Ocean, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāvikara, and others, and shall be protected and sustained by all these bodhisattvas."
"Śubhavyūha, you should know this!
When holding this mantra, perform the following ritual: first, as a preliminary practice, one should recite and maintain it for ten thousand eight times.

Next, in a dark room, adorn a maṇḍala; on the first day of the dark fortnight, bathe with purity, wear fresh and clean garments, burn incense, scatter flowers, and make various offerings including food and drink."

Upon entering the maṇḍala, one should first pay homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as previously described. Having sincerely and reverently repented of past transgressions, one should place the right knee on the ground and recite the aforementioned mantra one thousand and eight times. Then, sitting upright in meditation, one should contemplate and keep in mind one's aspirations.
Before sunrise, within the *maṇḍala*, one should consume pure black food and take only a single meal per day, remaining in the *maṇḍala* until the fifteenth day.

This will cause this person’s merit and power to become inconceivable, such that whatever they seek or pray for will be fulfilled without exception. If their wishes are not yet met, they should re-enter the *maṇḍala*; once their hearts’ desires are satisfied, they should constantly maintain [the practice] without forgetting it.

Chapter 9: Further Elucidation of Emptiness (5) The Golden Light Most Victorious King Sūtra, Chapter Nine: Further Elucidation of Emptiness At that time, having spoken this mantra, the World-Honored One, desiring to benefit the great assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, humans, and devas, and wishing to cause them to realize and understand the profound, true, and ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), further clarified the nature of emptiness by speaking these verses:
“I have already, in other profound sūtras, Extensively explained the subtle Dharma of true emptiness;
Now, within this king of sūtras, I shall briefly explain the inconceivable Dharma of emptiness.”
Regarding all vast and profound dharmas, sentient beings lack the wisdom to understand them;
therefore, I shall hereupon expound upon them again, so that they may attain awakening to the dharma of emptiness.
Out of great compassion for sentient beings, And by means of skillful expedients and supreme causes and conditions,
I shall now, within this great assembly, Proclaim and explain so that they may understand the meaning of emptiness.
Know that this body is like an empty village, where the six thieves dwell together yet do not know one another;
the thieves of the six sense-objects each rely on their respective faculties, and likewise they remain mutually ignorant of one another.
The eye faculty constantly observes the realm of forms; The ear faculty listens to sounds without ceasing;
The nose faculty perpetually smells the objects of fragrance; The tongue faculty always tastes delicious flavors;
The body faculty experiences light and soft touches; The mind faculty discerns phenomena without knowing weariness.
These six sense faculties arise according to their respective objects, each generating discrimination within its own domain.
Consciousness is like a magical illusion and lacks true reality; yet, depending upon the locations of the faculties, it falsely craves and pursues.
Just as a person runs through an empty village, so too do the six consciousnesses depend upon the faculties.
The mind roams everywhere in pursuit, shifting as it encounters objects; relying on the sense organs and engaging with their spheres, it completes all its tasks.
It constantly craves forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures, seeking and pondering phenomena without a moment’s rest.
Following conditions, it pervasively functions through the six sense faculties, like a bird flying through the sky without obstruction;
by taking these faculties as its basis, it is then able to discern external objects.
This body is insentient and lacks an agent; its substance is not solid, being formed by dependence on conditions.
It arises entirely from false conceptualization, like a mechanical device set in motion by karma.
Earth, water, fire, and wind together form the body; according to their respective causes and conditions, they bring about diverse results.
Though dwelling in the same place, they conflict and harm one another, like four venomous snakes residing in a single basket.
These four great serpents differ in their natures; though they dwell in one place, some rise while others sink.
Whether moving upward or downward throughout the body, they all ultimately return to the law of extinction.
Among these four kinds of venomous snakes, the two snakes of earth and water tend to sink downward;
the two snakes of wind and fire are by nature light and upward-moving. Due to this mutual conflict, a multitude of diseases arise.
The mind-consciousness relies upon this body to perform various kinds of wholesome and unwholesome karma;
it shall go to the realms of humans, devas, or the three evil destinies, receiving a physical form according to the power of its karma.
When one encounters various illnesses and the body dies, excrement and urine overflow everywhere;
putrid with pus and infested with maggots, it is no place for delight, cast away in the charnel ground like a piece of rotten wood.
You should contemplate all phenomena as such: how could you cling to the existence of a self or a sentient being?
All dharmas are entirely impermanent; they all arise through the power of the condition of ignorance.
All those great elements are entirely false and illusory; fundamentally they have no real substance and are without arising.
Therefore it is said that the nature of the great elements is empty; one should know them to be floating and void, not truly existent.
The intrinsic nature of ignorance is originally non-existent; it exists through the conjunction of the power of various conditions.
Because it causes the loss of right wisdom at all times, I designate it as ignorance.
With volitional formations and consciousness as conditions, name-and-form arises; the six sense bases, contact, and feeling follow in succession.
With craving, clinging, and becoming as conditions, birth, aging, and death arise, constantly pursued by sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
Constantly entangled and oppressed by manifold sufferings and evil karma, one revolves in the cycle of birth and death without a moment’s rest;
originally non-existent, its essence is empty, yet through improper mental engagement, conceptual discrimination arises.
I have severed all afflictions, And always manifest right wisdom before me;
Realizing that the house of the five aggregates is entirely empty, I seek to realize the true state of Bodhi.
I have opened the great city-gate of the ambrosia, And manifested the subtle and wondrous vessel of ambrosia;
Having attained the true flavor of the ambrosia, I constantly bestow this ambrosia upon all living beings.
I strike the most supreme great Dharma drum; I blow the most supreme great Dharma conch;
I light the most supreme great bright lamp; I let fall the most supreme great Dharma rain.
Having subdued the afflictions and all fetters of enmity, I shall raise the supreme banner of the Great Dharma;
rescuing the deluded masses from the ocean of birth and death, I shall close the gates to the three evil realms.
The blazing fires of affliction burn sentient beings, Leaving them without protection or refuge;
With the sufficiency of cool nectar, The feverish distress of body and mind is entirely removed.
Thus, throughout immeasurable eons, I have reverently made offerings to all Tathāgatas;
upholding the prohibitive precepts, I have pursued Bodhi, seeking to realize the blissful state of the Dharmakāya.
He gives away his eyes, ears, hands, and feet; his wife, children, and servants, with no stinginess in heart;
his wealth, treasures, the seven precious gems, and ornaments—he provides for all who come seeking them.
Having universally cultivated all perfections, such as patience, And having fulfilled the ten stages to attain perfect enlightenment,
I have thus earned the title of "All-Knowing One," For there is no sentient being who can measure me.
Suppose that throughout the entire trichiliocosm, all things growing upon this land—
every forest and tree, rice, hemp, bamboo, reeds, and their branches— [were gathered together].
All these various things are cut down and entirely ground into fine dust;
they are accumulated in every place in quantities difficult to measure, until they completely fill the realm of empty space.
All the lands throughout the ten directions, And all the trichiliocosm worlds therein;
If the earth and soil were all ground into dust, The measure of these motes of dust would be beyond counting.
Even if the wisdom of all sentient beings were given to a single person, such a wise one’s measure would be boundless;
yet the number of their atoms might still be known.
The Sage, the World-Honored One, with his wisdom of a single thought-moment, causes those wise ones to measure it together;
yet throughout many koṭis of eons, they cannot calculate or know even a small fraction of it.

At that time, when the great assembly heard the Buddha’s teaching on this profound emptiness, immeasurable sentient beings were all able to realize that the essential nature of the four great elements and the five aggregates is entirely empty, and that the six sense faculties and six sense objects give rise to false fetters. They vowed to abandon saṃsāra and correctly cultivate the path to liberation; with deep hearts filled with joy, they upheld the teaching as it was spoken.

Chapter Ten: Fulfilling Wishes by Relying on Emptiness (5). The Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra, the King of Sutras, Chapter Ten: Fulfilling Wishes by Relying on Emptiness. At that time, the goddess Maniratnaprabhāśrī, having heard the profound Dharma being preached within the great assembly, was filled with joy and exultation. She rose from her seat, bared her right shoulder, knelt with her right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I only pray that you will explain the method of practice for the profound principle.
Then he spoke in verse:
"I ask the Illuminator of the World, The Most Victorious Honored One among bipeds."
"The Bodhisattva’s practice of the Dharma— may you, out of compassion, grant me leave to hear it.
The Buddha said,
"O Goddess of Goodness!"
"If there are any who have doubts, ask whatever you wish in your mind, and I shall explain it to you in detail.
At that time, the goddess addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How do the various bodhisattvas practice the correct conduct of enlightenment?"
“Why is it that you remain apart from both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa for the sake of benefiting yourself and others?
The Buddha told the goddess Bhadrayaśā:
“Relying upon the dharma-dhātu, you practice the dharma of bodhi and cultivate the conduct of equanimity.”
How does one rely upon the dharma-dhātu to practice the dharmas of bodhi and cultivate the practice of equanimity?

It means being able to manifest the dharma-dhātu within the five aggregates; the dharma-dhātu is itself the five aggregates. The five aggregates cannot be described, nor can that which is not the five aggregates be described.
Why is this? If the dharma-realm were the five aggregates, it would be the view of annihilationism;
if it were apart from the five aggregates, it would be the view of eternalism.

Free from dualistic characteristics and unattached to the two extremes, it is invisible, transcending all that can be seen; being without name and without form—this is what is called the teaching on the dharma-realm.
"Good Goddess!
How is it that the five aggregates can manifest the dharma-realm?
These five aggregates do not arise from causes and conditions."
Why is this? If something arises from causes and conditions, does it arise because it has already arisen,
or does it arise because it has not yet arisen?
If that which has already arisen were to arise, what need would there be for causes and conditions?
If that which has not yet arisen were to arise, its arising could not be established. Why is this so?

All dharmas that have not yet arisen are simply non-existent; they are without name and without characteristic, beyond the reach of calculation or analogy, for they are not produced by causes and conditions.
Good Woman Devī!

For example, just as the sound of a drum arises in dependence upon the wood, the hide, the drumstick, and the hand, so too this sound of the drum is empty in the past, empty in the future, and empty in the present.
Why is this? This sound of the drum does not arise from the wood, nor from the hide, nor from the drumstick and the hand; it does not arise within the three periods of time, and thus it is unarisen.
If it cannot arise, then it cannot cease;
if it cannot cease, it has nowhere from which it comes;
if it has nowhere from which it comes, it likewise has nowhere to which it goes.
If there is no place to which one goes, then it is neither eternal nor subject to annihilation;
if it is neither eternal nor subject to annihilation, then it is neither identical nor different. Why is this so?
If this were one and the same, it would not differ from the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
If that were so, ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) should perceive the ultimate truth (*satyadarśana*) and attain unsurpassed peace and bliss in *nirvāṇa*;
since this is not the case, we know they are not one.

If one says they are different, then the modes of practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would be attachments; they would not have attained liberation from the fetters of affliction, and thus would not realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because for all noble ones (*ārya*), whether in regard to conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*) or non-activity (*asaṃskṛta*), they are identical in their true nature (*tathatā*);

therefore, they are not different. Thus one knows that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are neither existent nor non-existent; they do not arise from causes and conditions, nor do they arise without causes and conditions. This is what the noble ones know, as it is not the domain of others; furthermore, it cannot be reached by verbal expression, being nameless and signless, without cause or condition, and beyond analogy. It is quiescent from the beginning and end, empty by its very nature.
Therefore, the five aggregates can manifest the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
O Good Goddess!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family desires to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should understand that it is neither different from the ultimate truth nor different from the conventional; it is difficult to conceive, and within the spheres of both the ordinary and the holy, its essence is neither identical nor distinct. Without abandoning the conventional and without departing from the ultimate, they should rely upon the dharma-realm and practice the conduct of enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*).

At that time, having spoken these words, the goddess Bhadramāyākārī leaped for joy and, rising from her seat, bared her right shoulder, knelt with her right knee on the ground, joined her palms in reverence, and with single-minded devotion prostrated herself before the Buddha, addressing him thus:
“World-Honored One!
"I shall now train in the correct practice for enlightenment as it has been described above.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, asked the goddess Bhadramukhī, Radiant with the Light of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, within the great assembly:
"This practice for enlightenment is difficult to cultivate; how have you now attained mastery over the practice for enlightenment?"
At that time, the goddess Bhadramāyākārī replied to the Brahmā King:
"Great Brahmā King!
As the Buddha has taught, this is indeed most profound."
All ordinary beings do not understand its meaning; it is the realm of the sages, subtle and difficult to know.

If it is true that by relying on this Dharma I may now dwell in peace and happiness, then by this word of truth, may all immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings in the five turbidities of this evil world attain golden bodies with the thirty-two marks, being neither male nor female, sitting upon precious lotus flowers and experiencing immeasurable bliss. May celestial wonderful flowers rain down, and the music of the devas sound spontaneously without being struck, and may all offerings be fully provided.

When the Goddess of Good Women had finished speaking these words, all sentient beings in the five turbid and evil worlds became entirely golden in color, possessed the marks of a great man, were neither male nor female, sat upon precious lotus flowers, and experienced immeasurable bliss, just like the palace of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations. There were no evil realms; rows of jewel trees lined the way, and seven-jeweled lotus flowers filled the world. Furthermore, exquisite celestial flowers made of the seven jewels rained down from above, and celestial music was played.
The goddess Bhadramāyākarī, whose radiance is like that of a wish-fulfilling jewel, immediately transformed her female body into the body of a Brahmā.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King asked the Bodhisattva Bhadramāyākarī:
"O Noble One!"
"How does one practice the bodhisattva conduct?
He replied:
"Brahmā King!..."
If the moon in the water practices the bodhisattva path, I too shall practice the bodhisattva path;
if one practices the bodhisattva path within a dream, I too shall practice the bodhisattva path;
if a mirage practices the bodhisattva path, I too shall practice the bodhisattva path.
"If an echo practices the conduct of enlightenment, I too shall practice the conduct of enlightenment.
When the Great Brahmā King heard these words, he addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"In what sense do you say this?"
He replied: "Brahmā King!
There is not a single dharma that is of the nature of ultimate reality (lakṣaṇa), for all are established solely through causes and conditions."
The Brahma King said:
"If that were so, then all ordinary persons would surely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He replied:
“With what intention do you speak thus?
Are foolish people one thing and wise people another?
Is awakening one thing and non-awakening another?”
"Is liberation one thing and non-liberation another?
Brahmā King!
Such dharmas as these are equal and without distinction."
Within this *dharmadhātu-tathatā*, there is neither unity nor difference; there is no intermediate state to be grasped, and it neither increases nor decreases.
Brahmā King!

It is like a magician or a magician’s apprentice who is well-versed in illusory arts; at a crossroads, they take various sands, earth, grasses, trees, and leaves, gather them in one place, and perform various illusions, causing people to see multitudes of elephants, multitudes of horses, multitudes of chariots and infantry, and heaps of the seven treasures and various storehouses.
If there are sentient beings who are foolish and lacking wisdom, unable to reflect, and ignorant of the root of illusion, then upon seeing or hearing [these things], they think:
"The elephants, horses, and other multitudes that I see and hear are truly existent; all else is false."
Thereafter, they no longer examine or reflect upon it. A person of wisdom is not like this; having understood the nature of illusion, whether seeing or hearing [such things], they form this thought:

"The multitude of elephants, horses, and so forth that I see are not real; there is only an illusory phenomenon that deceives the eyes. To falsely claim these are elephants and such, or various storehouses, is to have names without reality. Just as I have seen and heard them, I do not grasp them as being real."
At a later time, through reflection, one realizes that these are false and illusory.

Therefore, the wise person understands that all phenomena lack any substantial reality; they merely conform to worldly convention, expressing matters exactly as they are seen or heard. However, when reflecting upon the principle of ultimate truth, it is not so; for it is by means of provisional designations that the true meaning is revealed.
“Brahmā! Foolish ordinary beings have not yet attained the supramundane eye of noble wisdom, and thus they do not know that the suchness of all phenomena is inexpressible.”

When these ordinary, foolish people see or hear of dharmas that are either practiced or not practiced, they engage in such reflections and give rise to attachment, claiming them to be real; they are unable to understand that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the true nature (*tathatā*) of all dharmas is ineffable.

When these noble ones perceive or hear of phenomena that are either active or inactive, they do not give rise to attachment or regard them as truly existent according to their capacity. They thoroughly understand that all phenomena—whether active or inactive—are without real existence; they are merely the products of false conceptualization regarding the characteristics of activity and inactivity, possessing only names but no substantial reality.
These noble ones, following worldly convention, speak in this way because they desire to cause others to know the true meaning.
Thus, O Brahmā King!

Because these noble ones, through their noble wisdom and vision, realize that the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena is inexpressible, they likewise treat both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena as such; yet, in order to cause others to realize and know them, they employ various conventional designations.
Then the Great Brahmā King asked the Bodhisattva Jewel-Light Radiance:
"How many sentient beings are able to understand such a profound and correct Dharma?
He replied:
“Brahmā King!
There are sentient beings with minds and mental factors who are able to understand such a profound and correct Dharma.
Brahmā King said:
"This illusory person has no substantial existence; from what, then, do these mental factors arise?
He replied:
"If one knows that the dharma-realm is neither existent nor non-existent, such a sentient being can understand this profound meaning."
At that time, the Brahma King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Bodhisattva Jewel-Radiance of Suchness is inconceivable; he has thoroughly penetrated such profound meanings.”
The Buddha said, “So it is! So it is!”
“Brahmā King!
As you have said, this Jewel Radiance of Wish-Fulfilling Power has already instructed you all to resolve to attain the Dharma of the Non-arising Endurance.

At that time, the Great Brahmā King and the assembly of Brahmās rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms in reverence, prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva Jewel Radiance of Wish-Fulfilling Power, and spoke these words:
"How rare! How rare!
Today we have had the good fortune to encounter this Great Being and have been able to hear the True Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Brahma King, saying:

"This Radiance of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel shall, in a future age, attain Buddhahood, with the name Ratnajvālāśrīgarbha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One."

When this chapter was being spoken, three thousand *koṭis* of bodhisattvas attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; eight thousand *koṭis* of devaputras, along with immeasurable and incalculable kings, ministers, and subjects, became free from dust and removed of defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, there were five billion bhikṣus in the assembly who were practicing the bodhisattva path but were on the verge of regressing from their resolve for enlightenment. When they heard the Bodhisattva Jewel-Light-Radiance (Ratnārci) expound this Dharma, they all attained firm, inconceivable, and fulfilled supreme vows; they once again gave rise to the mind of enlightenment and each offered his own robe as an offering to the Bodhisattva.
They further resolved upon the unsurpassed and superior aspiration, making this vow: "May our meritorious roots never regress, and may we dedicate them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Brahmā King!
These bhikṣus, by relying on these merits and practicing according to the teaching, shall attain realization after ninety great kalpas and transcend birth and death.”
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately bestowed upon them this prophecy:

"O bhikṣus, after thirty asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, you shall all become buddhas. The kalpa shall be named King of Invincible Radiance (Duṣpradharṣaprabhāsa-rāja), and the land shall be named Stainless Light (Vimalaprabhā). Simultaneously, you shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all shall bear the same title: King Adorned with the Ornament of Vows (Praṇidhāna-vyūha-alaṃkāra-rāja), fully endowed with the ten epithets."
“Brahmā King!
This subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* possesses great majestic power if it is correctly heard and upheld.
Suppose there were a person who, for hundreds of thousands of great kalpas, practiced the six pāramitās without skillful means;”

If there are good sons or good daughters who transcribe such a *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* and, for every half-month, recite it with single-minded devotion, this mass of merit will be such that the former merit does not equal even one hundredth part of it, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.
Brahmā King!
For this reason, I now command you to practice, recollect, uphold, and explain extensively to others. Why is this?

In the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, like a warrior entering the midst of battle, I did not begrudge my own body or life to circulate such a subtle and wondrous king of sutras, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining it for others.
Brahmā King!

It is like a wheel-turning sage king: as long as the king remains in the world, the seven treasures do not perish; but when the king passes away, all the seven treasures naturally vanish and come to an end.
Brahmā King!

If this subtle and wondrous King of Sutras, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, exists in the present world, the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure will not perish at all; yet if this sutra does not exist, it will vanish wherever it may be.

Therefore, one should single-mindedly listen to, receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this King of Sutras for others; one should encourage its transcription, practice the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), not begrudge body or life, and not shrink from weariness. This is the most supreme among merits, and my disciples should thus diligently cultivate and study it.

At that time, the Great Brahmā King, together with an immeasurable host of Brahmās, Śakra, the Four Kings, and all the yakṣas, rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We all vow to protect and propagate this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra; and should the Dharma-preacher encounter any difficulties, we shall dispel them, so that he may be endowed with manifold virtues, his physical strength and vitality fully restored, his eloquence unimpeded, and his body and mind at ease, while all those in the assembly who listen receive peace and happiness.

In whatever lands there may be famine, hostile bandits, or harm caused by non-human beings, we, the assembly of devas, shall provide protection for them all, ensuring that the people live in peace, security, and abundance, free from all unjust calamities; this is entirely through the power of us, the assembly of devas.
"If there are those who make offerings to this sutra, we shall likewise respectfully make offerings to them, no different from how we do for the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Great Brahma King, the assembly of Brahmas, and even the Four Heavenly Kings, yakṣas, and others:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!

You have heard this most profound and wondrous Dharma, and you are further able to resolve to protect and uphold this subtle and sublime King of Sutras. You shall obtain boundless and supreme merit and swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the Brahma Kings and the others received them with joy and reverence.

**Chapter Eleven: The Four Heavenly Kings Surveying Humans and Devas** *The Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra, King of Sutras* At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, and the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa all rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, King of Sutras, is constantly contemplated and observed by all Buddhas; it is revered by all Bodhisattvas; it is perpetually offered to by all devas and nāgas; and the hosts of devas always give rise to joy toward it. All the World-Protectors praise and extol it; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas alike uphold it together. It is able to clearly illuminate the palaces of all the devas, bestow supreme peace and happiness upon all sentient beings, and bring to rest the sufferings and afflictions of the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals. It can utterly eliminate all fears; all enemies shall immediately retreat and disperse; it can cause famine and evil times to become bountiful and prosperous; it can cause the pains of epidemics and diseases to be cleared away and healed; and all calamities and hundreds of thousands of sufferings shall be entirely extinguished.
"Bhagavān!
This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is able to provide such peace, security, benefit, and happiness for us. We pray that the Bhagavān will extensively proclaim it within this great assembly."

We four kings, together with our retinues, having heard this unsurpassed flavor of the nectar-like Dharma, find our vital strength fully restored, our majestic radiance increased, our diligence and valor enhanced, and our supernormal powers doubled in excellence.
"Bhagavān!

We four kings practice the True Dharma and constantly proclaim the True Dharma, transforming the world through the Dharma. We shall cause those devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kumbhāṇḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and all human kings to always transform the world with the True Dharma, warding off all evils. Furthermore, we shall cause all malevolent spirits and ghosts who suck the vital essence of humans and lack compassion to depart far away."
“World-Honored One!

We four kings, together with the twenty-eight yakṣa generals and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yakṣas, shall use our pure divine eyes, which surpass those of ordinary humans, to observe and protect this Jambudvīpa.”
World-Honored One!
For these reasons, we kings are called "Protectors of the World.

Furthermore, within this continent, if there are kings who are constantly harassed by enemy invaders, or if there is widespread famine, the prevalence of epidemics, and hundreds of thousands of such immeasurable calamities;
"World-Honored One!

We four kings shall reverently make offerings to this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. If there be any bhikṣu-dharma masters who receive, uphold, read, and recite it, we four kings will go together to awaken them and exhort such persons."

At that time, by the power of my supernormal knowledge and awakening, that Dharma Master shall go to that realm and widely proclaim and disseminate this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra; through the power of this sūtra, he shall cause all those immeasurable hundreds of thousands of afflictions, calamities, and misfortunes to be entirely dispelled.
“World-Honored One!
If there are human kings within whose realms a bhikṣu Dharma-master who upholds this sutra arrives, you should know that this sutra has also arrived in that kingdom.”
World-Honored One!

At that time, the king of that country should go to the place of the Dharma Master to listen to what he preaches; having heard it, he shall rejoice, reverently make offerings to that Dharma Master, and protect him with a profound heart so that he may be free from sorrow and affliction, as he expounds this sutra for the benefit of all.
"World-Honored One!

Because of this sutra, we four kings shall all with one mind protect this king and the people of his realm, causing them to be free from calamities and afflictions, and always to attain peace and security."
“World-Honored One!

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who uphold this sutra, may that king of men provide for their needs and offer them sustenance so that they lack for nothing. We, the four kings, shall ensure that both that sovereign and the people of his realm are all secure and free from calamities and afflictions.”
“World-Honored One!

If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and if a king of men provides them with offerings, respect, reverence, and praise, we shall cause that king to be the most honored and revered among all kings, and to be universally extolled by all other kings.”
Having heard this, the great assembly received and upheld it with joy.
*Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Fascicle Five.
*Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Fascicle Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śramaṇa Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Twelve: The Four Heavenly Kings Protecting the Nation (Part Six).

At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing that the Four Heavenly Kings had reverently made offerings to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* and were able to protect those who uphold this sutra, spoke in praise:
“Excellent! Excellent!

You Four Kings have, in the past, at the abodes of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, paid respectful offerings, honored and praised them, planted various roots of goodness, practiced the True Dharma, constantly preached the True Dharma, and transformed the world through the Dharma.”

Throughout the long night, you have constantly contemplated the benefit of all sentient beings, giving rise to great compassion and vowing to grant them peace and happiness; by these causes and conditions, you are now able to receive this supreme retribution.
If there is a king who reverently makes offerings to this most supreme sūtra, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, you all should diligently provide protection so that he may attain peace and security.

"You, the four kings and your immeasurable, innumerable retinues of hundreds of thousands of yakṣas who protect this sutra, are thereby protecting and upholding the true Dharma of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
"You four kings, along with the other hosts of devas and yakṣas, shall always achieve victory when fighting against the asuras;
if you are able to protect and uphold this sutra, by the power of this sutra, you will be able to eliminate all sufferings, hostile enemies, famine, and various epidemics."

Therefore, if you see members of the fourfold assembly who uphold, receive, read, and recite this King of Sutras, you should also diligently join together in protecting them, removing their decline and afflictions, and bestowing upon them peace and happiness.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra-rāja* is circulated in future ages—whether in kingdoms, cities, towns, villages, mountain forests, or wildernesses—at whatever place it may reach, if the king of that land listens to and receives this sutra with a sincere heart, praises and makes offerings to it, and furthermore provides for the fourfold assembly who uphold this sutra, deeply protecting them so they are freed from decline and affliction, then by these causes and conditions, I shall protect that king and all his people, causing them all to be peaceful and secure, far removed from sorrow and suffering, their lifespans increased, and their majesty and virtue fully perfected.
“World-Honored One!

If that king, upon seeing the fourfold assembly who uphold this sutra, honors and protects them as if they were his own parents and provides them with everything they require, we, the Four Kings, will constantly provide protection for them, ensuring that all sentient beings hold them in reverence.”

Therefore, we, together with immeasurable yakṣas and deities, shall follow wherever this King of Sūtras is disseminated and protect it in secret, ensuring there are no obstacles. We shall also guard and mind those kings and others who listen to this sūtra, removing their misfortunes and afflictions so that they may all be secure and at peace, and causing enemies and bandits from other regions to retreat and disperse.
World-Honored One, if there is a king who listens to this sutra, and the hostile enemies of neighboring states conceive such a thought as:
"We shall assemble the fourfold army to destroy that kingdom.
World-Honored One!

By the majestic spiritual power of this King of Sutras, at that time, neighboring enemies and other adversaries will come to invade and harass his realm, and many calamities and epidemics will spread.
When the king sees this, he will immediately array his fourfold army and set out for that country with the intent to punish them.

At that time, we, together with our retinues of immeasurable and boundless yakṣas and spirits, shall each conceal our forms to provide protection and assistance, causing those enemies to submit naturally so that they do not even dare to approach the borders of that kingdom, let alone engage in the punishment of war.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You Four Kings, you are indeed able to protect such a sutra as this.

Throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas in the past, I cultivated various ascetic practices, attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, realized all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), and now proclaim this Dharma."

If there is a king who upholds this sutra and reverently makes offerings to it, his decline and afflictions shall be eliminated and he shall be brought to peace and security; furthermore, he shall be protected within cities and villages, even to the point that all enemies and bandits will be driven back and dispersed. Moreover, he shall cause all kings throughout Jambudvīpa to forever be free from decline, distress, and strife.
"O Four Kings, you should know!

In this Jambudvīpa, there are eighty-four thousand cities and villages, and eighty-four thousand human kings who each enjoy various pleasures within their respective kingdoms and possess sovereign power. Their wealth and treasures are abundant for their enjoyment, and they do not encroach upon or seize one another's property. Receiving their retributions according to their past causes, they do not give rise to evil thoughts or greed for other nations; instead, they all develop a mind of few desires and seek the benefit and happiness of others, free from the sufferings of war, imprisonment, and the like."

The people of that land are naturally filled with love and joy; those above and below are harmonious and concordant like water and milk. They hold one another in mutual affection and esteem, delighting in playful pastimes, practicing compassion and humility, and increasing their roots of goodness.

By these causes and conditions, this Jambudvīpa will be peaceful, secure, and prosperous; its population will flourish, the earth will be fertile, and cold and heat will be harmoniously balanced. The seasons will not deviate from their proper order, the sun, moon, and stars will always move according to their courses without deficiency, and wind and rain will arrive at the appropriate times. Free from all calamities and misfortunes, resources and treasures will be abundant and overflowing. People will be free from stinginess and meanness, constantly practicing wise generosity, and being endowed with the ten virtuous actions (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*). When such people pass away, they will mostly be reborn in the heavens, increasing the number of celestial beings.
"Great King!
If in future ages there are kings who hear and accept this sutra, reverently make offerings to it, and uphold it, they shall be honored and praised by the fourfold assembly."

Furthermore, wishing to bring peace, happiness, and benefit to you and your retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yakṣas, that king should constantly listen to and receive this sublime King of Sutras. By obtaining the water of this True Dharma—the supreme flavor of ambrosia—your physical and mental strength shall increase, and your diligence, valor, merit, and majestic radiance shall all be made fully complete.
If these kings of men can listen to and receive this sutra with a sincere heart, it shall constitute a vast and rare offering—an offering made to me, Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
If one makes offerings to me, it is equivalent to making offerings to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
If one can make offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, one shall obtain an immeasurable and inconceivable mass of merit.

For these reasons, you all should protect that king, his queen, and their retinue, ensuring they are free from decline and affliction; furthermore, may the deities of the palace and the residence always enjoy peace and happiness. Their merit shall be inconceivable, and all the inhabitants of these lands shall likewise experience the various pleasures of the five senses, while all evil matters shall be utterly extinguished.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In future ages, if there should be a king who delights in hearing this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra*, desiring to protect himself, his queen, his princes, and even the various ladies of the inner palace, as well as his cities and palaces—so that they may all attain the foremost, inconceivable, supreme joy, tranquility, and peace; so that in this present life, his royal position may be exalted, sovereign, prosperous, and ever-increasing; and further, desiring to gather immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable masses of merit, such that within his own realm there shall be no enemies, nor any sorrows, afflictions, calamities, or misfortunes.”
World-Honored One!

Such a king of men should not be negligent or allow his mind to become distracted; he should give rise to reverence, sincerity, and profound earnestness to listen to and receive this most supreme King of Sutras.

When one wishes to listen, one should first adorn the most excellent palace—a spacious and prominent place held in high esteem by the king—sprinkling the ground with scented water and scattering various famous flowers. One should arrange a magnificent lion throne, embellishing it with all kinds of rare jewels, spreading various precious canopies, banners, and streamers, burning priceless incense, and performing various musical offerings.

At that time, the king should bathe himself thoroughly, anoint his body with fragrant perfumes, and put on fresh, clean garments and various necklaces. Sitting upon a low seat, he should not give rise to arrogance; relinquishing his position of sovereignty and abandoning all pride, he should listen to this King of Sutras with an upright mind and right mindfulness, regarding the Dharma Master as a Great Teacher.

Furthermore, he gave rise to a heart of compassion toward the queens, princes, court ladies, and retinues within the palace; they looked upon one another with joy, their countenances harmonious and their speech gentle, while a great sense of rapture filled his own body and mind.
One should form this thought:
"I have now attained inconceivable, supreme, and vast benefit by making abundant offerings to this King of Sutras.
Having made these preparations, upon seeing the Dharma Master arrive, one should give rise to a heart of devout reverence and yearning aspiration.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:
"One should not fail to welcome the Dharma Master in this manner.

At such a time, the King of Men should don pure, fresh, and clean robes, adorning himself with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments. Carrying a white parasol and fragrant flowers himself, he should fully arrange his military regalia and set forth a grand display of music. He should then step out from the city gates on foot to welcome the Dharma Master, directing his thoughts with reverent devotion as an act of auspiciousness."
"O Four Kings!
For what reason and by what causal conditions does that king of men personally perform such respectful offerings?

It is because with every step he takes—lifting his foot and setting it down—he is performing respectful offerings, serving, honoring, and respecting hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-Bhagavāns.
