Chapter Twenty-Two: The Devas and Yakṣas’ Protection and Sustenance (9) The Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra, King of Sutras, Chapter Twenty-Two: The Devas and Yakṣas’ Protection and Sustenance. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Auspicious Goddess, saying:

"If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who wish to present inconceivable, vast, and subtle articles of offering to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; and who wish to understand the profound sphere of practice of the Buddhas of the three periods of time—such persons should, with resolute and sincere hearts, wherever this King of Sutras may be located—in cities, towns, villages, or amidst mountains and marshes—extensively expound and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings."
Those who listen to the Dharma should eliminate distracted thoughts and listen with focused attention.
Then the World-Honored One, for the sake of that deva and the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to make inconceivable offerings to all Buddhas,
And furthermore seeks to understand the profound realm of all Tathāgatas,"
If one sees this most excellent *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* being expounded,
one should personally go to that place and arrive at the location where it is being taught.
This sutra is inconceivable, capable of generating all merits;
it liberates all sentient beings from the boundless great ocean of suffering.
As I contemplate this King of Sutras, it is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end.
Profound and unfathomable, it cannot be compared through analogy.
Even if one were to take the sands of the Ganges, the dust of the great earth, the waters of the ocean, the void of space,
and all the mountains and stones— none could serve as even a small fraction of a metaphor for it.
Those who wish to enter the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) should first listen to this sutra;
within the stūpa of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is profoundly and excellently established,
they shall behold me, the Honored Muni, inside that very stūpa.
With delightful and wondrous voices, they expound this sutra.
Because of this, for koṭis of eons, their number being inconceivable,
they are born among humans and devas, constantly experiencing supreme and sublime bliss.
If one listens to this sutra, one should cultivate such a thought:
"I have attained an inconceivable, boundless mass of merit.
Even if a great mass of fire were to fill a hundred yojanas;
To listen to this king of sutras, one would pass through even the most bitter hardships without complaint.
Once they have reached that dwelling place and heard such a sutra as this,
their karmic offenses will be extinguished and all evil dreams will be dispelled.
When malevolent stars and various portents, Witchcraft,
and malevolent spirits encounter this sutra, All evils shall be cast aside.
One should prepare a magnificent and lofty seat, Pure and exquisite like a lotus flower.
The Dharma Master sits upon it, like a great dragon seated;
having sat there in composure, he preaches this profound sutra,
transcribing it, reciting and upholding it, and further explaining its meaning.
The Dharma Master leaves this seat and departs for other regions;
yet within this high throne, his supernormal powers manifest in manifold ways.
Some see the image of the Dharma Master still remaining upon the high throne.
At times one may see the World-Honored One, as well as the various Bodhisattvas;
some appear in the form of Samantabhadra, others like Mañjuśrī;
or one may see the Honored Maitreya, seated upon a lofty throne.
Or one may see rare and wondrous signs, as well as the forms of various devas;
having briefly beheld their countenances and deportment, they suddenly vanish again.
All auspiciousness is accomplished, and whatever is done accords with one's wishes.
All merits are completely fulfilled; thus has the World-Honored One spoken.
Possessing the most excellent renown, one is able to extinguish all afflictions;
thieves from foreign lands are all eliminated, and one always attains victory in battle.
All evil dreams shall vanish, and all poisons and harms shall be dispelled;
the sins committed through the three karmas shall be extinguished by the power of this sutra.
Throughout this Jambudvīpa, its fame shall fill every corner.
All bonds of enmity and resentment are entirely cast aside.
Should any enemies approach, they shall retreat and disperse upon hearing his name;
without the need for the movement of weapons, both armies shall give rise to joy.
Brahmā, Lord Śakra, and the four World-Protecting Kings;
the Vajra Yakṣas and the Great General Vijñānagupta;
the Nāga King Anavatapta and Sāgara.
The Kinnara music gods, the Sura and Garuda lords;
the Great Goddess Sarasvatī, together with the Great Auspicious Goddess;
these and other preeminent deities, each leading their respective hosts of devas—
Constantly making offerings to all Buddhas and the inconceivable Dharma Jewel,
they always give rise to a heart of joy and maintain reverence for the sutras.
All these hosts of devas together contemplate thus:
Surveying all those who cultivate merit, they spoke thus together:
"One should observe these sentient beings; they all possess great merit.
By the power of their roots of goodness and diligence, they shall be reborn in our heaven in the future."
To hear this profound sutra, you have come here with a reverent heart;
To make offerings at the dharmic caitya, out of respect for the True Dharma.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, you bring them great benefit.
Regarding this profound sutra, one can become a vessel for the Dharma-treasure.
Those who enter this dharma-gate are able to enter into the nature of phenomena;
regarding this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, one should listen and receive it with a sincere heart.
"This person has once made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas;
by virtue of those roots of goodness, they have been able to hear this sutra.
Thus spoke the lords of the devas and the goddesses of great eloquence.
Together with the auspicious goddess Śrī, the hosts of the Four Great Kings,
and countless yakṣas— valiant and possessed of supernatural powers—
they shall constantly come from each of the four directions to provide protection.
The Sun and Moon, Śakra, Lord of Devas; the deities of Wind, Water, and Fire;
Vaiśravaṇa, Mahābhuja; Yama, Vāgīśvara, and the rest;
all the World-Protectors, valiant and endowed with majestic power;
They shall protect those who uphold this sutra, never leaving them by day or night:
the Great Powerful Yakṣa Kings, Nārāyaṇa and Īśvara;
led by Saṃjñeya, these twenty-eight yakṣas.
A further hundred thousand yakṣas, possessing great power through their supernormal faculties,
will constantly come to protect this person in places of terror.
The Vajra Yakṣa King, together with his retinue of five hundred;
The great assembly of bodhisattvas constantly comes to protect this person.
The Yakṣa King Ratnarāja, as well as Pūrṇabhadra;
Kāntārakṛtya, Kiṃpila, Piṅgala, and Bheruṇḍaka.
These yakṣa kings, each with a retinue of five hundred,
shall all come together to protect those who see or hear this sutra.
Citrasena, the gandharva, and Veṇu-rāja, ever victorious in battle;
Maṇikaṇṭha and Nīlakaṇṭha, together with King Bṛhaspati;
Mahāviśeṣa and Mahākāla, Subhadra and Kheṭa;
Pañcika and Eḍamūka, as well as Mahābhaga.
The Minor Stream and Dharmapāla, as well as the Monkey King;
Sūcīroma and Divākara, and Ratakeśa—all came to protect him.
The Great Stream, Nakula, Candana, and Kāmavara;
Śaila and Himavat, as well as Sātāgira;
all possessing great supernormal powers, heroic, fierce, and endowed with mighty strength—
upon seeing one who upholds this sutra, they shall all come to provide protection.
Anavatapta and Sāgara; Mucilinda and Nanda, as well as Upananda;
Among these hundreds of thousands of nāgas, They possess supernormal powers and majestic virtue.
Together they shall protect those who uphold this sutra, never departing from them day or night:
Vemacitra, Rāhu, Vepacitti; Mucilinda, Śaṃbara, Mahābāhu, and Nandika.
As well as other Sura kings, together with countless hosts of devas—
mighty, courageous, and valiant— all come to protect this person.
The goddess Hārītī, along with her five hundred yakṣa followers;
Whether that person is awake or asleep, they shall always come to protect them.
Caṇḍā and Caṇḍālī, Yakṣa and Yakṣiṇī;
Kuntī and Kuṭadantī, who suck the vital essence of living beings.
Such hosts of deities, possessing great power and supernormal faculties,
shall constantly protect and uphold those who recite this sutra, never departing from them day or night.
Foremost among them is the goddess Sarasvatī, along with immeasurable celestial maidens.
Śrī-devī at their head, together with all their other retinues;
this goddess of the great earth, the deities of fruit-bearing groves and forests;
the tree spirits, the river spirits, and the various deities of the caityas.
Thus all these celestial deities, their hearts filled with great joy,
will all come to protect those who read and recite this sutra.
Seeing those who uphold the sutra, they shall increase their lifespan, physical appearance, and strength.
With majestic radiance and merit, adorned with sublime marks,
may all calamitous portents of the stars and constellations, as well as the misfortunes that befall this person,
and all evil omens seen in dreams, be entirely extinguished.
This great earth goddess is firm and possesses majestic power;
by the power of this sutra, she is always fully satisfied with the flavor of the Dharma.
Even if the earth’s essence were to flow downward for more than a hundred yojanas, [it would still be sustained].
The Earth Deity causes the essence of the earth to rise upward, nourishing and moistening the great earth.
This earth is sixty-eight hundred million *yojanas* thick;
from its surface down to the limit of the vajra, she causes the essence of the earth to rise throughout.
By hearing this King of Sūtras, one obtains a great mass of merit;
it enables all the hosts of devas to receive its benefits,
and further causes the hosts of devas to possess majestic power and radiance.
Always joyful and ever at peace, they abandon all signs of decay.
Within this Southern Continent, the deities of forests, fruits, and crops—
through the power of this sutra— shall always find joy in their hearts.
The sprouts and fruits have all reached maturity, and wondrous flowers bloom everywhere;
the fruits are abundant and flourishing, filling the great earth.
All the fruit-bearing trees, as well as the various groves and gardens;
All produce exquisite flowers, their fragrances perpetually sweet and pervasive.
Among the various grasses and trees, all bring forth subtle and wondrous blossoms;
they also bear sweet and delicious fruits, filling every place to overflowing.
In this Jambudvīpa, immeasurable nāga maidens,
their hearts filled with great joy, all entered the ponds together.
There they planted padmas and puṇḍarikas.
Blue and white lotuses fill the ponds everywhere;
through the power of this sutra, the void is pure and without obscuration;
clouds and mist are all dispelled, and all darkness becomes radiant light.
The rising sun emits a thousand rays, its stainless flames pure and clear;
by the power of this King of Sūtras, its radiance flows and encircles the four continents.
By the majestic power of this sūtra, the Son of Heaven is assisted.
All are made of Jambūnada gold, serving as the palaces.
When the Sun Deity first rises, he beholds this continent with joy;
with his great radiance, he constantly shines everywhere throughout its entirety.
Within this great earth, all lotus ponds,
when touched by the light of the sun, will without exception blossom.
In this Jambudvīpa, the fields, fruits, and medicinal herbs—
May all beings be brought to full maturity, filling the entire earth.
By the power of this sutra, wherever the sun and moon shine,
the stars shall not deviate from their courses, and wind and rain shall follow their proper seasons.
Throughout this Jambudvīpa, all lands shall be prosperous and joyful;
wherever this sutra resides, it will be far more excellent than other regions.
Wherever this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* scripture is disseminated, [it shall be so].
"Those who are able to lecture upon or recite it shall all obtain the blessings described above.

At that time, the Great Auspicious Goddess and the various devas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they single-mindedly protected this King of Sutras and those who uphold it, ensuring they remain free from sorrow and affliction and always attain peace and happiness.

23. Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecy (9). The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Three: The Bestowal of Prophecy. At that time, after the Tathāgata had extensively expounded the Dharma within the great assembly, he desired to bestow the prophecy of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the Bodhisattva Subhaketu and his two sons, Rajaketu and Rajaprabha.

At that time, ten thousand devaputras, with Varaprabha as their leader, together came from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and listened to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, saying:

"In a future age, after immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas have passed, you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi in a world called Golden Radiance. You shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā deva-manuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named King of the Golden Jewel Mountain, appearing in the world.
At that time, after this Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, all his teachings shall likewise be extinguished."

At that time, his eldest son, named Silver Banner (Rūpyadhvaja), shall succeed him in this world-system to fill the seat of Buddhahood. At that time, the world-system shall change its name to Pure Banner (Vimaladhvaja). He shall become a Buddha, known as Golden Banner Light Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, after this Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, all his teachings shall also completely perish.

The second son, Silver Light (Rūpyaprabha), shall succeed him in the Buddha’s place and attain Buddhahood within this very realm; he shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Suvarṇaprabhāsa.

At that time, ten thousand devaputras, having heard that the three great beings had received their predictions and further having heard this most excellent King of Sūtras, gave rise to joy in their hearts; they became pure and stainless, like space.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that the roots of goodness of these ten thousand devaputras had matured, immediately bestowed upon them the prediction of great bodhi:

"O devaputras, in a future age, after immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas have passed, you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the world-system called Most Victorious Indra-Exalted Banner. You shall be of one and the same lineage and bear one and the same name—Pure Face and Utpala Fragrant Mountain—and shall be endowed with the ten titles. In this manner, ten thousand Buddhas shall appear in succession in the world."
At that time, the deity of the Bodhi tree addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

These ten thousand devaputras have come from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the place where the Buddha is in order to hear the Dharma; why has the Tathāgata immediately bestowed upon them the prediction that they shall attain Buddhahood?”
"Blessed One!

I have never heard that these sons of the gods have fully practiced the six pāramitās or performed difficult asceticisms—giving away their hands, feet, heads, eyes, marrow, and brains; their kinsmen, wives, and children; their elephants, horses, and carriages; their slaves, servants, and attendants; their palaces, gardens, and groves; and their gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, jade, conch shells, food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine—just as other immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas have done by offering all manner of requisites to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas in the past. Such bodhisattvas each pass through immeasurable and boundless kalpas before they finally receive the prediction of enlightenment."
“World-Honored One!

By what causes and conditions have these sons of heaven cultivated such superior practices and planted such roots of goodness that, having come from those heavens to hear the Dharma for a brief moment, they immediately receive their prediction of enlightenment?”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me and sever the net of my doubts.
The Buddha told the tree deity:
"O Good Goddess!
As you have said, all [who receive predictions] do so only after having diligently practiced with great hardship based on the causes and conditions of supreme and wondrous roots of goodness.

These sons of the gods, having abandoned the pleasures of the five desires within their sublime celestial palaces, have come here to hear this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra*. Having heard the Dharma, they have conceived a profound and reverent mind toward this sūtra, like pure lapis lazuli free from all blemishes. Furthermore, because they have heard the account of the predictions for these three great bodhisattvas—and due to the causes and conditions of the vows and right practices they cultivated over the distant past—I now bestow predictions upon them all that in a future age they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, that tree deity rejoiced and accepted it with faith.
Chapter 24: Removing Disease (9). *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Four: Removing Disease. The Buddha addressed the Bodhi-tree deity, the virtuous goddess:
"Listen attentively!"
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well.
I shall now explain for you the causes and conditions of the original vows of these ten thousand devaputras.
“Good Goddess!

In the past, immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Ratnaśikhin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
“Good Goddess!

After that World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma had ceased, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a king named Devendraprabha, who constantly transformed the people through the True Dharma, just like parents.”

In this king’s realm, there was an elder named Jālinīprabha who was well-versed in the science of medicine and skillfully mastered the eight branches of healing; he was able to cure all the ailments and sufferings of the sick, restoring balance to the four great elements whenever they were disturbed.
"Good Woman Devī!

At that time, the elder Jālinīprabha had an only son named Jalavāhana, who was handsome in appearance and pleasing for all to behold. He was of keen intelligence and nature, profoundly skilled in all treatises, and there was nothing he did not master, whether in writing, painting, calculation, or seals."

At that time, within the king’s realm, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of living beings who all encountered an epidemic; oppressed by manifold sufferings, they lacked even a single thought of joy.
"Good Woman Devī!

At that time, the elder’s son Flowing Water (Jalavāhana), seeing these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings suffering from various ailments, gave rise to a heart of great compassion and thought to himself:

'Immeasurable sentient beings are oppressed by extreme sufferings. Although my father, the elder, is skilled in medical formulas and has mastered the eight branches of medicine, capable of treating all diseases and the increase or decrease of the four elements, he is already advanced in years, decrepit, frail, and weak; he can only move forward with the support of a staff and is no longer able to go to cities, towns, or villages to rescue those from their suffering.'"

"Now there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who have all encountered grave illnesses, yet none can save them. I shall now go to my father, the Great Physician, to consult him regarding the secret methods of medical prescriptions for curing diseases. Once I have mastered them, I shall go to cities, towns, and villages to rescue sentient beings from their various ailments, enabling them to attain peace and happiness throughout the long night."

At that time, having formed this thought, the son of the elder went at once to his father’s place. He prostrated himself at his feet in salutation, joined his palms with reverence, and stood to one side. He then addressed his father with a verse, requesting:
“Compassionate father, please have pity on me; I wish to save sentient beings.
I now request the various medical prescriptions; I pray you will explain them to me.”
How does the body decay and disintegrate? How do the great elements undergo increase and decrease?
At what time do various diseases arise?
By consuming food and drink in what manner can one obtain peace and happiness?
How can one cause the internal fires within the body not to diminish?
Sentient beings have four ailments—wind, bile, phlegm, and their combination; how are these to be treated?
When does the wind disorder arise?
When does the heat disorder manifest?
When does the phlegm-mucus become agitated?
"When will they all assemble and be born?
Then, having heard his son's request, the elder replied to him with a verse:
"I shall now rely upon the methods for treating illness as used by the ancient seers."
I shall explain this to you in due order; listen well, for it is for the salvation of sentient beings.
Three months constitute the spring season; three months are called summer;
three months are called autumn; and three months are known as winter.
This is based on one year, explained by dividing it into groups of three;
with two [periods] making one section, there thus become six seasons in a year.
The first two are the time of flowers; the third and fourth are called the heat season.
The fifth and sixth months are called the rainy season; the seventh and eighth are said to be autumn;
the ninth and tenth are the cold season, and the final two are named for ice and snow.
Having understood these distinctions, administer medicine so as not to cause error.
At such times, one should regulate the intake of food and drink;
by allowing it to be digested within the belly, no manifold ailments shall arise.
When the seasonal energies shift and change, the four great elements undergo transformation.
At this time, lacking the resources for medicine, one will inevitably give rise to the suffering of illness.
A physician understands the four seasons and further knows the six periods;
he is clear and proficient in the seven constituents of the body, administering food and medicine without error.
That is to say, the realm of taste, blood, and flesh, Fat, bone, marrow, and brain;
when disease enters within these, Do you know whether it can be cured?
There are four distinct types of disease, Namely: wind, heat, phlegm, and mucus.
And regarding the combined disorders of the humors, one should know the times when they are provoked:
phlegm (kapha) is provoked during spring; wind (vāta) diseases arise within summer;
yellow-fever (pitta) increases in autumn; and all three arise together during the winter season.
In spring, consume astringent, hot, and pungent; in summer, unctuous, hot, salty, and sour;
in autumn, cold, sweet, and unctuous; in winter, sour, astringent, unctuous, and sweet.
Within these four seasons, one should take medicine and food accordingly.
If one relies on such flavors, no illnesses will have cause to arise.
Illness after eating arises from phlegm; when the food is being digested, it arises from heat;
after digestion has occurred, it arises from wind—one must recognize the illness according to these stages.
Having identified the source of the ailment, one prescribes medicine according to the disease;
even if the symptoms differ, one must first treat the root.
For wind disorders, oily substances are taken; for heat disorders, purgation is beneficial.
For phlegm disorders, one should induce vomiting; for those where [phlegm] is accumulated, three medicines are required.
When wind, heat, and phlegm are all present, this is called "accumulation";
although one knows when the illness arose, one must observe its fundamental nature.
Having observed and understood this, one administers medicine according to the proper time;
when food, drink, and medicine are applied without error, such a person is called a skilled physician.
Furthermore, one should know the eight branches of medical science, which encompass all therapeutic methods.
If one is clear and proficient in this, one may heal the ailments of the multitude:
namely, injuries from needle-accidents and wounds, physical diseases as well as those caused by spirits;
malignant poisons and childhood illnesses, extending years of life and increasing vital strength.
First observe their physical form, speech, and temperament;
then inquire about their dreams to distinguish between wind, heat, and phlegm disorders.
One who is emaciated, has little hair on the head, and whose mind lacks stability—
One who speaks much, dreams of flying, and has white hair growing in youth,
as well as excessive sweating and anger, and whose intelligence perceives fire in dreams—
such a person is of the wind-nature (vātika). One who is wise and sees fire in dreams— such a person is of the heat-nature (paittika).
The mind is settled and the body is upright; one’s thoughts are discerning and the head feels oily.
To dream of water or white objects—know that these are the characteristics of phlegm (śleṣman).
These natures may arise collectively, appearing either as two or all three together.
Whichever [defilement] is present in excess, one should know that to be its nature.
Having understood this fundamental nature, one administers medicine according to the illness;
only when one verifies the absence of signs of death can one be called capable of saving a person.
When the sense faculties perceive objects perversely, when the eminent physician gives rise to pride,
and when kinsmen harbor anger— know these to be signs corresponding to death.
When the left eye changes to white, the tongue turns black, and the bridge of the nose slants;
The lobes of his ears differ from those of ordinary men, and his lower lip hangs down.
The harītakī fruit possesses all six tastes;
it can eliminate all diseases and is the king among medicines that require no dietary restrictions.
Furthermore, the three fruits and the three pungents are easily found among various medicinal herbs;
sugar, honey, ghee, and milk can cure many diseases.
As for all other medicinal substances, they may be added according to the specific ailment.
First arouse a heart of compassion, and do not scheme for wealth or profit.
I have already explained to you the essential matters for treating illness;
by using this to save sentient beings, you shall obtain boundless fruit.

“Good Woman Devī! At that time, the elder’s son, Flowing Water, personally questioned his father regarding the essentials of the eight branches of medicine: the increase and decrease of the four elements, the variations of the seasons, and the methods for administering medicinal herbs. Having thoroughly mastered these, he considered himself capable of curing all manner of ailments. He then traveled everywhere to cities, towns, and villages; wherever there were hundreds of thousands of millions of beings suffering from illness, he went to their side, comforted them with kind words, and spoke thus:
‘I am a physician!’”
"I am a physician!
Well-versed in prescriptions and medicines, I shall now treat your many ailments so that they may all be cured.
Thus spoke the goddess Kṣemadattā.

At that time, when the multitude heard the kind words of consolation from the elder’s son and his promise to treat their illnesses, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who were afflicted with extremely grave diseases felt their bodies and minds leap with joy upon hearing these words; they experienced what they had never known before.
By this cause and condition, all their illnesses and sufferings were completely eliminated; their physical strength was restored and they returned to their original state.
Good Goddess!

At that time, there were again immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings whose illnesses were so profound and severe as to be difficult to treat; they went together to the place where the son of the elder was and earnestly requested his medical treatment.
At that time, the son of the elder immediately administered the wondrous medicine, and they all received relief and were cured.
O Goddess of Goodness!
Within this kingdom, the son of the elder treated the sickness and suffering of hundreds of thousands of millions of beings, and all were completely healed.

Chapter 25: The Son of a Householder, Flowing Water (9). *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Five: The Son of a Householder, Flowing Water. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhi-tree goddess:
"O Good Goddess!

At that time, the elder’s son Flowing Water, in times past, within the realm of King Sovereign Light of Heaven, treated all the ailments and sufferings of sentient beings, causing them to recover and attain peaceful and secure happiness.
At that time, because their illnesses had been cured, the sentient beings cultivated many meritorious deeds, practiced extensive acts of giving, and enjoyed themselves.
They then went together to where the son of the elder was, all conceiving feelings of reverence and saying:
"Excellent!..."
Excellent, noble son of a great householder!

You are truly skilled at cultivating meritorious deeds and increasing our peace, security, and lifespan. You are indeed a Great Physician-King of compassion, a Bodhisattva who is profoundly proficient in medicine and excels at healing the immeasurable sufferings and illnesses of sentient beings.
Thus he praised her, his voice resounding throughout the city and its suburbs.
"O Good Woman Devī!
At that time, the wife of the elder’s son was named Jaladhārāgarbha, and she had two sons: the first was named Jalapūrṇa;..."
The second was named Water-Treasury (*Jalagarbha*).

At that time, Flowing Water took his two sons and traveled gradually through cities, towns, and villages, passing through deep and perilous places within the empty wilderness. There he saw various birds and beasts—jackals, wolves, foxes, monkeys, vultures, and eagles—who feed on flesh and blood; they all fled and flew away in one direction.
At that time, the son of the elder had this thought:
"For what reason are these birds and beasts all flying and running in one direction?
I should follow after them for a moment to observe."
He then followed along and saw a great pond named Wild Growth; its water was nearly exhausted, yet within this pool there were many fish.
Upon seeing this, Shrotasvatī gave rise to a heart of great compassion.
At that time, a tree spirit manifested half of its body and spoke these words:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
Son of good family,
since you possess the true meaning of the name "Flowing Water," you should have compassion for these fish and provide them with water.
There are two causes and conditions for which one is named "Flowing Water":
first, the ability to flow with water; second, the ability to provide water.
You should now act in accordance with this name.
At that time, Flowing Water asked the tree deity,
"How many heads do these fish have?
The tree deity replied:
"Ten thousand in total.
"O Virtuous Goddess!
When the merchant’s son heard this number, his compassion increased all the more."

At that time, this great pond was scorched by the sun until little water remained; these ten thousand fish were approaching the threshold of death. As they writhed and turned their bodies, they saw the elder and felt a sense of hope, following him with their gaze and never once averting their eyes.
At that time, having witnessed these events, the son of the elder galloped toward the four quarters, seeking water, but was ultimately unable to find any.
Looking again toward one side, he saw a great tree; he immediately climbed it, broke off branches and leaves, and fashioned them into a cooling shade.
He further investigated from where the water in the pond came.

Searching without ceasing, he saw a great river named Jalamukha. At that time, by the side of this river, there were fishermen who, for the sake of catching fish, had diverted the water at a steep and dangerous point upstream so that it would not flow downstream; the breach they had made was extremely difficult to repair.
He then thought to himself:

"This cliff is deep and precipitous; even if a hundred thousand people were to work for three months, they might not succeed in cutting through it, let alone a single person like myself being able to accomplish the task."

Then the son of the elder quickly returned to his native city and went to the place where the Great King was. Prostrating himself at the King’s feet, he withdrew to stand to one side and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words:

“For the sake of the Great King’s realm and its people, I have treated various ailments until all were made secure and at ease. As I traveled by stages, I arrived at a desolate marsh where I saw a pond called Wild Growth. Its waters were nearly exhausted, and ten thousand fish were being scorched by the sun; they would soon die. I only pray that the Great King will look upon them with compassion and pity, and send twenty great elephants to go and carry water for a moment to save the lives of those fish, just as I have preserved the lives of the sick.”
At that time, the Great King immediately commanded his ministers to quickly provide this Elephant-King to the Physician-King.
Having received the King’s command, the ministers said to the son of the elder:
"Excellent, Great Being!"
"Virtuous One, you may now go yourself to the elephant stables and select twenty elephants at your discretion to benefit sentient beings and bring them peace and happiness.

At that time, Flowing Water and his two sons took the twenty elephants and borrowed many leather bags from a wine shop; they went to the place where the water was being diverted, filled the bags with water, and had the elephants carry it to the pond, pouring it into the pool until the water was completely full and restored to its former state.
“Good Woman Devī!
At that time, as the son of the elder paced about and gazed at the four sides of the pond, those many fish likewise followed him, moving along the bank.”
Then the son of the elder thought again:
"For what reason do these many fish follow me?
They must surely be tormented by the fire of hunger and wish to seek food from me; I shall now give it to them."
At that time, the elder’s son Shrotas said to his son:

"Take one of the elephants of greatest strength and go quickly to our home to inform your father, the elder. Gather all the edible things in the house, including the portions set aside for your parents to eat, as well as the portions for your wife, children, and servants; you may bring them all here."

At that time, having received their father’s instructions, the two sons mounted the largest elephant and proceeded swiftly to their home. Arriving at the place where their grandfather was, they related the aforementioned matters.
They gathered all the edible items from the house, placed them upon the elephant, and quickly returned to their father’s location, arriving at the edge of that pond.

At that time, when Flowing Water saw his son arrive, his body and mind leaped with joy; he then took the cakes and scattered them throughout the pond, and once the fish had received the food, they were all fully satiated.
He then thought:
"I have now given food to these fish so that they may live; I vow that in future lives I shall provide the food of Dharma to sustain and relieve the infinite.
He further reflected:
"In the past, while I was in a secluded forest, I saw a bhikṣu reciting a Mahāyāna sūtra that expounds the profound essentials of the Dharma of the twelvefold dependent origination.
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtra:
'If there are sentient beings who, at the time of their death, hear the name of the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin, they shall immediately be reborn in the heavens.'"
"I shall now expound for these ten thousand fish the profound twelvefold dependent origination, and I shall also proclaim the name of the Buddha Ratnaśikhin.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of people in Jambudvīpa: first, those who have deep faith in the Mahāyāna; second, those who lack faith and disparage it. I shall also cause their confidence to increase."
At that time, the son of the elder thought to himself:
"I shall enter the pond and preach the profound and wondrous Dharma for the sake of the fish.
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered the water and proclaimed:
Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān of the past, Ratnaśikhin.
When this Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, he made this vow:
"May all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions who hear my name at the time of their death be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven after they pass away."
At that time, Flowing Water further expounded this profound and wondrous Dharma for the fish in the pond: "Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. That is to say:

with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair arise."

With the cessation of this, that ceases: namely, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease; with the cessation of aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus, this entire mass of pure suffering is utterly extinguished.
Having spoken this Dharma, he further proclaimed the *dhāraṇī* associated with the twelve links of dependent origination, saying:
"Tadyathā vi-jñe..."
vicarṇi vicarṇi saṃsargini
saṃsajini saṃsajini virini
Vīriṇi vīriṇi svāhā tadyathā.
namini namini namini saciṇi!
Kill the peacock!
Kill the peacock! Spharisa! Spharisa!
Sapariśānti svāhā.
Tadyathā: vaidani.
Vedani vedani trishnini.
Ciriṣiṇi ciriṣiṇi upadani upadani.
Upadine svāhā tadyathā.
Bhavini bhavini bhavini jātini.
jatiṃ jatiṃ jamaniṃniṃ
"Jāmanini jāmanini svāhā.
At that time, as the World-Honored One recounted this past karmic connection of the elder’s son to the great assembly, the multitude of humans and devas marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, each in their respective place, spoke with one voice in unison:
"Excellent, Honored Śākyamuni! You have proclaimed this sublime Dharma and vidyā-mantra;
it generates merit and eliminates all evils, corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination."
We, too, shall recite mantras to protect such a Dharma;
should there be those who give rise to opposition or fail to comply with it,
their heads shall split into seven pieces, just like the tips of a *lāngakha* flower.
In the presence of the Buddha, we shall together recite this mantra:

"Tadyathā | Hirimī | Kṣānti-gaṇṭhāri | Caṇḍālidṛśe | Sāvarī | Śikhivarī | Purabhuve gu-gu-mati | Kṣīramati | Dṛḍhamukhe | Jūrupe | Mūrupe | Kutamūru-gaṇṭhe | Dhuru dhuru | Vire | Ene sise ḍat-tu-ha | Huṇḍa-huṇḍa | Oṣṭharī | Utsaṭarā-vati | Apsaravati-padmavati | Kusumavati | Svāhā. The Buddha addressed the Good Goddess:
"At that time, the elder’s son Flowing Water and his two sons, having provided water and food for the fish in that pond and preached the Dharma to them, returned home together."
Later, at another time, the merchant’s son, Flowing Water, was attending a gathering where various musical performances were provided; he became intoxicated with wine and lay down to sleep.
At that moment, ten thousand fish simultaneously passed away and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where they had this thought:
"By what causes and conditions of wholesome karma have we been born in this heaven?"
They then said to one another:

"Previously, within Jambudvīpa, we fell among the animals and together took birth as fish. The elder’s son, Jalavāhana, gave us water and food, and further expounded for our sake the profound Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination and the dhāraṇī. He also invoked the name of the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin; by these causes and conditions, we have been able to be born in this heaven."
"Therefore, we should now all go to that son of a householder to repay his kindness and make offerings.
At that time, the ten thousand devaputras vanished from the heavens and arrived at the place of the Great King of Physicians in Jambudvīpa.

At that time, the son of the elder was sleeping peacefully atop a high tower. Then, ten thousand devaputras together placed ten thousand pearl necklaces at his face, another ten thousand at his feet, another ten thousand at his right side, and another ten thousand at his left side. They rained down *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers until they reached his knees; their radiance shone everywhere, and various celestial music produced wondrous sounds, causing all those in Jambudvīpa who were asleep to awaken, and the elder’s son, Jalavāhana, likewise awoke from his slumber.

At that time, after making their offerings, the ten thousand devaputras soared away through the air. Throughout the kingdom of King Devendraprabha, they rained down exquisite celestial lotuses everywhere. These devaputras then returned to their original location, where they rained down various celestial flowers upon a pool in a desolate marsh; thereupon they vanished and returned to their celestial palaces, enjoying the pleasures of the five senses with sovereign ease as they pleased.
When King Divyendraprabha reached the break of dawn, he asked his ministers:
"For what reason did such a rare and auspicious omen suddenly appear last night, emitting such great radiance?"
The minister replied, "Great King,
you should know that hosts of devas have rained forty thousand pearl necklaces and celestial māndārava flowers upon the house of the elder’s son, Jalavāhana, so that they accumulate up to his knees."
The king said to his minister,
"Go to the house of the elder and summon his son.
Having received the command, the great minister went immediately to that house and, proclaiming the king's decree, summoned the elder’s son.
Then the son of the elder went to the king's presence.
The king asked,
"For what reason did you manifest such a rare and auspicious omen last night?"

The son of the elder said, "As I reflect upon it, these must surely be the various fish from within that pond who, as stated in the sutras, were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven after their lives ended; they have come now to repay my kindness, and thus manifest such a rare and wondrous sign."
The King asked,
"How do you know this?
Flowing Water replied:
"The King should dispatch a messenger along with my two sons to that pond to verify its reality or falsehood: are those ten thousand fish dead or alive?

Upon hearing these words, the King immediately dispatched the messenger and his sons toward the edge of the pond. There they saw that the pond was filled with many *mandārava* flowers, accumulated in great heaps, and all the fish were dead. Having seen this, they returned in haste and related the matter extensively to the King.
Having heard this, the king felt great joy in his heart and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhi-tree goddess:
"O virtuous goddess!
"You should now know that the elder’s son Flowing Water of former times was none other than myself;
the elder Sustainer of Water was the Elder Subtle Banner;
and those two sons—the elder, Water Full, was Silver Banner, and the younger, Water Treasury, was Silver Light."
That King Sovereign Light of Heaven was none other than you, the Bodhi-tree deity;
the ten thousand fish were none other than the ten thousand devaputras.

Because in the past I rescued those fish with water, gave them food until they were full, and for their sake expounded the profound twelvefold dependent origination along with the corresponding dhāraṇī-mantra, and further invoked the name of that Ratnaśikhin Buddha, they have attained birth in the heavens by virtue of these roots of goodness. They have now come to me to joyfully listen to the Dharma.
"I shall bestow upon all of you the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and proclaim your respective names.
O Goddess of Goodness!

Just as I, in the past, while wandering through the various realms of existence within saṃsāra, extensively benefited others, so now I cause immeasurable sentient beings to successively achieve unsurpassed enlightenment and grant them their predictions. You all should diligently seek liberation and not be negligent."

At that time, having heard this teaching, the great assembly all attained awakening and understanding; realizing that only through great compassion to protect and rescue all beings and through the diligent practice of asceticism can one realize unsurpassed bodhi, they all gave rise to profound resolve, receiving it with faith and joy.
The Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra, King of Sutras, Scroll Nine;
The Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra, King of Sutras, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śramaṇa Yijing by Imperial Command.

Chapter 26: Sacrificing the Body (10) At that time, after the World-Honored One had already related to the great assembly these past causes and conditions of ten thousand devaputras, he further addressed the Bodhi-tree goddess and the entire multitude:

"In the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I did not merely bestow water and food to save the lives of those fish; I even sacrificed my own beloved body. You should all observe the causes and conditions of such events together."

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—the most supreme and most venerable one above and below heaven—whose hundred-thousandfold radiance illumines the worlds of the ten directions, who possesses all-knowledge and whose merits are perfected, led the bhikṣus and the great assembly to the village of Pañcāla and proceeded to a certain forest.
The ground was level and even, free from thorns and brambles, and covered everywhere with fragrant flowers and soft grass.
The Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda,
"You may spread a seat for me beneath this tree."
Then Ānanda, having received the instruction and spread the seats, said:
"World-Honored One!
The seats have been prepared; may the Noble One know the proper time."
At that time, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged upon his seat, straightening his body and establishing right mindfulness, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you wish to see the original relics of that Bodhisattva who practiced austerities in the past?"
The bhikṣus said, "We wish to see it.

The World-Honored One then pressed down upon the ground with his hand, adorned with the marks and signs of a hundred merits. At that moment, the great earth shook in six ways and split open; suddenly, a stūpa made of the seven treasures emerged, its summit adorned with nets of various jewels.
When the great assembly saw this, they were struck with wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, paid homage, circumambulated it to the right, returned to his original seat, and addressed Ānanda:
"You may open the door of this caitya."
Then Ānanda opened the door and saw a casket made of the seven precious gems, adorned with various rare jewels. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, there is a casket of the seven precious gems, decorated with many kinds of jewels."
The Buddha said, "You may open the casket.
Then Ānanda, having received these instructions, opened it and saw the śarīra, white as a conch shell, snow, or a kumuda flower. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The casket contains relics, their color wondrous and extraordinary.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
"You may take these bones of the Great Being and bring them here.
At that time, Ānanda immediately took the bones and presented them to the World-Honored One.
Having received them, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“You all should contemplate the bodily relics of the Bodhisattva who practiced asceticism.
Then he spoke in verse:
“The wisdom of the Bodhisattva accords with supreme virtue; Through courageous diligence, the six perfections were perfected.”
"Constantly practicing without ceasing for the sake of Bodhi, never abandoning the firm resolve, and remaining free from weariness.

You bhikṣus, all should pay homage to the original body of this Bodhisattva; these relics are perfumed by the incense of immeasurable morality, concentration, and wisdom—the supreme field of merit, most difficult to encounter."
At that time, all the bhikṣus and the great assembly, with single-minded devotion, joined their palms, paid homage by bowing their heads to the śarīra, and marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.
Then Ānanda stepped forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
“The Tathāgata, the Great Teacher, transcends all things and is revered by all sentient beings; for what reason and by what cause do you pay homage to these skeletal remains?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Because I attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of these bones, I now pay homage to them to repay my past debt of gratitude.”
He further addressed Ānanda:

"I shall now, for your sake and that of the great assembly, sever all doubts by recounting the past causes and conditions of these relics. You should reflect well upon this and listen with a single-minded focus."
Ānanda said: "We wish to hear it; we pray that you will explain it for us.
[The Buddha replied: "Ānanda!"

In a past age, there was a king named Mahāratha, who was immensely wealthy and possessed vast riches; his treasuries were overflowing, and his army was brave and martial, such that all held him in awe and submission. He constantly governed the common people through the True Dharma; his subjects flourished, and he had no enemies or adversaries.

The Great Lady of the State gave birth to three sons, whose countenances were upright and handsome, bringing joy to all who beheld them. The eldest son was named Mahāpuruṣa; the second son was named Mahādeva; and the youngest son was named Mahāsattva.

At that time, the Great King, wishing to travel and enjoy the sights of the mountains and forests, was followed by his three princes; seeking flowers and fruits, they left their father and wandered until they reached a great bamboo grove, where they rested.
The first prince spoke these words:
"Today my heart is filled with great alarm; will there not be some fierce beast in this forest that will harm me?"
The second prince spoke again, saying:
"I have no initial reluctance toward my own body, but I fear the suffering of separation from those I love.
The third prince addressed his two elder brothers, saying:
"This is the dwelling place of the divine seers; I have no fear, nor sorrow of separation.
My body and mind are suffused with joy, and I shall attain all manner of supreme merits."

Then each of the princes spoke of the matters they had been contemplating in their own hearts. Continuing further on their journey, they saw a tigress who had recently given birth to seven cubs; only seven days had passed since their birth, and as the cubs crowded around her, she was tormented by hunger and thirst, her body so emaciated that she would soon die.
The first prince spoke these words: "Alas!
This tigress has given birth for seven days; her seven cubs surround her, leaving her no leisure to seek food. Driven by hunger and thirst, she will surely devour her own offspring."
The Prince Sattva asked,
"What does this tigress usually eat?
The eldest prince replied:
“Tigers, leopards, jackals, and lions feed only upon warm flesh and blood;
they have no other food or drink that can sustain such emaciated bodies.”
When the second prince heard these words, he spoke thus:
"This tigress is emaciated and oppressed by hunger and thirst; her remaining life is but brief. How can we possibly seek such food and drink that is so difficult to obtain?"
"Who else would sacrifice their own life for the sake of such a person to relieve them from the suffering of hunger?
The first prince said,
"Of all things difficult to relinquish, nothing surpasses one's own body."
Prince Sattva said:

"We now each harbor attachment to our own bodies; furthermore, lacking wisdom, we are unable to bring benefit to others. Yet there are superior beings who, cherishing great compassion, constantly sacrifice their own lives for the sake of benefiting others."
Again, he thought:

"In hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, this body of mine has been wasted and decayed in vain, never providing any benefit; why can I not today cast it away to relieve the suffering of hunger, as if discarding mucus or spittle?"

When the princes had finished this deliberation, each gave rise to a heart of compassion; moved by sorrow and pity, they gazed together at the emaciated tigress without averting their eyes for even a moment. After lingering there for a long time, they all departed together.
At that time, Prince Sattva thought to himself:
"Now is the very moment for me to sacrifice my body and life. Why is this?"
"I have sustained this body for a long time, Foul, putrid, and flowing with pus, utterly unlovely;
Yet I have provided it with bedding and requisites, As well as food, clothing, elephants, horses, carriages, and precious wealth."
The nature of things subject to decay is impermanent; they are ever difficult to satisfy and difficult to preserve.
Though constantly provided for, they harbor resentment and malice; in the end, they abandon me, ungrateful as they are.

"Furthermore, this body is not solid; it is of no benefit to me, as terrifying as a thief and as impure as excrement. On this day, I shall cause this body to cultivate vast deeds, acting as a great vessel upon the ocean of birth and death, abandoning saṃsāra and enabling its transcendence."
He further thought:
"If I relinquish this body, I shall relinquish immeasurable abscesses, malignant diseases, and hundreds of thousands of fears.

This body contains nothing but excrement and urine; it is as unsubstantial as a bubble, a gathering place for various worms, held together by veins, arteries, sinews, and bones—it is truly loathsome."

Therefore, I should now renounce [these things] in order to seek unsurpassed, ultimate *nirvāṇa*, forever departing from sorrow, affliction, impermanence, and suffering; bringing rest to birth and death, severing all worldly entanglements, and through the power of concentration and wisdom, fully cultivating and adorning myself with a hundred merits to achieve omniscience. Having realized the subtle and wondrous *dharmakāya* praised by all Buddhas, I shall bestow immeasurable Dharma-joy upon all sentient beings.

At that time, the prince aroused great courage and resolve, generating a vast vow and strengthening his mind with thoughts of great compassion. Fearing that his two elder brothers, harboring feelings of terror, might together create obstacles and prevent the fulfillment of his prayer, he immediately said:
"Elder brothers, you go on ahead; I shall follow behind."
At that time, Prince Mahāsattva returned to the forest and went to where the tigress was. He stripped off his clothes and placed them upon a bamboo stalk, making this vow:
"For the sake of all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm, I resolve to seek the state of unsurpassed Bodhi;
Arising a Great Compassionate Mind that is unshakable, I shall relinquish this body, so cherished by ordinary folk."
Bodhi is free from affliction and free from feverish distress; it is that which all the wise delight in.
For all sentient beings within the ocean of suffering of the three realms, I now rescue and deliver them, bringing them peace and happiness.
"Then, having spoken these words, the prince threw himself down to lie before the starving tigress.
By the power of this Bodhisattva’s compassion, the tiger was rendered powerless."

Having seen this, the Bodhisattva immediately ascended a high mountain and threw himself to the ground; at that moment, various seers and deities caught the prince in their arms, so that he suffered no injury whatsoever.
He then thought to himself:
"The tigress is now so emaciated and weak that she will not be able to eat me."
He immediately rose to seek a knife, but in the end he could not find one; he then pierced his own neck with a dry bamboo stalk to draw blood and gradually drew closer to the tiger's side.

At that moment, the great earth shook in six ways, like water agitated by a violent wind, surging and subsiding in unrest. The sun lost its brilliance, as if obscured by Rāhu; all directions were shrouded in darkness, devoid of any radiance. The heavens rained down named flowers and exquisite fragrant powders, falling in profusion and covering the entire forest.
At that time, there were hosts of devas in the void who, having seen this event, gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, saying in unison:
"Excellent, Great Being!"
He then spoke in verse:
“The Great Being, moving with a heart of compassion to rescue and protect, Regards all sentient beings as his only child;
With courageous joy and a mind free of stinginess, He gives up his body to relieve suffering—his merit is inconceivable.”
One shall reach the truly eternal, supreme, and wondrous state, forever freed from the various bonds of birth and death;
before long, one shall attain the fruit of Bodhi, realizing the unborn within tranquil peace and bliss.
At that time, having seen the blood flowing from beneath the Bodhisattva’s neck, the starving tigress immediately licked the blood and devoured the flesh until nothing remained but the bones.
Then, having witnessed the earthquake, the eldest prince said to his younger brother:
“The great earth, mountains, and rivers all tremble; The quarters are shrouded in darkness and the sun has no light.”
"Flowers from heaven fall in profusion throughout the sky; this must surely be the sign of my younger brother’s self-sacrifice.
Having heard his elder brother’s words, the second prince spoke these verses:
"I have heard the compassionate words of the Sattva, And I see that hungry tigress, her body emaciated."
"Bound by the suffering of hunger, she fears eating her own offspring; I now suspect my younger brother has sacrificed his body.
At that time, the two princes were overcome with great sorrow and grief; weeping and lamenting, they immediately followed one another back to where the tigress was.

Seeing his younger brother’s clothes upon the bamboo branches, his bones and hair strewn about in every direction, and the blood flowing into mud that defiled the ground, he fainted and could not support himself.
He threw himself onto the bones and only after a long time regained consciousness; immediately rising, he raised his hands and wailed aloud with great lamentation.
Simultaneously they sighed and said:
"Our younger brother’s appearance was so dignified and handsome that our parents loved and cherished him especially;
why have you both gone forth together, abandoning your bodies and not returning?"
"If our parents should question us, how shall we answer?
It would be better for us to sacrifice our lives together than to preserve our own bodies.
At that time, the two princes, weeping with grief and distress, gradually departed. Then the attendants whom the younger prince had brought along said to one another:
"Where is the prince?
We ought to search for him together.

At that time, the Queen Mother was sleeping on a high tower when she saw inauspicious signs in a dream: her two breasts were cut off, her teeth fell out, and she caught three young pigeons, one of which was snatched away by a hawk while the other two were terrified.
At the time of the earthquake, the lady was awakened; her heart was filled with great sorrow and distress, and she spoke these words:
"Why does the great earth now tremble, Causing rivers, forests, and trees to shake and quiver?
The sun lacks its brilliant radiance as if it were shrouded, And my eyes, limbs, and breasts throb unlike any other time."
As if an arrow had pierced my heart, I am oppressed by grief and suffering; my whole body trembles and finds no peace.
This dream I have seen is an inauspicious omen; there must surely be some extraordinary calamity or change.
The lady’s two breasts suddenly began to flow with milk, and she thought to herself, "There must surely be some portentous event.
At that time, a maidservant heard outsiders say:
"We have been searching for the prince, but have not yet found him."
His heart was filled with great alarm and fear; he immediately entered the palace and said to the lady:
"Do you know, my lady?
I have heard outside that people are searching for the prince everywhere, yet they cannot find him."
When the lady heard these words, she was overcome with great distress; her eyes filled with tears of sorrow as she went to the Great King and said to him:
"Great King!"
"I have heard outsiders say these words:
'I have lost my youngest and most beloved son.
Upon hearing these words, the king was struck with such alarm and confusion that he could not find his bearings; choking back his sobs, he spoke:"
"Alas! Today I have lost my beloved son.
He then wiped away his tears, comforted the lady, and said to her:
"O Worthy One! Do not grieve;
let us now go forth together to search for our beloved son.
The king, together with his ministers and the multitude of people, immediately departed the city, dispersing in various directions to search everywhere.
Before long, a high minister came forward and addressed the king, saying:
"I have heard that the prince is alive; pray do not grieve. Only his youngest son has not yet been seen."
Upon hearing these words, the king sighed with grief and said:
"Alas! Alas! How bitter!"
"I have lost my beloved son.
"When first having a child, joy was slight; Later, when losing that child, sorrow and suffering were great.
If only my son could regain his life, Even if my own body perished, it would not be a hardship."
When the lady heard this, she was bound by grief and distress as if struck by an arrow, and she sighed, saying:
"My three sons and their attendants All went together to the forest to enjoy themselves;
Yet my youngest beloved son alone has not returned— Surely there must be some calamity or misfortune of separation."
"Next, the second minister came to the king's presence.
The king asked the minister:
'Where is my beloved son?'"
The second minister was distressed and wept; his throat and tongue became parched, and he could not speak, remaining utterly unable to offer a reply.
The lady asked:
"Quickly report where my young son is now!"
"My body is tormented by fever and burns all over;
I am distressed, confused, and have lost my original mind—do not let my chest burst asunder now!
At that time, the second minister reported in detail to the king the matter of the prince’s self-sacrifice.

When the king and his consort heard this account, they could not overcome their grief and choked sobs. Longing for the place where he had sacrificed his body, they hurried forward in their carriage until they reached the bamboo grove.

Upon arriving at the site where the Bodhisattva had given up his life, they saw his bones scattered and strewn about; they both threw themselves to the ground, fainting and on the verge of death, like great trees toppled by a violent wind, their minds lost and their senses utterly bewildered.
Then the ministers and others sprinkled water everywhere upon the king and the queen; after a long while, they regained consciousness, raised their hands and wept, lamenting and sighing:
"Alas for our beloved son of such dignified appearance! Why does the suffering of death come to press us first?"
"If I had died before you, how could I have witnessed such a great tragedy?

At that time, the lady’s fainting fit gradually subsided; her hair was disheveled and wild, and she beat her breast with both hands, rolling upon the ground like a fish cast up on dry land or a cow that has lost its calf. Weeping bitterly, she said:
"Who has butchered and cut my son? His remaining bones are scattered upon the earth."
Having lost my beloved son, I am overcome by grief and sorrow.
Alas! Who has killed my child, bringing about such a cause for distress?
My heart is not made of diamond; how could it not shatter?
What I saw in my dream: both breasts were cut off;
all my teeth fell out, and now I suffer great agony.
Furthermore, I dreamed of three young pigeons, one of whom was seized and carried away by a hawk.
"Now that I have lost my beloved son, it is clear that the evil omens were not false.

At that time, the Great King, the Queen, and the two princes all wailed in grief; casting aside their jeweled necklaces and ornaments, they joined the multitude in collecting the relics of the Bodhisattva’s remains for the purpose of making offerings, enshrining them within a stūpa.
Ānanda! You should know that these are the śarīra relics of that very Bodhisattva.
He further addressed Ānanda:

"In the past, although I was possessed of afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, I was able to provide relief according to circumstances within the five destinies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, causing them to attain liberation."

How much more so now, when all afflictions are completely exhausted and no further habitual tendencies remain, and one is titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans, endowed with all-encompassing wisdom—how could such a one fail to be able to undergo various sufferings in the hells and other realms for the sake of each and every sentient being throughout many kalpas, thereby causing them to transcend birth-and-death and the cycle of afflictions?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"I recall past lives, Throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas;
At times I was a king, And at others, a prince."
Constantly practicing great giving, and relinquishing even his beloved body;
may he emerge from birth and death, and reach the state of sublime Bodhi.
Long ago there was a great kingdom, and its sovereign was named Mahāratha.
The prince was named Courageous; his mind was ever generous, free from stinginess.
The prince had two elder brothers, known as Mahānagna and Mahādeva.
The three of them went out together on an excursion and gradually reached a mountain forest.
Seeing the tiger oppressed by hunger, he immediately gave rise to this thought:
"This tiger is scorched by the fire of hunger and has nothing else left to eat.
Observing this, the Great Being feared that the beast would devour his children.
He cast away his body without hesitation, saving his son so that he would not be harmed.
The great earth and all its mountains shook all at once;
the rivers and seas surged upward, their startled waves flowing against the current.
Heaven and earth lost their radiance; in the gloom, nothing could be seen.
The birds and beasts of the forests and wilds fled in haste, losing their refuge.
His two elder brothers, wondering why he did not return, were filled with anxiety and sorrowful suffering.
Immediately, together with his attendants, he searched everywhere through the forests and thickets.
The brothers consulted one another and went further into the deep mountains;
looking in all directions, they found nothing, until they saw a tiger in the empty woods.
The mother and her seven sons had blood staining their mouths;
scattered bones and remaining hair lay strewn across the ground.
Furthermore, one saw flowing blood spread throughout the grove of trees.
When the two elder brothers saw this, great terror arose in their hearts.
They fainted and fell prostrate upon the ground, bewildered and unconscious;
dust covered their bodies, and all six sense faculties lost their mindfulness.
The prince’s various attendants wept with hearts filled with grief;
they sprinkled water to revive him, raising their hands and wailing aloud.
When the Bodhisattva relinquished his body, his compassionate mother was within the palace.
Together with five hundred court ladies, she enjoyed exquisite pleasures;
yet suddenly, milk flowed from both her breasts,
and her entire body felt as if pricked by needles, such that the pain left her no peace.
Suddenly the thought of losing her son arose, and the arrow of grief pierced her heart;
she immediately informed the Great King, recounting this matter of her distress.
Unable to endure her sorrowful weeping, she spoke to the King in a mournful voice:
"Great King, you should now know: I am beset by great suffering and distress.
My two breasts suddenly flow with milk, which I cannot restrain or control.
It is as if needles were piercing my body all over; my chest is so agitated that it feels as though it will burst."
I previously had a dream of evil omens; I shall surely lose my beloved son.
I pray that Your Majesty will save my life by letting me know whether my child lives or dies.
In the dream I saw three young pigeons; the smallest one was my beloved son.
Suddenly snatched away by a hawk, her grief and sorrow are beyond description.
Now I am submerged in an ocean of anguish; my end will come before long.
Fearing that my child’s life may not be spared, I pray you seek him out with all speed.
Furthermore, I have heard the words of outsiders that my young son could not be found;
my mind is now ill at ease, so I pray the King will have compassion for me.
Having thus addressed the King, the lady threw her whole body to the ground.
Overwhelmed by grief, her heart fainted; in her confusion, she was unconscious.
Seeing the lady lying on the ground in a swoon, the court ladies raised their voices and all wept aloud, filled with anxiety and despair, having lost their refuge.
When the king heard these words, he was overcome with grief and could not bear it;
he then commanded his ministers to search for his beloved son.
Together they all went outside the city, each seeking him out in their respective places.
Weeping and wailing, he asked the people:
"Where is the prince now?
Is he alive or dead? Who knows where he has gone?"
"How may I see him? How may you dispel my heart's grief and sorrow?
Thus all the people spread the word, saying that the prince was dead;
those who heard it were all stricken with lamentation, their wailing and sighs of grief beyond measure.
At that time, King Mahāratha, wailing in grief, rose from his seat;
he went to the Queen’s side and sprinkled water upon her body.
Once the Queen had been sprinkled with water, she regained consciousness only after a long while.
Weeping, she asked the king,
"Is my son still alive?
The king said to the lady:
"I have already dispatched people to search for the prince in all four directions, yet no news has been received.
The King further addressed the Queen:
"Do not give way to distress; rather, comfort yourself, and let us go together to search for him."
The King, together with his consort, immediately prepared their carriage and proceeded forward;
their cries were mournful and moving, and their hearts burned with grief like fire.
Hundreds of thousands of commoners and officials likewise followed the King out of the city.
Each seeking the prince, their cries of lamentation never ceased.
Because the king sought his beloved son, he gazed toward the four quarters;
then he saw a man approaching, with disheveled hair and his body smeared with blood.
His entire body was covered in dust as he came forward weeping and wailing;
seeing these evil omens, the King’s grief and distress redoubled,
and he raised both hands, crying out in lamentation beyond restraint.
At first, there was a high minister who, in great haste,
went to the king’s presence and addressed the Great King, saying:
"I pray that you will not grieve;..."
The king’s beloved son, though sought now, has not yet been found;
before long he shall arrive and dispel the Great King’s sorrow.
The king proceeded further and saw the next minister arrive.
The minister went to the king’s presence and, with tears streaming down his face, addressed the king, saying:
“The two sons are currently alive, yet they are tormented by the fire of grief;
as for the third prince, he has already been swallowed up by impermanence.”
Seeing a starving tigress who had just given birth, And was about to devour her own cubs;
That Prince Sattva, seeing this, gave rise to a heart of compassion,
Vowing to seek the unsurpassed path To deliver all sentient beings.
Fixing his mind on the wondrous Bodhi, vast and deep as the ocean,
he ascended to the summit of a high mountain and threw himself before a starving tigress.
The tiger was too weak to devour him, so he wounded his own neck with a bamboo splinter.
"He then devoured the prince’s body, leaving nothing but his skeletal remains.
Upon hearing this, the king and his consort both fainted;
their hearts sank into an ocean of sorrow, consumed by the blazing fires of affliction.
I, your servant, sprinkled sandalwood water upon the King and the Queen;
together they rose up with great cries of sorrow, raising their hands to beat their breasts.
Then the third minister came and addressed the King with these words:
"I saw the two princes, fainting in the forest.
My ministers sprinkled them with cold water, and only then did they briefly regain consciousness;
looking toward the four quarters, it was as if a fierce fire were spreading everywhere."
Rising for a moment, he fell back down again, wailing with grief beyond his own control;
raising his hands, he spoke these words of lamentation, extolling his brother’s rarity.
When the King heard these words, the fire of his sorrow flared up all the more.
The lady wailed aloud, speaking these words in a loud voice:
"My youngest son, whom I cherished most dearly, has already been swallowed by the rākṣasa of impermanence;
my two remaining sons are now present, yet they too are tormented and oppressed by the fire of grief."
"I shall now quickly go to the foot of the mountain to comfort him and ensure he preserves his remaining life.
He then immediately drove his carriage toward the path ahead, with single-minded resolve proceeding to that precipice where he was to sacrifice his body.
On the road he encountered two sons walking along, weeping and wailing; beating their breasts in anguish, they had lost all composure.
Seeing them, their parents were filled with grief and sorrow, and together they went to the place in the mountain forest where [the father] had abandoned his body.
Having arrived at the place where the Bodhisattva had relinquished his body, they gathered together and wailed in grief, giving rise to great suffering;
casting off their jeweled necklaces and exhausting their hearts with sorrow, they collected the remaining bones of the Bodhisattva’s body.
Together with the multitude of people, they made offerings and collectively constructed a stūpa of the seven precious gems;
having placed those relics within a casket, they prepared their carriages and, filled with sorrow, proceeded toward the city.
Again he addressed Ānanda:
"The being of that former time was none other than I, the Muni; do not harbor any other thought."
The King is his father, Śuddhodana; the Queen is his mother, Māyā;
the Crown Prince is Maitreya, followed by Mañjuśrī;
the tiger is Mahāprajāpatī, and the five cubs are the five Bhikṣus.
One was Mahāmaudgalyāyana, The other was Śāriputra.
For your sake I shall relate The causes for their past altruistic deeds;
Such bodhisattva practices, Which are the cause for attaining Buddhahood, you should study.
When the Bodhisattva relinquished his body, he made this great vow:
"May the remaining bones of my body benefit sentient beings in future lives.
This is the site where he gave up his body; here stands a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels.
Having remained for immeasurable time, it was eventually submerged deep within the earth.
By the power of its original vows from the past, it arises to provide salvation according to conditions;
to benefit humans and devas, it wells up forth from the ground.

At that time, when the World-Honored One was speaking of these past causes and conditions, an immeasurable asaṃkhyeya of the great assembly of devas and humans were all filled with great compassion and joy; they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He further addressed the tree deity:
"I have paid this homage out of gratitude.
The Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, and the stūpa sank back into the earth.

Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Praise of the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions (10) The Golden Light Most Victorious King Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Praise of the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions At that time, while the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was preaching this sūtra, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions who each departed from their own lands for Vulture Peak Mountain. Arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground. Having paid homage to the World-Honored One, they joined their palms with single-minded devotion and, in one voice, praised him, saying:
